#1384. Phelan's Momentum Ahead of Spurs Test

Coming off the back of a 6-0 victory at Goodison last night, Scott Phelan's Blues head into this weekend’s clash against Spurs with a four-game unbeaten streak and unrivalled confidence.

On last night’s cup match against Durham, the head coach highlighted the squad’s “top of their game” performance. Everton dominated possession for the full 90 minutes of the game, using additional "time on the ball" to net six goals – with a hattrick from Japanese forward Yuka Momiki.

Phelan now hopes that the team can gain momentum from the impressive victory.

"Last night was an opportunity to show the top of our game and have a lot of the ball," said Phelan in his pre-match press conference on Thursday afternoon. "That will hopefully give the players a confidence boost."

On the WSL season so far, Phelan commended the players' “excellent” performance in a series of “challenging” fixtures. The last two weekends seeing the Blues hold a strong fort against high-flying Manchester United and Chelsea, bringing both matches to a draw.

"It has been a positive last three fixtures," he continued. "We knew this run of fixtures would be challenging, but to see the players performing has been excellent.

The 2026/27 season has also seen the introduction of the Subway Players Cup. An excited Phelan maintains that this is a “positive addition” to the league, as “more games and opportunities” are available to players.

"It enhances the league so there's more games and more opportunities. Overall. it has been a positive addition.

The overall strong form of the team has seen them progress further in the league, with the former Under-21s captain noting that this was one of the “challenges” they were up against this season.

"Four games, four wins," he stated. "That gives us a real strong chance of progressing which was one of the challenges for this season.

Saturday’s game sees Everton face Spurs away from home, with no fresh injuries in the squad heading into this weekend.

Recovering centre-back Megan Finnigan started in Wednesday’s cup match, with Phelan saying he is "pleased to see her getting 90 minutes on the pitch after a long time injured."

Last season saw Everton beat the Londoners 2-1 away from home. The Blues’ head coach is confident that his squad can bring fierce competition and good form into this weekend’s reunion.

#1383. Rio Ferdinand labels Man United's Michael Carrick sacking 'like ChatGPT' - with 142-word statement sent by communications department and no message from club chiefs

Published: 07:20 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 07:22 EST, 12 November 2026

Man United legend Rio Ferdinand has called for 'a face' to explain the decision to sack Michael Carrick after comparing the club's statement announcing his dismissal to ChatGPT.

Carrick's dismissal was confirmed in a 142-word statement released at 10.37am, which was sent out by Man United's communications department.

Man United have moved closer to appointing former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer.

Man United's key decision makers, including chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox, have not issued a message following the decision to part ways with Carrick.

Ferdinand, who played alongside Carrick at Man United, has called for officials to front up to the decision in a post on social media.

'Man United statement like Chat GPT… I wanna hear a voice!' Ferdinand wrote. 'I want to see a face to this…'

Michael Carrick - pictured arriving at Carrington on Thursday morning - has been sacked after Manchester United's disastrous start to the season

Man United's leadership, including minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox, were not named in the club's statement

Man United legend Rio Ferdinand called for 'a face' to speak about the decision after comparing the club's statement to ChatGPT

Man United's club statement confirming the decision read: 'Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

'Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

'The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.'

Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, along with the Glazer family, who dialled in virtually from the United States, Berrada and Wilcox reached a verdict in the south of France yesterday, all while Carrick remained in limbo back in Manchester.

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am this morning and was dismissed. He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later.

United States boss Mauricio Pochettino is ready to take over as United's new manager

Ferdinand, speaking on Rio Presents, claimed Carrick had been disrespected in the way his dismissal had been handled.

'You do everything you can to make this end in the most amicable and respectful and pleasant way possible,' Ferdinand said.

'I think the way it has been done, it could have been done better. I think the leaks coming out of the club are terrible, they don't reflect well on anybody at all.

'It adds to the disrespect to the person in charge at the time. It is terrible to play out in the public like this. The minimum you should get is a bit of respect.'

#1382. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

Liverpool arrive at their team hotel for their game against Manchester City! https://t.co/M8CizGPQXg

😤 "They're about to find out how angry every other club is." 🗣️ Alan Shearer shares his thoughts on the Man City charges. https://t.co/9Oby6XT60j

The Liverpool head coach was asked for his reaction to City’s guilty verdict in his pre-match press conference and, as with many of his peers, he kept his response brief.

“Uncertainty is not good for anyone involved,” he said. “But there is the process ongoing and we have to be patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end.”

It is the most unlikely Oasis song title for a banner but, in a sea of canvas, the word will jump out from the Kop: Acquiesce.

The simplest flags frequently carry the most profound messages and, on a red background, below Acquiesce is the declaration: “MCFC Cheats”. It has been prepared specially and specifically for the return of domestic football to Anfield.

Given the tone coming out of the Etihad Stadium, nobody will be acquiescing to any alleged wrongdoing, certainly not on Sunday, but minds were made up on Merseyside about how far City had pushed the boundaries in pursuit of success a long time ago.

“There has been a lot of talk about various things,” explains John Gibbons, host of Anfield Wrap, the popular Liverpool podcast. “Manchester City trying to say they are going to be hard done to, but there are no great surprises among Liverpool fans about these charges, are there?

“Everyone who goes to the match, who supports Liverpool, have known all along that a lot of those sponsorship deals looked questionable. Did they pass the smell test? That’s why the atmospheres in the past when City came were always brilliant and I’m expecting it will be the same again.”

So that is why Anfield will be a maelstrom of sound and fury for one of the most significant occasions in Premier League history.

The half-and-half scarves have been replaced by more topical match-day merchandise this afternoon...

Here is what City’s head coach said during his first press conference after the guilty verdict:

“There is a process ongoing and in this moment I completely trust the club … I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. And then there is not another club in the world where I would [rather] be.”

“Absolutely not. The last time I was here was the treble season. I know the effort from the players, from the club, from the manager in that time that was Pep [Guardiola]. I know exactly the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target.”

“I won the Championship with Leicester. League One, we will see, but we are thinking about something that we don’t know.”

I’m not worried at all. The environment [among] the players is nice. In this moment we are top of the league so the players have all the reason to be happy and excited.

“One hundred per cent… Because I know the organisation from years ago, and I know how serious they are, I know that they do the right things. I would like to speak about this when we win the appeal.”

While Liverpool have struggled for wins in this fixture of late, it’s worth noting that this run includes five draws.

Liverpool have won just three of their last 13 Premier League clashes with Man City 👀 https://t.co/OxkeDpLjQq

On Saturday Manchester United fans resurrected their “ticker” mocking Manchester City’s trophy drought following their rivals’ cheating scandal:

There was also a nod to Rui Pinto, the whistleblower whose Football Leaks documents prompted the Premier League’s investigation into City:

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

"Enjoy the ride and smile" Erling Haaland with a message for Man City fans ahead of their trip to Anfield this weekend 🎙️🩵 https://t.co/H7so0fk6XE

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1380. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1379. Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers1,2. However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples3, collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

Cancers develop through a process of Darwinian evolution within tissues1,4,5,6. Mutation, drift and selection in the large cell populations making up our tissues can result in the emergence of a clone that has acquired multiple genetic and epigenetic ‘driver’ alterations that disrupt tissue homeostasis and promote uncontrolled proliferation7,8,9,10. Although large-scale sequencing efforts over the last 20 years have provided comprehensive catalogues of the driver genes responsible for cancer development11,12,13, a complete quantitative understanding of the evolutionary dynamics governing how these drivers arise, expand and compete is lacking. Why are cancer driver mutations widespread across many healthy human tissues2,14,15,16,17, yet cancers of many of these tissues are comparatively rare? Why in some people do initial clonal expansions progress to lethal cancers whereas in others they remain benign? What are the relative roles of chance and determinism in the evolution of cancer? Answers to these questions could guide more rational approaches to early cancer detection18, risk prediction19,20,21,22,23 and personalized intervention24,25.

Theories of oncogenesis on the basis of somatic evolution have existed since the 1950s and were used to explain the nonlinear increases in cancer incidence with age26. These multi-stage models highlighted important roles for mutation26,27, selection28,29 and stem-cell population sizes30. However, these models have proven difficult to falsify with age-incidence data alone. The dynamics of molecular evolution, read-out using deep sequencing of serial samples, provide a more direct measure of the evolutionary dynamics and have transformed our understanding of microbial evolution31,32,33,34,35. Applying similar approaches to cancer development, however, has proven challenging as serial samples of pre-cancerous tissue from asymptomatic individuals are difficult to obtain. Even when these tissues are available, they typically provide only a static snapshot of the somatic diversity present. To better understand the dynamics of pre-cancerous evolution requires serial samples collected with high temporal resolution.

The haematopoietic system provides a unique opportunity to understand and quantify pre-cancerous evolution because serial blood samples in asymptomatic individuals can be collected antecedent to cancer development. Healthy blood displays ubiquitous and pronounced age-related changes driven by positive selection for genetic alterations that are recurrently mutated in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) (for example, DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1)19,20,21,22,23,36,37. This phenomenon, termed clonal haematopoiesis, increases the risk of future blood malignancies such as AML19,20,21,22,23. Although some aspects of clonal haematopoiesis evolution have begun to be understood quantitatively38,39,40,41,42,43, our understanding of how these age-related changes evolve into AML is incomplete. We reasoned that serial blood samples collected regularly over decade-long timescales in people who subsequently develop AML could be used to better understand the evolutionary origins of AML. By leveraging developments in error-correctable sequencing44,45 and insights from evolutionary theory32,46,47, we sought to characterize when in life the key driving events of AML occur and to gain insights into the rules governing their establishment, growth and competition.

The United Kingdom Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS) study enrolled 202,638 cancer-free post-menopausal women, aged 50–74 years, between 2001 and 2005, of whom 50,640 were randomized into a ‘multimodal arm’ involving annual blood serum samples for up to 11 years (refs. 3,48). We identified all the women who subsequently developed AML during more than 12 years of follow-up, of whom 47 had sufficient blood sample available from at least two timepoints before AML diagnosis. These 47 women were diagnosed with AML at a median age of 72 years (range 53–83 years) and had up to 10 serial blood samples (median 5) available before diagnosis (Fig. 1a, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Note 1). We obtained 249 pre-AML blood serum samples from these 47 women, as well as 249 timepoint-matched samples from 47 age-matched controls who remained cancer free. One control was subsequently excluded owing to development of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). To precisely track the evolutionary dynamics in these longitudinal samples, we designed a highly sensitive sequencing strategy called TETRIS-seq. This approach incorporates duplex error-corrected sequencing44 of a panel that comprehensively covers clonal haematopoiesis- and AML-associated genomic alterations, including gene mutations, chromosomal rearrangements and mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs), in combination with a custom in silico de-noising algorithm (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Note 2). Using TETRIS-seq we reliably achieved a duplex consensus depth of greater than 1,500×, enabling robust detection of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and indels at variant allele frequencies (VAFs) ≥0.1% (Supplementary Note 2f). Using the longitudinal nature of our samples, we phased single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) on sections of chromosomes affected by mCAs, enabling detection of chromosomal gains, losses and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH) events ≥5 Mb down to approximately 1% cell fraction (Supplementary Note 2k,l).

a, Longitudinal blood samples collected annually from 47 future AML cases and 46 age-matched controls from the UKCTOCS cohort, up to ten samples per individual (one per timepoint). No technical replicates were performed. b, TETRIS-seq workflow for deep duplex targeted sequencing of AML-associated genetic alterations combined with an in silico de-noising algorithm. c, Cell fraction trajectories of all variants detected at more than one timepoint in the pre-AML cases (above; n = 132 variants) and controls (below; n = 59 variants), coloured by mutation gene class (see key). Characteristic dynamic behaviours are labelled and highlighted. Histograms (right) show the distribution of cell fraction measurements across all sampled timepoints (that is, one count per variant per timepoint).

Applying TETRIS-seq revealed strikingly different somatic evolutionary dynamics between the pre-AML cases and the controls (Fig. 1c). In controls, we detected clonal haematopoiesis in 72% (33 of 46) of people, consistent with previous studies37,39. Variants observed in controls were typically at cell fractions less than 20% and trajectories seemed relatively stable over time (Fig. 1c). These variants were mostly in well-known clonal haematopoiesis driver genes, including DNMT3A and TET2 (Extended Data Fig. 2). In pre-AML cases, we detected clonal haematopoiesis in 89% (42 of 47) of people. Compared with controls, variants observed in pre-AML cases were substantially more abundant and exhibited large cell fraction changes over the sampling period (Fig. 1c). These variants occurred in a broader range of AML-associated genes, including spliceosome, cell signalling and tumour suppressor genes (Extended Data Fig. 2).

The cell fraction trajectories observed in pre-AML samples exhibit a broad range of qualitative behaviours, which are distinct from the controls (highlighted trajectories, Fig. 1c). We observed many examples of classic selective sweeps whereby a single variant expanded to dominate the blood. Most of these somatic sweeps had already reached fixation before the sampling period (‘completed sweeps’). We did not detect any selective or completed sweeps in the controls. We also observed examples of clonal expansions whose growth stalled, reversed or experienced multiple reversals in fortune (Fig. 1c) suggestive of frequent and strong clonal interference between parallel lineages within the same individual. These behaviours were almost exclusively observed in the pre-AML cases. Clones expanding at low cell fraction were a common feature of both pre-AML cases and controls, but were more common in pre-AML cases (histograms, Fig. 1c) and seemed to expand at faster rates pre-AML.

The highly quantitative time-series data generated by TETRIS-seq enabled us to unambiguously infer the order of driver mutation acquisition and patterns of co-occurrence in many of the 47 pre-AML cases (Fig. 2, Supplementary Note 3, ‘Inferring clonal architecture’ in the Methods and Supplementary Table 8). In 55% (26 of 47) of pre-AML cases, we observed ‘linear evolution’, characterized by the sequential acquisition and expansion of driver mutations along a single dominant ‘trunk’, with minimal evidence of side-branching (Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Fig. 40). Within this class, however, there was substantial variation in the clonal composition of the blood in the decade before diagnosis. In 23% (11 of 47) of cases, we observed clear evidence of clonal interference, characterized by the acquisition and expansion of multiple driver clones on parallel evolutionary branches, which grew to high cell fractions (more than 10%) and interfered with each other’s growth, causing complex evolutionary trajectories (Fig. 2e–h and Supplementary Fig. 41). There was substantial variation in the dynamics observed within this class too, with examples of competition between quadruple-mutant clones (Fig. 2e), triple-mutant clones (Fig. 2h) and double-mutant clones (Fig. 2g). In both the linear and clonal interference patterns, most of the blood already derived from clones harbouring at least one pathogenic mutation in the decade pre-AML diagnosis. The remaining 21% (10 of 47) of cases are characterized by ‘late evolution’, for which the pre-leukaemic clone was detectable only 1–2 years pre-AML, if at all (Fig. 2i,j and Supplementary Fig. 42). This suggests that in some cases AML may evolve through the acquisition of uncommon driver mutations not covered by our targeted sequencing panel, that the pre-leukaemic evolution may play out while clones are below our detection limit or that the acquisition of the key drivers in these cases occurs without a long pre-leukaemic phase.

Muller plots showing inferred clonal dynamics in ten pre-AML cases, demonstrating ‘linear evolution’, ‘clonal interference’ or ‘late evolution’. Each panel is one pre-AML case. In each plot the vertical extent of a band is the fraction of cells belonging to that clone, with nested bands showing daughter clones arising within their parent, across age (x axis). Colour denotes the number of observed driver mutations in each clone (see legend); dark grey denotes the wild-type (non-driver) cell fraction. White vertical dashed lines indicate timing of UKCTOCS blood samples. Thick grey vertical dashed lines indicate time of AML diagnosis. The timing of any diagnosis of MDS, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML) or myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN), or pre-AML chemotherapy exposure, is indicated by labelled grey arrows (see Supplementary Table 10 for more details). a, Linear evolution: a double-mutant clone sweeps through the blood in the ~5 years before diagnosis. b, Linear evolution: a large single-mutant clone acquires further drivers in the final years before diagnosis. c, Linear evolution: a quadruple-mutant clone expands to dominate the blood. d, Linear evolution: the founding clone has already swept through the blood before sampling began, with a triple-mutant subclone expanding before diagnosis. e, Clonal interference between quadruple-mutant clones. f, Clonal interference between triple-mutant clones. g, Clonal interference between double-mutant clones. h, Clonal interference between triple-mutant clones. i, Late evolution: a putative pre-leukaemic clone first detected in the final year before diagnosis. j, Late evolution: a germline DDX41 carrier, with a small somatic DDX41/SRSF2-mutant clone detected only at the final sample. MF, myelofibrosis.

We reasoned that the high sensitivity and temporal resolution of our data could be used to gain a quantitative understanding of how driver mutations expand and compete in the decades preceding AML diagnosis (Fig. 3). We developed a mathematical framework for predicting how clones expand and compete through time inspired by models of microbial evolution32,46. In this framework the dynamics of a given clone are determined by its occurrence time, fitness effect and the simplest interaction term: an increasing ‘mean fitness’ of all other clones in the population that ensures the population frequencies of all clones sum to 1. The dynamics of a specific variant are determined by summing the frequency of the original parental clone (that is, the first clone to acquire the variant) and all daughter clones that inherited the variant (Fig. 3a–c).

a–c, Schematics demonstrating how clonal composition (left, phylogenetic trees) and the fitness and occurrence time of each clone (top plot) interact via the population mean fitness (black line, top plot) to produce different variant frequency trajectories (bottom plot). Annotations (for example, \(\bar{x}\) > s1) mark where the population mean fitness overtakes a clone’s fitness, driving the reversals seen in the trajectory. a, A single clone expands exponentially, slowing as the mean fitness rises and it sweeps to fixation. b, Competition between two independent clones: the less fit clone declines once its fitness is overtaken by the mean fitness. c, Competition within and between branches produces multiple reversals of fortune. d–g, Measured cell fractions (data points) compared with variant frequency trajectories (coloured lines) predicted from maximum likelihood estimates of each clone’s fitness and occurrence time, during UKCTOCS blood sampling (left plots) and since birth (right plots). Uncertainties (95% optimizer range and standard deviation) are provided in Supplementary Table 9. Grey shading indicates the UKCTOCS sampling window. Grey and thick black vertical dashed lines indicate blood samples and AML diagnosis, respectively. Labelled grey arrows indicate any other haematological malignancy, pre-AML cancer diagnosis or pre-AML chemotherapy exposure (Supplementary Table 10). Phylogenetic trees (right) show each clone’s inferred occurrence time (number in circles, years), fitness effect (% per year) and number of driver mutations (colour; see key). d, Linear evolution: a TET2-mutant clone acquired at ~39 years expands slowly until two further drivers are acquired 3 years before diagnosis. e, Linear evolution: an SRSF2/IDH2 double-mutant clone sweeps the blood, while low-frequency CHEK2 and IDH1 variants decline. f, Clonal interference on the background of a triple-mutant clone that had already swept the blood, resolved by an inferred missing driver (dashed line). g, Clonal interference with two inferred missing drivers (dashed lines).

After surviving an initial stochastic drift phase, a single clone carrying a driver mutation expands exponentially at a rate determined by its fitness (where ‘fitness’ is the growth rate relative to wild-type haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) assuming a constant effective population size). This clonal expansion causes the population mean fitness (\(\bar{x}\)) to increase, eventually causing the clonal expansion to slow down as it sweeps to fixation (Fig. 3a). Competition between two independent clones with different fitnesses can lead to the variant frequency trajectory of the less fit clone decreasing once its fitness is overtaken by the population mean fitness (Fig. 3b). Competition between clones within a branch and between branches can drive more complex variant frequency dynamics involving multiple reversals of fortune due to clones jumping ahead of, or falling behind, the population mean fitness (Fig. 3c). Using this framework, we developed a maximum likelihood approach (Methods) to infer fitness and occurrence time estimates for each clone and compare the predicted variant frequency trajectories (lines) with the measured trajectories (data points) in pre-AML cases (Fig. 3d–g, Extended Data Figs. 3–9 and Supplementary Fig. 47) and controls (Supplementary Figs. 48–55).

We observe a remarkably close agreement between the variant frequency trajectories predicted by this simple framework and the observed data. We first consider a case of linear evolution with no evidence of clonal competition (C92_005, Fig. 3d). Here we infer that a TET2 variant was acquired at around 39 years of age and expanded exponentially with a doubling time of about 2.4 years (fitness of 30% per year). Approximately 30 years later (at age approximately 67) this lineage acquires two further driver mutations that cause rapid clonal expansion, with a doubling time of about 8 weeks (fitness of ≥474% per year). Diagnosis occurs 3 years later at 70 years of age. Case C92_007 also exhibits a predominantly linear pattern of evolution (Fig. 3e). Here we infer that the first pre-leukaemic clone (SRSF2 p.P95L) is acquired at approximately 47 years of age and expands with a doubling time of about 2.5 years (fitness of 30% per year). Approximately 20 years later (at age around 67), this lineage acquires an IDH2 p.R140Q mutation, which creates a double-mutant clone that expands rapidly, with a doubling time of around 7 months (fitness effect of 115% per year). This double-mutant clone sweeps the blood when the person is in their late 70s and they are diagnosed with AML at age 80, 13 years after acquisition of the IDH2 mutation. The sweep of the double-mutant clone harbouring SRSF2 and IDH2 variants causes two low-frequency variants (in CHEK2 and IDH1) to be outcompeted, highlighting that high-frequency clones provide important information about the behaviour of low-frequency clones and vice versa.

We next considered cases with clear evidence of clonal interference (Fig. 3f,g). In C92_022 there has already been a full sweep of the blood by a clone harbouring three driver mutations (SRSF2 p.P95H and bi-allelic loss of TET2) by the time of the first sample, 8 years before diagnosis (Fig. 3f). On the background of this triple-mutant clone there is rapid evolution involving the acquisition of multiple further driver events. First, two independent clones caused by the acquisition of JAK2 V617F and MPL W515L arise at age approximately 55 and expand with doubling times of 4.3 and 6.7 months, respectively (fitness effects of about 195% and about 124% per year). These are soon outcompeted by a substantially fitter clone carrying 19p CN-LOH that is acquired at around 59 years of age and expands with a doubling time of just 2.4 months (fitness effect of about 345% per year). Remarkably, however, this lineage does not sweep. Instead, the JAK2 V617F lineage acquires two further events: a 9p CN-LOH and a subsequent event of unknown origin (‘missing driver’) that grows with a doubling time of about 1 month and sweeps the entire blood in under 2 years. Without invoking a highly fit missing driver (dashed trajectory, Fig. 3f), the variant frequencies measured at age 65 would be inconsistent with the behaviour of the observed clones. Thus, the internal consistency between the variant frequency trajectories can be used to detect events missed by our sequencing panel (Methods). C92_012 (Fig. 3g) highlights another example of clonal interference in which the observed VAF trajectories suggest the presence of two missing drivers. Despite these driver events being missed, the dynamics of the other observed driver events enable us to estimate their occurrence times and fitness effects.

Overall, these findings demonstrate that, once established in the HSC pool, the dynamics of pre-leukaemic clones are surprisingly predictable. Although we cannot exclude extrinsic effects altering some clones, one does not need to invoke more complex scenarios to explain the data: one can achieve remarkably close fits to variant trajectories by assuming clones have an intrinsic fitness and compete globally for one resource with minimal spatial structure.

Applying our framework to all pre-AML cases enabled us to estimate the fitness and occurrence time of many of the key events driving AML development in these 47 cases (Fig. 4) and 46 controls (Supplementary Figs. 48–56). In approximately 80% of pre-AML cases, our data suggest that the acquisition of the key driver events plays out over decades. In two-thirds of individuals who develop AML, the first driver mutation has already been acquired by age 20 (Fig. 4b). On average, these first driver events occur more than 50 years before AML diagnosis, but expand with relatively modest fitness advantages of around 10% to 30% per year (doubling times of about 2–7 years, Fig. 4c). A third of individuals have acquired their second driver mutation by age 50 (Fig. 4b). On average, these second ‘hits’ occur around 30 years before AML diagnosis and confer a substantially larger fitness advantage to cells, causing them to expand at rates of between about 20% and 100% per year (doubling times of about 1–3 years, Fig. 4c). Remarkably, this pattern continues as the pre-AML clone acquires further driver mutations. Clones with three driver mutations grow with fitness advantages of between around 50% and 200% per year, and quadruple-mutants range from around 100% to 1,000% per year, doubling in weeks to months (Fig. 4c). This remarkable increase in fitness with the number of driver mutations acquired is close to geometric: each driver mutation acquired confers a 2–3-fold increase in the growth rate. This finding strongly suggests that pre-leukaemic mutations combine synergistically.

Grey data points are clones on side branches (not ancestral to the AML). Dashed circle outlines denote a missing driver. Colour denotes the number of somatic driver mutations detected in the clone. Cases are ordered by time from first inferred driver to AML diagnosis. b, Cumulative incidence of a clone carrying one (blue), two (green), three (orange) and four or more (red) driver mutation acquisitions across all 47 pre-AML cases (n = 42, 29, 17 and 8 cases, respectively; for each case, the earliest clone harbouring at least that number of driver mutations was used). c, Cumulative distributions of fitness effects for driver mutations occurring in clones harbouring one (blue), two (green), three (orange) and four or more (red) driver mutations (n = 79, 33, 29 and 15 clones, respectively). Uncertainties in fitness and occurrence time estimates (95% optimizer range and standard deviation) are provided in Supplementary Table 9.

The quantitative picture of the evolutionary dynamics afforded by our data highlights several important features. First, transformation usually involves the acquisition of multiple driver mutations in the same clone (range, 2–6), with considerable inter-patient variation in when these driver events are acquired. Second, pre-leukaemic clones are subject to strong positive selection, with fitness advantages that vary by two orders of magnitude: ranging from 10% per year for the least fit single-mutant clones to 1,000% per year for the fittest quadruple-mutant clones. Third, the variant frequency trajectories exhibit diverse qualitative behaviours, suggesting strong clonal competition in some cases (for example, C92_012 and C92_022) but a complete absence of competition in other cases (for example, C92_005 and C92_007).

We hypothesized that many of these features may be emergent properties of a stochastic evolutionary model governed by a simple set of rules. To test this, we developed a model of the clonal dynamics inspired by previous models of microbial evolution32,46,47, which we modified to incorporate key experimental observations (Methods). In this model, blood is maintained by a population of N cycling HSCs that divide symmetrically every \(\tau \) years (Fig. 5a). HSCs acquire driver mutations at a rate of U per year. Driver mutations vary in the fitness effects they confer to HSCs. A driver mutation arising in a wild-type HSC, creating a single-mutant clone, confers fitness advantages drawn from a distribution with a median and range controlled by a single parameter, s ≈ 16% per year (Methods). A driver mutation arising in a single-mutant clone confers a median fitness effect that is r = 2.5-fold larger (s ≈ 40% per year), creating a double-mutant clone. Triple-mutant and quadruple-mutant clones follow the same geometric pattern (with median fitness effects of s ≈ 100% and s ≈ 250% per year, respectively). In this framework, transformation to frank AML is defined by the acquisition of four driver mutations within the same clone that reaches greater than 50% of the cell fraction before the age of 85. Using established estimates for \(N\tau \)  = 105 (refs. 38,39,41), U ≈ 10−5 per year (ref. 40) and s ≈ 16% per year for single-mutant fitness effects39,42,43, we simulated the clonal dynamics in 200,200 simulations and considered the evolutionary dynamics observed in the decades preceding the around 900 virtual incidental AMLs (Fig. 5b–d).

Simulated AMLs are defined by clones that acquire four driver mutations (red star). Clone growth rates are determined by relative fitness (Δ) between the clone and the mean fitness of all other clones in the population (\(\bar{x}\)). b, Fraction of observed pre-AML cases (grey, n = 47) and simulated AMLs (red, n = 943; from 200,200 simulations) assigned to linear, branched or late evolutionary patterns (classified as in the Methods). The vertical line marks largest VAF = 30%; points to its right have undergone at least one somatic sweep (VAF > 30%). f, As in e, for variants at one of 27 clonal haematopoiesis hotspot positions (Methods) detected in the UK Biobank (age approximately 40–70). Future myeloid leukaemia cases (red; n = 114) and controls (grey, n = 4,920).
