a, Developmental rate of embryos injected with H2B-mCherry mRNA (20 ng/µl) for live imaging assays. Left panel, representative images of embryos captured at the indicated time points (hpi). Two independent experiments with similar results (a). Tiled images from a large-field scan. b, 3D rendered images of mid 2-cell nuclei, related to Fig. 1b (additional examples from one experiment). The images labelled “paired” are from two blastomeres in a single embryo. c, Confocal 2D timelapse images of nuclei during the 1-cell, 2-cell and 4-cell stages. Representative from three independent experiments. The corresponding movies are provided in Supplementary Videos 1−3. The bright circular spots are nucleolus precursor bodies. d, Representative line profiles of local nuclear deformation, calculated as in inset. Negative signs indicate concave nuclear deformation. e, Time-dependent change in nuclear size, as measured by the mean nuclear radius R (mean ± s.d., n = 6 embryos). f, Time-dependent change in nuclear shape (traced outlines are overlaid). g, Representative confocal images of nuclei visualized using mCherry-NLS (red) and the traced outlines from two independent experiments. Statistical test, chi-square test (a). n, numbers of embryos analysed. Traces are representative from three independent experiments with similar results (d, f). Scale bars, 100 µm (a); 10 μm (b, c, g).

a–c, Influence of cytoplasmic viscosity. A viscous drag can oppose nuclear movement and affect the measurement; the effect may be larger at faster nuclear movement (a). The speed of nanocapillary movement among the developmental stages (b). The stage-dependent difference in nuclear deformability at varying nanocapillary speed (c). Coloured lines are linear regression slopes: 0.02, −0.01, 0.08, 0.06, and 0.01 (min) for the 1-cell, early 2-cell, mid 2-cell, late 2-cell and 4-cell stages, respectively. The values in b are 0.26 ± 0.19 µm/sec (1-cell), 0.24 ± 0.05 µm/sec (early 2-cell), 0.28 ± 0.18 µm/sec (mid 2-cell), 0.28 ± 0.12 µm/sec (late 2-cell) and 0.29 ± 0.18 µm/sec (4-cell) (n = 27, 17, 18, 20 and 25 embryos, respectively). d–f, Influence of cytoplasmic elasticity. An elastic restoring force can oppose nuclear movement and affect the measurement (d). The movements of nuclei before and after micromanipulation from their original location in embryos (D1 and D2 in d, respectively) (e). The stage-dependent difference in nuclear deformability at varying nuclear travel distance (f). Coloured lines are linear regression slopes: 0.22, 0.18, 0.26, 0.19, and 0.22 for the 1-cell, early 2-cell, mid 2-cell, late 2-cell and 4-cell stages, respectively (the identical numbers of embryos per condition as in a–c). g, h, Nuclear stiffness measured using different imaging probes (g) and label-free differential interference contrast (DIC) imaging (h). H2B-mCherry: n = 18, 13, 12, 13 and 13 embryos (from Fig. 1j,k), emerin-EGFP: n = 12, 6, 14, 6 and 9 embryos; label-free DIC imaging: n = 12, 6 and 7 embryos, from the 1-cell to 4-cell stages, respectively. i, Nuclear stiffness variation in individual embryos. The lines connecting the plots indicate paired data from each (pro)nucleus in the same embryos (8 and 16 pairs for 1-cell and 2-cell, respectively). j, Influence of nanocapillary pressure levels on the measured nuclear stiffness (n = 13 and 45 embryos for 2.1 × 101 kPa and 1.2 × 101 kPa among the population that reached the blastocyst stage at 96 hpi, respectively). k, Influence of nanocapillary pressure levels on the frequency of development. Data from three to four independent experiments per condition (black circles). Total numbers of embryos: n = 55, 64, 75 embryos, from left to right columns. Bars are s.d. H2B-mcherry (20 ng/µl mRNA) was used as nuclear marker (i–k). l–n, Alternative mechanical measurement using aspiration force. Nuclear surface was aspirated using an incremental suction pressure (6 × 103 Pa/min) applied to a capillary (l). Confocal images (m, H2B-mCherry) were used to determine the pressure level at which the nucleus began to be aspirated (>1 µm) (n). The values are 11.5 ± 5.5 kPa (1-cell), 3.8 ± 1.4 kPa (2-cell) and 10.4 ± 2.5 kPa (4-cell) (n = 12, 14 and 12 embryos, respectively). Statistical tests, Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test (b, e, h, n) (comparison was performed independently for D1 and D2 in e); Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided) (g, j); Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-sided) (i); one-way ANOVA followed by Turkey’s multiple comparison test (k). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. Scale bars, 10 μm.

a, Snapshots (overlay of bright-field and H2B-EGFP) of 2-cell nuclei in IVF (left panels) and SCNT (right panels) embryos subjected to nanocapillary-based mechanical analysis, associated with data in Fig. 2. Representative from three independent experiments. b, Effect of nuclear imaging marker on nuclear stiffness measurement examining IVF embryos (H2B-mCherry: n = 53 embryos, H2B-EGFP: n = 28 embryos; from Fig. 2b). c, Expression levels of nuclear imaging marker in IVF embryos that reached the blastocyst stage versus ones that exhibited impaired development (pooled from H2B-mCherry and H2B-EGFP samples). Blue-coloured plots are samples that showed stiff 2-cell nuclei, defined as more than twice the mean in normally developed embryos. The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. d, Representative images and the frequency of preimplantation development for SCNT embryos with and without nanocapillary-based measurement (n = 46 and 52 embryos, respectively) from three independent experiments. e, Tables show the developmental impairment of each embryo and the corresponding nuclear stiffness measured at the 2-cell stage. Statistical test, Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided) (b, c). Scale bars, 10 µm (a); 50 μm (d).

a, Quantification of lamin A/C and B2 levels from assays in Fig. 3a, as analysed in Fig. 3b (lamin A/C: n = 21, 20, 22, 26 and 18 embryos; lamin B2: n = 22, 36, 27, 28 and 27 embryos, from the 1-cell to the 4-cell stages, respectively). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. b, Representative immunostaining images of Lap2β. Two independent experiments with similar results. c, Representative time-lapse images of mEGFP-lamin B1 for assays in Fig. 3c from one experiment. Numbers below images are mean signal intensities normalized to 21 hpi. d, Effects of wortmannin on lamin B1 clearance. Representative immunofluorescence images and quantification of lamin B1 signals (32 hpi). Control (DMSO): n = 30, wortmannin: n = 36 embryos. e, Nuclear localization of LC3. Live-embryo images of EGFP-LC3 (upper panels) and EGFP alone (lower panels) at 8, 21 and 24 hpi. Two independent experiments with similar results. f, LC3 inhibition via antibody microinjection. Representative immunofluorescence images of lamin B1 and DAPI counterstain, and quantification of lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope at 24 hpi versus control IgG microinjection. The red horizontal bars represent the means. Control IgG: n = 19 embryos, anti-LC3: n = 23 embryos. g, Cell-cycle progression in the presence of wortmannin or the anti-LC3 antibody as examined using an EdU incorporation assay (22–24 hpi). Aphidicolin (10 µM) was used as a control. Numbers of embryos are shown in the panel. h, Nuclear localization of sfLB1 and sfLB1Δ. H2B-mCherry was coexpressed to visualize nuclear location. The white dashed lines indicate the embryo contours. Two independent experiments with similar results. i, Immunoblotting of p62. Lysates of 2-cell embryos (32 hpi; 60 embryos per sample) injected with EGFP-sfLB1 mRNA (right lane) were blotted along with control (left lane). j, Immunoblotting of endogenous lamin B1 in 2-cell embryos perturbed via sfLB1 (28 hpi; 25 embryos per sample, middle lane). The left and right lanes are controls (non-injection and sfLB1Δ, respectively). k, In-vitro pull-down assay results for the interaction of LC3 with sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ. Statistical tests, Kruskal–Wallis followed by uncorrected Dunn’s multiple comparisons test (a); Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided) (d, f); chi-square test (g). Western blot data are representative from two independent experiments (i); one (j); and three (k). The thick horizontal bars (red) represent the means. Source blot data are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. Scale bars, 10 µm.

The total numbers of embryos analysed are provided in the main text panel. #1368. Mauricio Pochettino should TURN DOWN the Man United job unless he gets TWO new signings to fix 'the worst back four in the Premier League', says Gary Neville

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:19 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 10:08 EST, 12 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino has been warned against taking the Manchester United job, by Gary Neville unless the club's hierarchy promise to back him in the January transfer window and bolster 'the worst back four in the Premier League'.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport, Pochettino is expected to be named as the new Red Devils head coach, replacing Michael Carrick. Carrick was pictured arriving at Carrington on Thursday morning before being sacked just hours later.

Director of football Jason Wilcox was pictured arriving to the club's training ground on Thursday morning too. He had been in Monaco the day before with the club’s chief executive Omar Berrada, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe ratified their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

United moved closer to putting Pochettino in charge at Old Trafford after reaching a verbal agreement with the US national team boss on Wednesday. The club then made a formal approach to US Soccer.

Upon Pochettino's expected arrival, he will join a club languishing in the relegation zone - with United 18th in the Premier League with just one win from their opening 10 matches.

United have conceded 19 goals across those 10 games - with only 14th-placed Ipswich Town (20) and bottom side Crystal Palace (24) having conceded more.

Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) has been warned against becoming the new Manchester United head coach by Gary Neville unless they promise him defensive reinforcements in January

Michael Carrick arrives at Carrington on Thursday morning ahead of his Man United sacking

Director of football Jason Wilcox was pictured arriving to the club's training ground on Thursday morning after being in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick's fate at the club

And speaking about Pochettino's pending arrival, Neville insists on the Argentine making ultimatums to the board if they want him - starting with improving the defence.

'If I was Mauricio Pochettino now, I would be literally protecting myself up to the high heaven,' he said on The Overlap.

'He'll do that with a pay-off. So do that in your contract. But secondly, he needs two defenders in January. So he's got to insist that he gets two defenders in January. He's got to insist that he gets a minimum budget next summer for the transfer we're not to be able to turn this around. He's got to insist that he gets a budget that follows.

'They have to give it to him or else he shouldn't take the job.'

Expanding further, the former United right back didn't hold back in his criticism of the current defensive options at the club.

'I mean look the back four that he finished with on Sunday was [Diogo] Dalot left back, [Noussair] Mazraoui right back, Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven,' he said.

'That is probably the worst back four in the Premier League. I don't know a back four that is worse than that in the Premier League right now if I watch it. That is I can't believe Manchester United have ended up with that back four.'

Pochettino is currently at the US Soccer base outside Atlanta preparing for a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final double header against Haiti, and is due to speak to the media on Friday.

Neville believes Manchester United have 'the worst back four in the Premier League'

Diogo Dalot (left) gave away a penalty during United's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday

It’s unclear if he will remain in charge for those games, with United said to be relaxed over the Argentine taking the team. It is possible he could stay for the first leg in Kingston, Jamaica at the weekend and then travel to Manchester.

The second leg in Cincinnati is not until the early hours of Thursday, and Pochettino may even would only take over at United on Friday with a huge game against Liverpool at Anfield 48 hours later.

It’s understood that the US Soccer Federation are ready for this contingency and have a succession plan in place should he leave.

It will cost Pochettino around £7million to buy himself out of his contract with the US Soccer Federation, with United ready to foot the bill.

The cost of bringing in his back-room team, including trusted assistants Jesus Perez and Miguel D’Agostino, will take the cost above £10m.

The 54-year-old only signed a new deal after the World Cup meaning that United could have got him for nothing in the summer.

#1367. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. We had a fantastic season last season but in order to compete we needed to buy more players. Many teams buy many players and Atletico Madrid did. They have an amazing team and deserved to win today.

I expected more. [Are you saying you expected more investment in the squad this summer?] Yes 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. As players we have to do more but it is important to make a strong squad to be ready for for this kind of night.

In general, in general [should you have invested more in defence and attack given all the midfielders]. Last season we made a strong base to build an amazing team. It’s annoying and disappointing coming here and trying to get a result.

I don’t think so [was the manager backed?] He does his best. You can’t [live on] what you did last season. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season is a big problem.

It’s changing, changing, changing the manager [after a poor run]. But what about other areas? I can’t say more.

Tonight is it easy to say the coach, easy to say the players [are at fault]. But we have to look at other areas.

So far this season there have been more times when the performances have been worse than the results. This was the other way round but there is a sizeable quality gap between Carrick’s squad and the company they are keeping. They can point to a soft red card but they still shot themselves in the foot with their doziness in the first minute and squandering the good chances they created.

Maguire strays offside when Mount, from the short corner, tries to pick him out at the back post.

Amad, now on the right, tries to dribble past Grimaldo who wins the ball off him but Atletico give it straight back. Man Utd work it into the box for Zirkzee to cushion and then dither so long over a shot he has to lay it off to Cunha who hits it straight at the keeper with two-thirds of the goal vacant. Oblak turns it wide.

Five minutes of stoppage time are signalled.

Alan Shearer says there has been improvement tonight since Saturday. “They have stuck together and have not been outrun.” This is a very low bar but OK. He goes on to say that the glaring weakness is not attitude but a lack of finishing quality.

And Le Normand is booked within seconds of his introduction for a tug of the shirt.

Dalot lofts a deep cross way beyond Zirkzee. I think Dalot encompasses Man Utd’s recruitment over the past eight years or so in that it’s hard to see any progression or improvement since the day they signed him. Maybe he always had a low ceiling. But where on earth is the coaching?

Manchester United have had their chances but they have lacked an elite or even merely decent finisher.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#1365. Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene1, and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats2,3,4,5,6,7, yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.

Plastic pollution, once thought to be a predominantly aquatic issue, is increasingly being recognized as a threat to terrestrial ecosystems1. Microplastics (synthetic polymer particles with diameter less than 5 mm) are a particularly problematic form of plastic pollution, as these small particles are easily dispersed through pathways that include atmospheric deposition, precipitation, river transport and groundwater flow2,3,4,5,6,7. The high environmental mobility of microplastics has allowed them to infiltrate even the most pristine habitats8 where they can persist for centuries9,10. For wildlife exposed to microplastics, the small size and diverse chemistry of these particles facilitate ingestion11 and the penetration of biological membranes12,13. Once internalized, microplastics can bioaccumulate, biomagnify through food webs and pose severe health risks14,15,16,17,18.

Although much work has been done on detecting microplastics in different biological compartments (reviewed in ref. 19), studies in terrestrial ecosystems have largely been limited to descriptive surveys that document the presence of microplastics without investigating how these pollutants accumulate within wildlife20,21,22. Although such studies have proven informative for identifying the scope and scale of plastic pollution, this approach has left the bioaccumulation dynamics of microplastics in terrestrial environments poorly understood. As a result of this knowledge gap, even high-profile studies on plastic ingestion risk in wildlife have had to rely on assumptions about the relationship between individual habitat use and the uptake of microplastics rather than empirically grounded associations23. Because both sources and dispersal pathways for microplastics are amplified by land-use change24,25,26, the intensity of human landscape modification should have a key role in shaping the internal microplastic burdens of terrestrial wildlife. Whether this is the case, however, is still largely unknown. With the continuing expansion of human-modified landscapes into wild spaces27 and the concomitant increase in global plastic production28, there is an urgent need to move beyond presence/absence studies and towards understanding the ecological and landscape-level factors that shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial species29.

Here we integrate movement ecology, land-use data and in vivo contaminant measurements within the same individuals to investigate how the intensity and proximity of anthropogenic land-use change shape systemic microplastic burdens in terrestrial mammals. The role of anthropogenic disturbance in shaping internal plastic burdens is particularly pressing in regions facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil, where the extent of anthropogenic land-use change since the turn of the century has substantially outpaced the global average30,31 and deforestation, resource extraction, urbanization, agricultural intensification and an expanding road network are rapidly transforming the country’s landscapes30,32. By pairing in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking data, we provide quantitative evidence that links individual-level habitat use and human landscape modification to systemic microplastic burdens in free-ranging terrestrial wildlife.

Between February 2021 and November 2022, we collected blood samples and high-resolution GPS-based movement data from lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris; n = 26) and giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla; n = 21) sampled at the Arc of Deforestation in the Amazon, an agricultural mosaic in the Cerrado, and a relatively undisturbed cattle ranch in the Pantanal (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Table 1). For each individual, we quantified blood microplastic concentrations and polymer profiles using confocal Raman spectroscopy, detecting particles larger than 1 μm. We then paired these data on in vivo microplastic burdens with the GPS tracking data to understand how inter-individual differences in habitat use and disturbance exposure shaped internal microplastic burdens. In particular, we quantified each individual’s exposure to human disturbance through the Human Footprint Index (HFI), a globally standardized measure of cumulative anthropogenic pressure ranging from 0 (undisturbed) to 50 (most heavily modified)33. We also examined local-scale effects through each animal’s proximity to the nearest human development (that is, the built environment including urban areas, mining infrastructure and power plants)34 and waste management facilities34.

a, Locations of the monitored lowland tapirs (blue, n = 26 animals) and giant anteaters (green, n = 21 animals) throughout Brazil, overlaid on top of the HFI. The numbers depict the sample sizes within each study area. b, Heat map depicting the concentration of the analysed microplastic polymers for lowland tapirs (blue) and giant anteaters (green). Each row in the heat map corresponds to an individual animal. Polymers categorized as ‘other’ were those that occurred at low abundance, and included polyvinyl butyralolyethyleneimine, poly(butylene terephthalate), polyvinylformal, polyacetal, polymethylpentene, polyurethane and polyethylene glycol. Giant anteater image credit: Steven Traver via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0); tapir image credit: Christophe Mallet via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0).

Across all samples, we identified a total of 17,165 particles with a hit quality index (HQI) > 75, of which 2,815 (16.4%) were identified as microplastic. Microplastics were near-ubiquitous and found in the blood of all but four animals (three giant anteaters and one tapir), but systemic concentrations varied markedly across individuals (mean: 73.8 particles per ml; range 0 to 1,211.3 particles per ml). Lowland tapirs had the highest microplastic burdens (98.9 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 52.0–188.0 particles per ml), followed by giant anteaters (42.8 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 26.7–68.6 particles per ml); however, concentrations did not differ significantly between species (β = 0.84, t = 1.88, P = 0.067). Tapirs and giant anteaters did differ in polymer composition (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Information), with additional inter-individual variation detailed in the Supplementary Discussion and Extended Data Fig. 2. Although comparable data on systemic microplastic burdens are not presently available for other species of terrestrial wildlife, the mean concentration of 73.8 particles per ml found in these animals is within the range reported in human blood using spectroscopic methods35 (1.9 to 108 particles per ml).

Across species and sampling sites, individual differences in blood microplastic burdens were consistently associated with anthropogenic disturbance. Of the 47 animals from which blood samples were collected, 40 had sufficient GPS tracking data for inclusion in the habitat use analyses. These animals spanned a wide gradient of human pressure (Fig. 2a), with the maximum HFI individuals experienced ranging from as low as 2.6 to 40.5. The home ranges of these animals were 12.6 km from the nearest human development on average, ranging from 95 m to 67.4 km. There was a significant positive relationship between blood microplastic concentrations and the maximum HFI within an animal’s home range (β = 0.07, t = 2.66, P = 0.011; Fig. 2b), although weighted mean HFI exposure was non-significant (β = 0.061, t = 1.73, P = 0.092; Extended Data Fig. 3).

a, Map of the difference in the HFI between 2001 and 2020; examples of HFI and animal movement, as well as land-use class and animal movement data (scatter points), are shown for animals with high, medium and low blood microplastic concentrations. b,c, The scatter plots (n = 20 lowland tapirs and 20 giant anteaters) show the relationships between microplastic concentrations and the maximum HFI in home range (b; β = 0.07, t = 2.66, P = 0.011) and the mean distance to development (c; β = −0.032, t = −2.94, P = 0.0057). Lines in b,c show the fitted population-level trend from a hierarchical generalized linear model (Tweedie distribution; log link) with species-specific random intercepts and slopes; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals. P values are based on two-sided tests, with no correction for multiple comparisons; coefficients are on the link scale. Giant anteater image credit: Steven Traver via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0); tapir image credit: Christophe Mallet via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0).

Although these results highlight how direct exposure to human-modified landscapes shapes internal microplastic burdens, plastic pollution is a transboundary issue with complex dispersal pathways36. Atmospheric deposition and waterborne transport are likely contributors, as airborne microplastics from urban, industrial and agricultural sources can travel long distances before settling in remote ecosystems, and rainfall runoff, river discharge and seasonal flooding redistribute particles across landscapes to habitats far from their original sources2,3,4,5,7,37. Focusing on direct HFI exposure alone can obscure such effects. Indeed, we found that the local-scale effects of human land use were particularly important in shaping the systemic microplastic concentrations of the monitored animals, with significant effects of distance to development (β = −0.032, t = −2.94, P = 0.0057) and distance to the nearest waste management facility (β = −0.026, t = −2.73, P = 0.0096) (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3). Additional data on giant armadillos (Priodontes maximus) living in the Pantanal corroborate this trend (see Supplementary Discussion). These relationships were all robust to sensitivity analyses (Extended Data Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Discussion) and highlight the role of anthropogenic land use in driving species’ exposure to plastic pollution. The polymer profiles also varied across sampling sites in patterns that were broadly consistent with the dominant human activities at each site (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 and Supplementary Discussion).

Recent estimates38 reveal that the mean global HFI increased from 5.26 in 2001 to 6.63 in 2020, representing a 26% increase. This trend in land-use change was even more pronounced in Brazil, where the HFI rose by 42% over the same period, from 4.17 to 5.92. Problematically, anthropogenic land-use expansion often outpaces the development of waste management infrastructure39,40. This infrastructural gap leaves regions experiencing the most rapid change the least equipped to contain plastic waste. Across large parts of rural and interior Brazil, for example, solid waste collection remains inadequate and wastewater treatment is limited or absent altogether41,42,43. The plastic materials tied to the expanding human footprint thus have few barriers preventing them from becoming highly mobile environmental pollutants42. The relationship between human disturbance and blood microplastic concentrations identified here suggests that microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife will continue to rise as land-use change intensifies. Notably, even at an HFI of zero the model predicted blood microplastic concentrations of 10.5 particles per ml (95% confidence interval 4.6–24.2 particles per ml; intercept: β = 2.36, t = 5.58, P < 0.001). While we can not discount the potential that this non-zero intercept was the result of an unmodelled non-linear relationship at low HFI exposure, it does provide support that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. The seemingly pervasive reach of microplastic pollution is most strikingly illustrated by our findings from the animals in the Pantanal. The Pantanal is the world’s largest and most pristine wetland, supporting an extraordinary diversity of wildlife within a relatively undisturbed landscape44. Unlike other biomes in Brazil, much of the Pantanal has remained ecologically intact owing to its remote location, limited infrastructure and seasonal flooding, which naturally regulate many human activities. Yet, we found microplastics in the blood of all of the individuals we sampled in the Pantanal, despite these animals living more than 65 km from the nearest development and more than 112 km from the nearest waste management facility. This finding is corroborated by several recent studies that reported substantial concentrations of microplastics in both aquatic environments and sediments throughout the Pantanal45,46,47, with the highest levels of microplastics (up to 1,174.2 items per m2) found near rivers flowing from urban areas46. The presence of microplastics in the blood of animals living many tens of kilometres from the nearest development or waste facility highlights how microplastics are a threat not only to wildlife with direct exposure to human-modified landscapes, but also to species across even the most remote and ecologically intact environments8. Developing a mechanistic understanding of the pathways through which microplastics reach remote terrestrial ecosystems will be essential for protecting wildlife from this highly mobile pollutant. Although environmental sampling across these sites would strengthen the causal inference of these relationships by directly linking environmental polymer profiles to those detected in blood, isolation protocols for chemically diverse samples such as blood and soil complicate spectroscopy-based comparisons48,49. Paired blood–environment sampling designs thus represent a productive, albeit challenging path forward.

By combining in vivo microplastic measurements with fine-scale movement data and high-resolution landscape disturbance indices, our study moves terrestrial microplastic research beyond detection surveys towards a spatially informed quantitative framework for predicting wildlife burdens from landscape context. This approach revealed how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics, and is readily transferable to other species and regions, offering a scalable tool for identifying vulnerable populations and informing targeted conservation responses. While no ecosystem is likely to be entirely free of microplastics50, we did find that animals in less disturbed habitats carried substantially lower burdens than those in close proximity to human infrastructure. These findings suggest that management efforts aimed at limiting animals’ exposure to human-modified environments and reducing their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure can serve to reduce the microplastic burdens carried by wildlife.

Lowland tapir (T. terrestris) samples were collected across three sites in Brazil. The agricultural mosaic site in the Cerrado was located between the municipalities of Nova Alvorada do Sul and Nova Andradina, in Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−21.99° N, −53.83° E). It features a mosaic of natural habitats, including Cerradão fragments, gallery forests and marshlands, which constitute approximately 12% of the study area. The remainder is heavily influenced by human activities, including agriculture (for example, sugarcane, soybean and corn), cattle ranching, eucalyptus plantations, highways and rural settlements. Precipitation exhibits marked seasonality, with approximately 70% of the total annual rainfall occurring between November and March51.

The field site in the Pantanal was situated on Baía das Pedras Ranch, in the Nhecolândia Sub-Region of the Southern Pantanal, Municipality of Aquidauana, Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−19.33° N, −55.72° E). This private property spans 145 km² and comprises a mosaic of seasonally inundated grasslands, lakes, gallery forests, scrub, and deciduous forests. The Pantanal is a nearly pristine biome with a low human footprint, and is far removed from areas experiencing deforestation and other anthropogenic pressures. The ranch supports abundant wildlife and extensive cattle grazing on native grasses. The average annual temperature is 25 °C, and the annual rainfall is 1,185 mm.

The site in the Amazon was located at Tanguro Farm, a privately owned 103,000 ha property in Querência, Mato Grosso state, that sits at the transition between the Cerrado savanna and the Amazon rainforest along the southern Arc of Deforestation. Owned by AMAGGI, a major actor in Brazil’s soybean industry, the farm comprises 59,000 ha (57%) of croplands (soybean, corn, and cotton) and 44,000 ha (43%) of legally protected forest reserves. This region is the driest portion of the Amazon basin and experiences a prolonged dry season (May–September) with annual rainfall of 1,700–2,200 mm. Forests in this region are shorter (~20 m) than the moist Amazon rainforest (~30 m). About 40% of the farm was cleared for pasture (1976–1992) and later converted to soy cultivation (2003–2010), leaving riparian forests surrounded by croplands.

The giant anteater (M. tridactyla) data collection was conducted in the Cerrado savanna of Mato Grosso do Sul state, Brazil, as part of the Anteaters and Highways Project (ICAS, www.icasconservation.org.br), which investigates wildlife-vehicle collisions and their impacts on wildlife populations. Sampling areas were located near two federal roads: BR-267 (−21.64° N, −53.51° E) and BR-262 (−20.86° N, −52.04° E). As described above, the study region is a mosaic landscape dominated by open areas, including grasslands, pastures, and croplands, interspersed with small remnants of native savanna and forest vegetation, as well as eucalyptus plantations52.

In addition to the tapir and giant anteater data, we also obtained a smaller amount of data from three giant armadillos (P. maximus). The giant armadillo data collection was also conducted at the Baía das Pedras Lodge and Ranch in the Pantanal, which served as the base of operations for the Giant Armadillo Conservation Program (GACP).

All animal capture, handling, and blood sampling procedures were approved by the Brazilian Ministry of the Environment (MMA) and the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio) under license numbers 14603-25 (lowland tapirs), 53798-18 (giant anteaters) and 27587-1 (giant armadillos). All procedures were performed in accordance with the terms of these licenses and with relevant national and institutional animal welfare guidelines. Chemical immobilization was performed under veterinary oversight, and all animals were released at their capture sites following full recovery.

Lowland tapirs were captured using a combination of methods, including darting, following physical restraint in box-traps or pitfall traps, or darting from a distance. Box traps and pitfall traps were deployed in areas frequently visited by tapirs. Tapirs captured by these methods were anaesthetized intramuscularly with a combination of butorphanol (0.17 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.012 mg kg−1) and ketamine (0.7 mg kg−1). Reversal agents, including atipamezole (0.04 mg kg−1) and naltrexone (0.35 mg kg−1), were administered at the conclusion of procedures. For tapirs darted from a distance, anaesthetics included tiletamine-zolazepam (1.25 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.006 mg kg−1), ketamine (0.6 mg kg−1) and atropine (0.03 mg kg−1). Darts (3 ml or 5 ml) were used to deliver anaesthetics. Midazolam (0.03 mg kg−1) was administered 30 min later to maintain anaesthesia. Captured tapirs underwent a range of procedures, including subcutaneous microchip insertion, morphometric measurements, sex and age determination, physical examinations, blood sample collection and telemetry collar placement for adults.

Tapirs were equipped with GPS collars (Telonics TGW SOB and GPS IRIDIUM models) programmed to obtain hourly location fixes, with a median operational life of 15.4 months. Additional location data were collected from stationary tags placed in the Pantanal (n = 883) and Cerrado (n = 174) to calibrate the measurement error in the GPS datasets.

Giant anteaters were captured between February 2021 and November 2022 using motorized active searches between 15:00 and 17:00, when they exhibit higher diurnal activity due to colder temperatures53,54. Searches were conducted along dirt roads in open areas, with two team members stationed in the back of a truck to improve detectability. Upon spotting an individual, technicians approached the animal on foot and captures were performed using two long-handled dip nets (1.5 m handles, 0.7 m diameter hoops). Physical capture typically lasted around 1 min.

Captured giant anteaters were chemically immobilized, equipped with GPS radiotelemetry harnesses (Telonics) as previously described55 and blood samples were collected. In brief, animals were anaesthetized using a protocol of butorphanol tartrate (Zoetis Indústria de Produtos Veterinários; 0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (Agener-União; 0.1 mg kg−1) and midazolam hydrochloride (Cristália; 0.2 mg kg−1), adapted from ref. 55. The induction period averaged 8.27 ± 4.78 min.

Giant armadillos were captured between February 2021 and November 2022, using a method tailored to their natural behaviour56. Researchers tracked footprints and signs of recent predation, such as termite mounds, to locate burrows. When a burrow was identified and confirmed to contain an armadillo (indicated by the entrance being sealed with sand), an iron funnel trap (jequi-type) was placed at the entrance. Once captured, animals were transported in iron-reinforced wooden crates and held overnight for nocturnal species, with procedures beginning the following morning at the capture site.

Captured giant armadillos were anaesthetized for the collection of blood samples and surgical implantation of intra-abdominal transmitters. Anaesthetic protocols included an intramuscular injection of butorphanol tartrate (0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1), and midazolam hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1) into the hind limbs. Before surgery, intradermal local anaesthesia with lidocaine hydrochloride (2 mg kg−1, Eurofarma) was infiltrated into the infra-umbilical region. Ketamine hydrochloride (10 mg kg−1) was administered intramuscularly as a supplementary anaesthetic immediately after the animals were completely washed. Transmitters (IMP 310 model, Telonics; 9.4 × 2.3 cm, 42 g, 36-month operational life) were surgically implanted within the abdominal cavity under sterile conditions. Following surgery, anaesthesia was reversed using a combination of naloxone hydrochloride (0.02 mg kg−1), yohimbine hydrochloride (0.125 mg kg−1), and flumazenil (0.01 mg kg−1). Armadillos were released at their capture sites upon recovery, typically remaining in their burrows for 24 to 120 h (average of 48 h) before emerging. Daily monitoring was conducted for 12–22 days post-release using telemetry receivers (model TR-4, Telonics) and VHF antennas (model RA-23K). After the initial monitoring period, armadillos were monitored monthly until the end of the transmitter’s operational life.

Approximately 10 ml of blood was collected within 20 min of immobilization via venipuncture of the medial saphenous or cephalic veins using a sterile glass vacutainer system (BD Vacutainer). Tapir captures were conducted in remote forest sites without access to field refrigeration. Blood samples were therefore stored in pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept shaded at ambient temperature, and transferred to a −20 °C freezer on return to the base camp within 5–6 h.

Blood samples (~5 ml) were collected approximately 20 min after induction from the cephalic or saphenous veins using a sterile vacutainer system with 23G or 25G needles (BD Vacutainer). Samples were transferred to pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept refrigerated at 4 °C on site, and frozen at −20 °C within 12–24 h for subsequent processing. We note that blood samples were obtained from three individual giant armadillos, however we obtained repeat samples at two time points for two of these animals. Although these blood samples were processed individually, they were pooled (that is, averaged) in our statistical analyses.

Cold storage under the above-mentioned conditions is standard practice in microplastic analyses and does not affect particle abundance or polymer identity. Microplastics are chemically stable over these timescales, and method reviews emphasize that environmental samples containing microplastics are routinely stored at 4 °C for days to weeks prior to processing, or frozen at −20 °C for longer periods, without alteration of polymer composition (reviewed in ref. 57).

Blood microplastic isolation was performed following a protocol previously developed by our team58,59,60. Depending on the sampling date, blood samples were stored at −20 °C for ~1–22 months between collection (Feb 2021–Nov 2022) and digestion (Dec 2022). On the first day of isolation, 1 ml of each blood sample was placed in an Erlenmeyer flask along with 50 ml of 10% KOH solution (sample ratio of 1:50). The mixture was incubated on a shaker at 60 °C and 250 rpm for 24 h. After the initial 24-h incubation, 10 ml of 47% NaClO were added to each sample to achieve a final concentration of 7.7%. The samples were then incubated under the same conditions (60 °C and 250 rpm) for an additional 24 h.

Following the second day of digestion, all samples were filtered through a 47 mm polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size (Merck Omnipore) and rinsed 3 times with filtered ultrapure water. The membranes containing the particles were then submerged in 50 ml of 20% HNO3 and placed in an ultrasonic bath with sweep function at 100% power and 45 kHz frequency for 15 min to transfer the particles from the membrane to the solution. The samples were further incubated for 30 min at 40 °C and 250 rpm.

After removing the membranes, the samples underwent a 24-h incubation at 40 °C and 250 rpm. On the final day, the samples were filtered through a 13 mm PTFE membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size, rinsed three times with filtered ultrapure water, and mounted on glass slides for microscopy and spectroscopy analysis. The resulting filter membranes were then stored in pre-cleaned glass Petri dishes and analysed by Raman spectroscopy over the subsequent ~12 months (Jan–Dec 2023). After digestion, a proportion of non-plastic particulates remained on the membrane, such that microplastics accounted for an average of 16.4% of imaged particles with HQI > 75 (range 0–89.9%).

Quality assurance and quality control methods used throughout the process are detailed in the Supplementary Methods (see also Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7).

Microplastic identification and characterization were conducted using a confocal Raman microscope (alpha300 R, WITec) equipped with a UHTS 300 spectrometer (WITec) and a 532-nm laser. The microscope was operated using Control Five software, and the acquired data were processed with Project Five software to compensate for background noise and cosmic radiation signals.

As an initial step, a whole membrane image was captured using a 10× NA 0.25 Zeiss objective with the Area Stitching option. From this image, a specific field was selected for detailed imaging with a 50× NA 0.75 Zeiss objective, employing both the Area Stitching option and Z-stack autofocus. Particle identification was facilitated by the Particle Scout software, which enabled the acquisition of Raman spectra for all identified particles across the entire membrane. Raman spectra were then obtained using a 100× DIC NA 0.9 Zeiss objective, with a laser power of 10 mW, an accumulation of 4, and an integration time of 0.45 s. Spectra autofocus was used throughout the measurements. The acquired spectra were then compared against the S.T. Japan database (S.T. Japan Europe GmbH) and the SLoPP MPs Raman library61 using the True Match-Integrated Raman Spectra Database Management software. Microplastic characterization was based on an automated, 3-step process that was optimized for spectra acquisition rather than image sharpness. This precluded the manual assessment of particle shape (for example, fibres or fragments) or colour. Only matches with an HQI greater than 75% were considered for further analysis.

To assess changes in the HFI over time, we obtained and processed global HFI rasters at a 300 m resolution for the years 2001 and 2020 from the Wildlife Conservation Society Human Footprint dataset (https://wcshumanfootprint.org/). After ensuring projections and resolutions were consistent between the HFI rasters, a difference raster was generated by subtracting the 2001 HFI from the 2020 HFI to visualize areas of increasing and decreasing human influence. We cropped and masked the HFI rasters to remove areas outside of Brazil and then computed the mean HFI for 2001 and 2020, as well as the absolute differences. These analyses were conducted in R using the terra (v1.8-54)62, sf (v1.0-21)63,64, tmap (v4.0.0.9000)65, fields (v16.3)66, rnaturalearth (v1.0.1)67, and geobr (v1.9.1)68 packages.

Before analysis, we pre-processed the GPS location data in order to calibrate the measurement error and filter outliers. Pre-processing was done via the methods implemented in the R package ctmm (v1.2.1)69. For each location estimate, the GPS trackers recorded a unitless Horizontal Dilution of Precision (HDOP), a value which is a measure of the accuracy of each positional fix. We converted the HDOP values into calibrated errors by specifying 20-m error at an HDOP of 1 for 2D fixes, and 10-m error at an HDOP of 1 for the 3D fixes70. For each individual dataset, we then removed outliers based on error-informed distance from the median location, and the minimum speed required to explain each location’s displacement. Through this process we identified a total of 16,656 outliers, which represented ca. 3.55% of the total 469,410 locations. After filtering outliers, the final dataset consisted of 343,913 GPS locations across 20 individual giant anteaters, 6,072 GPS locations across 2 individual giant armadillos, and 102,769 GPS locations across 20 individual lowland tapirs.

For each of the tracked animals, we used a continuous-time approach to estimate their movement rates and home ranges, enabling robust comparisons across individuals71. We first fitted a series of continuous-time stochastic process movement models to the location data. Parameters were estimated using perturbative-hybrid residual maximum likelihood (pHREML)72, and identified the best model via small-sample-sized-corrected Akaike’s information criterion (AICc). From both visual inspections of the semi-variograms, and the parameters of the fitted movement models, all animals occupied stable home ranges throughout the monitoring period with no indication of range shifts or large-scale dispersal events.

From the selected models, we estimated each animal’s diffusion rate (in km2 day−1) as a measure of their movement rate. We next estimated each animal’s home range, using autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE)73. AKDE home range estimates were conditioned on the autocorrelation structure of the fitted movement model, and we implemented the small-sample-size bias correction of Fleming & Calabrese (2017)74, as well as the optimal weighting of Fleming et al. (2018)75 to correct for uneven sampling. Home range areas (in km2) were estimated as the area contained within the polygon delimited by the 95% isopleth of the probability density.

We estimated the mean and maximum HFI within each individual’s home range. HFI is an aggregate measure of human disturbance that ranges from 0 in natural habitats to 50 in the most anthropogenically modified habitats33. A raster of HFI data with a spatial resolution of 100 m was obtained from Gassert et al.38. The weighted mean HFI within an individual’s home range was estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean of HFI values:

with weights (wu) determined by the probability density at each location u. Maximum HFI exposure was estimated by identifying the maximum value of HFI within each animal’s home range. We also estimated more nuanced patterns of habitat use via the MapBiomas database34, which details land use throughout Brazil at a spatial resolution of 10 m. We focused on habitats classified as water, development, agriculture, pasture, and native forest, which represented the majority of the land classes within the monitored animals’ home ranges. The proportions of each of these land classes within each animal’s home range were again estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean. Lastly, we used the MapBiomas land classification data, the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI), and the Waste Methane Assessment Platform 1.5.0, 2025 (https://wastemap.earth) to generate spatial rasters of distance to development, and distance to the nearest waste management facility (both in m). Development was a compound measure that captured the built environment, and was composed of the MapBiomas collection 10 classes: urban areas (24), mining (30), photovoltaic power plants (75), and other non-vegetated areas (25). From these spatial data, we estimated each animal’s mean distance to development and to the nearest waste management facility, estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean.

To study how human land-use change shaped blood microplastic concentrations, we fit hierarchical generalized linear regression models using the methods implemented in the mgcv package (v1.9-1)76. Because the microplastic concentrations scaled between [0,∞], we used a Tweedie distribution with a log link for the error distribution77, with parameters estimated via restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The regression models testing for correlations between individual habitat use and microplastic concentrations included a population-level effect, as well as random intercepts and slopes for each of the species, with the following general form

where β0 represents the population-level intercept, β is the population-level slope, us[i] is the species-specific random intercept, vs[i] is the species-specific random slope, and s[i] indexes the species of individual i. This structure was used for all of the habitat covariates xi. From these models, inference was then made on the population-level trend.

All analyses were conducted in R (v4.3.3). Weighted means and proportions of land-use exposure were computed with the weights package (v1.0.4). Figures were produced with ggplot2 (v3.5.2), ggspatial (v1.1.9), tidyterra (v0.7.0), rphylopic (v1.5.0; animal silhouettes), fmsb (v0.7.6) and gridExtra (v2.3).

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Sample sizes were determined by the number of animals that could be safely captured during the study period (February 2021 to November 2022) given the logistical constraints of live-capturing large, threatened, free-ranging mammals under national permits, and all animals captured during this period were sampled. This was an observational field study, so randomization was not applicable; animals were not allocated to experimental groups, and exposure to human land use was determined by each individual’s own space use. The investigators were not blinded to species or sampling site during laboratory processing or analysis; however, particle detection and polymer identification were automated (Particle Scout and True Match software) and based on a fixed spectral-match threshold (HQI > 75%), which limits observer bias. Each animal contributed one blood sample, with the exception of two giant armadillos sampled at two time points, whose values were averaged before analysis. Seven animals lacked sufficient GPS tracking data and were excluded from the habitat use models but retained in descriptive analyses. Samples were processed in two batches, each with a procedural blank (Supplementary Methods); all lowland tapir samples were processed in the same batch. The polymer-integrity test shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 was repeated three times independently with similar results.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The blood microplastics data (particle-level measurements, polymer identifications and per-individual summaries underlying Figs. 1 and 2, Extended Data Figs. 1, 2 and 4–7 and Extended Data Tables 1–3), raw GPS tracking data, and the per-individual movement and land-use summaries (underlying Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3) are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34001445 (ref. 78) and on GitHub (https://github.com/QuantitativeEcologyLab/microplastics_brazil). This study also used the following publicly available datasets: the 100 m HFI79 (https://source.coop/repositories/vizzuality/hfp-100/description); the Wildlife Conservation Society 300 m Human Footprint rasters for 2001 and 2020 (https://wcshumanfootprint.org/data-access); MapBiomas Brazil Collection 10 land use and land cover maps (https://brasil.mapbiomas.org/, downloads at https://brasil.mapbiomas.org/en/downloads/); waste management facility locations from the Waste Methane Assessment Platform (WasteMAP) v1.5.0, developed by RMI and Clean Air Task Force (https://wastemap.earth); and Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) and geobr68 basemap data. Raman spectra were matched against the SLoPP library61 (openly available) and the S.T. Japan commercial spectral database (S.T. Japan Europe GmbH), which is available under licence from the vendor. Source data are provided with this paper.

The code and data required to reproduce all of the analyses and figures in the manuscript are openly available at: https://github.com/QuantitativeEcologyLab/microplastics_brazil, and are permanently archived at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34001445 (ref. 78).

The radial bar plots show the mean concentrations (particles per ml) of the different plastic polymers within the blood samples of a, lowland tapirs (n = 26 animals) b, giant anteaters (n = 21 animals), and c, giant armadillos (n = 3 animals). The barplots in d, show the concentrations of the plastic particles in each animal. Histograms of the e, length and f, width of the individual particles are also shown (n = 2,815 particles). The average particle length was 10.2 μm (SD: 10.6, range: 2.0–167.2), and the width was 6.3 μm (SD: 5.2, range: 0.6–76.0). In panels a,d, polymers categorized as ‘other’ were those that occurred at low abundance, and included: Polyvinyl Butyralolyethyleneimine, Poly(butylene terephthalate), Polyvinylformal, Polyacetal, Polymethylpentene, Polyurethane, Polyethylene Glycol, amongst others. Data from giant armadillos are shown for visual comparison but were not included in the analyses presented in the main text. In d,e, Giant anteater image credit: Steven Traver via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0); tapir image credit: Christophe Mallet via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0); giant armadillo image credit: Steven Traver via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0).

The scatter plot in a, shows the relationships between microplastic concentrations (particles per ml) and age for lowland tapirs (n = 24 animals). The boxplots compare microplastic concentrations (particles per ml) between females and males for the b, lowland tapirs (n = 26 animals; 12 females, 14 males) c, giant armadillos (n = 3 animals; all females), and d, giant anteaters (n = 21 animals; 10 females, 11 males). All boxplots depict centre line, median; box limits, 25th and 75th percentiles; whiskers, 1.5× interquartile range; points, individual animals. Scatter plots show the relationships between microplastic concentrations (particles per ml) and body weight (kg) for the e, lowland tapirs (n = 24 animals), f, giant armadillos (n = 3 animals), and g, giant anteaters (n = 21 animals). Lines in a),e,f,g, show the fitted population-level trend from a hierarchical generalised linear model (Tweedie distribution; log link) with species-specific random intercepts and slopes; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals. P-values are based on two-sided tests, with no correction for multiple comparisons; a: β = −0.26, t = −3.13, P = 0.0049 (not robust to removal of the two youngest animals: β = −0.16, t = −1.44, P = 0.17); b: β = 2.05, t = 3.36, P < 0.005; d: β = −0.49, t = −1.01, P = 0.327; e: β = −0.016, t = −1.10, P = 0.29; g: β = 0.012, t = 0.49, P = 0.63. Coefficients are on the link scale. Data from giant armadillos (c,f; β = 0.06, t = 0.62, P = 0.58) are shown for visual comparison but were not included in the analyses presented in the main text. In a–e, Created in BioRender; Ferraz, M. https://BioRender.com/vp3npr1 (2026). The scatter plots show the relationships between microplastic concentrations (particles per ml) and a, home-range size; b, diffusion rate; c, proportion of home range in agricultural land; d, proportion of home range in water and wetlands; e, weighted mean HFI exposure; and f, distance to the nearest waste management facility for all three species. In all panels, solid lines depict statistically significant relationships, whereas non-significant relationships are depicted with dashed lines. Lines in a,b,c,d,e,f, show the fitted population-level trend from a hierarchical generalised linear model (Tweedie distribution; log link) with species-specific random intercepts and slopes; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals. P-values are based on two-sided tests, with no correction for multiple comparisons; a: β = 0.0039, t = 1.49, P = 0.14; b: β = 0.037, t = 0.89, P = 0.38; c: β = 9.40 × 10−4, t = 1.20, P = 0.24; d: β = −0.17, t = −3.50, P = 0.0011; e: β = 0.061, t = 1.73, P = 0.092; f: β = −0.026, t = −2.73, P = 0.0096. Coefficients are on the link scale. Data from giant armadillos are shown for visual comparison but were not included in the analyses presented in the main text. Heatmap in a, depicting the concentration (particles per ml) of the analyzed microplastic polymers for data from the field sites at the Amazon deforestation frontier, the Cerrado agricultural mosaic, and the Pantanal cattle ranch. Each row in the heatmap corresponds to a unique blood sample. Rows are grouped by site and separated by dashed lines; the top lines are from the Pantanal cattle ranch (Baía das Pedras Ranch, Nhecolândia, Aquidauana, Mato Grosso do Sul), the middle lines from the Cerrado agricultural mosaic (between Nova Alvorada do Sul and Nova Andradina, and along the BR-267 and BR-262 highways, Mato Grosso do Sul), and the bottom lines from the Amazon deforestation frontier (Tanguro Farm, Querência, Mato Grosso). The radar bar plots show the mean concentrations (particles per ml) of the different plastic polymers within the blood samples of animals from the b, Amazon deforestation frontier site (n = 14 animals) c, Cerrado agricultural mosaic (n = 22 animals), and d, Pantanal cattle ranch (n = 14 animals). In all panels, polymers categorised as ‘other’ were those that occurred at low abundance, and included: Polyvinyl Butyralolyethyleneimine, Poly(butylene terephthalate), Polyvinylformal, Polyacetal, Polymethylpentene, Polyurethane, Polyethylene Glycol, amongst others. Pairwise site comparisons used a hierarchical generalised linear model (Tweedie distribution; log link) with species-specific random intercepts and slopes. P-values adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure; Cerrado versus Pantanal PVC: β = 3.54, t = 3.36, adjusted P = 0.037; Amazon versus Cerrado polyamide: β = 3.19, t = 3.47, adjusted P = 0.037. No other pairwise polymer differences were detected. Overall concentrations did not differ across sites (generalized likelihood-ratio test, λ = 3.39, P = 0.61). All P-values are based on two-sided tests.

Scatterplots of the number of polymers identified in blood samples, as well as the Shannon and Simpson’s diversity indices as a function of the sample size. The top row a–c, shows results for data from the agricultural mosaic in the Cerrado (n = 22 animals), the middle row d–f, the cattle ranch in the Pantanal (n = 14 animals), and the bottom row g–i, the Amazon deforestation frontier site (n = 14 animals). In all panels, the dashed line represents the value estimated from the full dataset, the coloured lines connecting the points are included as a visual aid, and the shaded areas represent the 95% confidence intervals. Note how all curves exhibit saturating behaviour, however, clear convergence was limited for the data from the Pantanal site, and results from that site should be interpreted with caution.

Representative image of 1.1 μm polystyrene beads after the complete digestion and filtration workflow. Black arrows indicate polystyrene beads. Scale bar, 10 μm. The digestion test was repeated three times independently with similar results. Created in BioRender; Ferraz, M. https://BioRender.com/o4creek (2026).

Histograms of the a, length and b, width of the individual particles are shown (n = 108 particles). The two blank controls were processed in parallel with each of the two sample batches to monitor background contamination. The average particle length in the controls was 38.4 μm (SD: 69.6, range: 9.3–497.4), and the width was 14.9 μm (SD: 16.4, range: 1.7–124.0). Panels c,d, show the size distributions of the particles in the blank controls contrasted against the blood samples (n = 2,815 particles). The heatmap in e, shows the particle counts for the polymers in each of the two controls, while the radial bar plots show the polymer distributions in the f, blood samples, and g, controls.
