(a) Tumors 4 and 7 analyzed as in Fig. 1h. Cells are colored by classification or the indicated feature levels. (b) Heatmap of mean feature levels in each subpopulation across all HR+ tumors analyzed by CyTOF (n = 14, including 3 anchor repeats, see Table S3). Rows present standardized values. (c) Two luminal PDX models analyzed by CyTOF after removal of mouse cells (human CD298-positive; mouse MHC class 1-negative), and classification into three subpopulations (Fig. 1j). PDX-1 comprised of six tumors, with equal cell sampling per tumor; PDX-2 comprised of one tumor. Heatmaps show the mean feature levels within each subpopulation for each model. (d) UMAP of MCF7 CyTOF data using all measured markers. Points are colored by cluster (left) or the indicated feature or signature (right).

(a) Distribution of DBSACN-defined cell subpopulations across independent MCF7 CyTOF experiments of MCF7 cells, showing consistent proportions of the different cell states. (b) UMAP representation and DBSCAN clustering of two different MCF7 parental cells or single-cell derived clones analyzed by CyTOF, using only epigenetic features. Points are colored by the classification of different subpopulations or the expression levels of the indicated feature or signature (PermCell). (c) The distribution of cells among the populations defined by DBSCAN clustering in the MCF7 parental (p) or single-cell derived clones (c). The single-cell derived clones recapitulate the entire spectrum of heterogeneity observed in the parental population. (d) UMAP representation of CyTOF analysis of six independently grown tumors from the PDX-1 model (n = 6 tumors, each grown in a different mouse), colored by subpopulations. Cells from each individual tumor are mapped onto the joint UMAP, and the distribution of cells among the three subpopulations for each tumor is shown.

(a) Confusion matrix of XGBoost model predictions for all 3 subpopulations across HR+ tumors (n = 14) using only epigenetic features, excluding cell identity markers. Rows were normalized to show predictions as percentages of cells within each true class. (b) Representative examples of XGBoost-based noise prediction procedure. UMAPs of individual tumors are shown before (left) and after (right) prediction. Points are colored by classification; non-clustered cells before prediction, or cells in which prediction confidence <95% are marked in gray. (c-d) XGBoost models distinguishing Cycling cells from all other tumor cells (c) or specifically the basal-like cells (d) within the HR+ CyTOF cohort. SHAP scores show feature contributions to classification, ranked in descending order. (e) Percentage of proliferating cells (assessed by the levels of pRb, as in Fig. S3) in each epigenetic sub-populations (Cycling, luminal and basal-like). The basal-like and luminal sub-populations do not differ due to differences in the proliferative state. (f) The differences in the average levels of the indicated features between the basal-like and luminal sub-populations in the luminal PDX models. Basal-like cells show a recurrent pattern of both up and downregulated histone PTMs, highly similar to the pattern observed in fresh human tumors.

(a) UMAP of CyTOF data from tumors (as in Fig. S4), colored by the assigned clusters (top) or the basal-like epigenetic signature (basal PermCell score, bottom), which is derived solely from histone modifications. (b) UMAP of two MCF7 parental cultures and three single-cell-derived clones analyzed by CyTOF using only epigenetic features, colored by assigned clusters (top) or the basal-like epigenetic signature (bottom).

(a) Scatter plot comparing basal-like cell fraction with estrogen receptor (ER) positivity by IHC across tumors (n = 11). Spearman correlation coefficient and two-sided p-value are indicated. (b,c) Basal-like cell fraction in HR+ tumors stratified by progesterone receptor (PR) IHC (b; 100% PR-positive, n = 7; lower PR positivity, n = 4) or TP53 status (c; wild-type, n = 8; mutant, n = 3). Two-sided Wilcoxon tests. Boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend within 1.5xIQR. (d) Differential protein abundance between K5High and K5Low populations in tumor 19. Axes show protein intensity difference (K5High-K5Low) and -log10(p-value), respectively. Two-sided Student’s t-tests with FDR correction; Green and pink dots depict proteins significantly deregulated (Fold change>1.5, q-value < 0.05). Labeled are chromatin regulators differentially expressed between the two populations. (e) Principal component analysis (PCA) of RNA-seq profiles from sorted MCF7 subpopulations. Basal-like cells (K5High GATA3Low, n = 3), extreme luminal cells (K5Low GATA3High, n = 3), and bulk MCF7 cells (n = 2). Points represent independently sorted population. Axes indicate variance explained. (f) Differential gene expression between basal-like (K5High GATA3Low, n = 3) and bulk MCF7 cells (n = 2). Significantly upregulated (pink) and downregulated (green) genes are indicated (DESeq2, Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p-value < 0.05, log2FC > 1). EMT-associated genes (hallmark epithelial-mesenchymal transition gene set) are enriched among upregulated transcripts in the basal-like population and highlighted with a black outline. CD74, a membrane-bound protein upregulated in the basal-like cells, is marked in dark pink. (g) CD74 expression across basal-like (n = 3), bulk (n = 2), and extreme luminal (n = 3) MCF7 populations. Points represent independently sorted population; expression is shown as rld values. Statistical significance was derived from DESeq2 differential expression analysis with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. (h) Representative wound-healing assay images of sorted CD74Low and CD74High MCF7 cells at the indicated times. Three independently recovered sorted populations from the same sort were analyzed. The gap area is highlighted in green. Scale bar = 300 μm.

(a) TCGA-BRCA DNA-methylation dataset (n = 782)51 was deconvoluted into three archetypes. Dots show tumor archetype composition and colored by PAM50 subtype. The archetype V3 is associated with basal-like triple-negative tumors. The composition of archetypes within the three tumors analyzed in this study (T18, T19, and T23, highlighted) clusters with luminal breast tumors from the TCGA cohort. (b) Genes were ranked by correlation between methylation archetypes and matched TCGA-BRCA expression, followed by GSEA111 against MSigDB hallmark gene sets (Table S4b). V1 and V2 archetypes are associated with luminal transcriptional programs while V3 archetype is enriched for the EMT program. Normalized Enrichment Scores (NES) of representative terms are shown. Black outline denotes BH-adjusted p-value < 0.05. See Fig. S5a for all terms. (c-d) K5High and K5Low sorted cells from tumors 5 and 23 were subjected to enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq, n = 4 replicates, 200 cells/replicate), and differentially methylated gene promoters were identified. For each sample, functional enrichment analysis was performed separately for genes with hypermethylated or hypomethylated promoters. Shown are the top 10 enriched terms from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection (c) or a curated list of breast cancer cell identity signatures (d) with nominal p-value < 0.05 (one-sided hypergeometric test). Circle size represents the number of genes from the input list overlapping each gene set, and transparency reflects -log10(p-value). (e) A CpG-island (CGI) methylation signature distinguishing K5High and K5Low states, derived using CGIs showing concordant differential methylation between the states in both tumor 5 and 23. Shown is the projection of this signature into DNA methylation profiles from the TCGA-BRCA dataset. Positive scores indicate greater similarity to the EM-seq-derived K5High methylation program, whereas negative scores indicate similarity to the K5Low state. Boxplots show the distribution of signature scores across basal-like (n = 96) or luminal (n = 418) tumors with points representing individual tumors. Boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend to the largest/smallest value within 1.5×IQR. The K5High methylation program is enriched in basal-like breast tumors. Two-sided Mann–Whitney U test. (f) TCGA-BRCA DNA-methylation dataset deconvoluted into three archetypes as in a, with K5high and K5low-sorted populations from tumors 5 and 23 projected onto the archetype space. K5high populations are shifted toward the V3 archetype, consistent with enrichment for basal/EMT-associated methylation programs. (g) Representation of tumors from the TCGA-BRCA cohort based on the four-archetype decomposition described in Fig. 3a, colored by V1 contribution. K5high and K5low-sorted populations from tumors 5 and 23 are projected onto the UMAP embedding. K5high populations are localized to regions characterized by higher V1 contribution, consistent with the EMT-associated methylation programs.

(a) WGBS reads were clustered by DNA methylation patterns over 100 bp bins55, and each bin was scored for entropy, reflecting DNA methylation pattern heterogeneity; bins containing one pattern have zero entropy. Illustration, rows represent methylation patterns, filled/open circles indicate methylated/unmethylated CpGs and #r denotes supporting reads. Histograms show mean entropy scores of CGIs in tumor 19 (n = 17,434), tumor 18 (n = 20,845) and tumor 23 (n = 22,440). Most CGIs are unmethylated and have zero entropy scores. The intermediate and high-entropy bins are marked in pink and red. (b) Intermediate- and high-entropy CGIs (entropy>0) were linked to genes and analyzed for enrichment against MSigDB Hallmark genesets85. Pathways significantly enriched in all three tumors are shown (one-sided hypergeometric test, nominal p-value < 0.05). Dot size indicates overlapping genes; color indicates -log10(p-value). Variable CGIs are significantly enriched for genes related to EMT. (c) The Basal-luminal index was used to score the transcriptional identity of tumor cells13, and cells from each tumor were divided into quartiles; a low index score corresponds to expression of luminal identity genes (Q1) and a high index score corresponds to expression of basal-like identity genes (Q4). Cell-to-cell distance was calculated within each quartile to assess transcriptional heterogeneity; medians are shown for each sample. Bottom, representative UMAP and quartile definition for tumor 12-R. (d) Vendi score96 was used to calculate epigenetic heterogeneity within luminal or basal-like subpopulation (as defined in Figs. 1, 2, across n = 11 luminal tumors) using single-cell CyTOF histone PTMs measurements. Points show the mean across 5,000 rarefactions; error bars indicate uncertainty intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) of the rarefied score distribution. Histone PTM levels are more variable in basal-like cells.

(a) UMAPs of H3K4me1 (left, n = 17,062 cells) and H3K4me3 (right, n = 12,883 cells) snCUT&Tag 50 kb bins matrices from three tumor samples (PC1 representing read counts excluded; CD45-negative cells). Shared stroma clusters are outlined. (b) UMAPs as in a, colored according to H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 enrichment over fibroblast identity genes: FAP, COL3A1 and DCN (left) or endothelial identity genes: EMCN, PECAM1 and NOTCH3 (right). Higher UCell scores indicate stronger enrichment at genes associated with the corresponding stromal identity. (c,d) H3K4me1 (c) or H3K4me3 (d) UMAPS from all three tumors (50k bins matrix), colored by cluster. The portion of cells from each tumor that constitutes the clusters is shown below. Shared clusters were classified as stroma, as verified by gene activity; Boxed tumor clusters were analyzed further. For H3K4me3, limited number of cells passed quality control thresholds for tumor 8, thus data quality for this sample is lower. (e) Genomic annotation of H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 snCUT&Tag pseudo-bulk peaks, after stoma removal. Stacked bar plots show percentage of peaks assigned to genomic features. (f) For each tumor sample, removing the stroma compartment, a scTransform-normalized H3K4me3 gene activity was generated (excluding read counts information), represented by UMAP and clustered using Louvain clustering. Cell numbers are indicated. (g) Tumor 8 H3K4me1 UMAP (Fig. 3e), colored by UCell scores derived based on the genes contributing to the enrichment of the indicated terms. Cluster 2 shows high H3K4me1 signal on genes associated with basal-like cell identity. While the EMT signature was not significantly enriched for this cluster (FDR-adjusted p-value > 0.05), the corresponding UCell score is shown for comparison using EMT-associated genes contributing to the cluster. (h) Differentially H3K4me3-bound genes identified for each cluster shown in f (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2FC > 1, adjusted p-value < 0.01) were tested against MSigDB Hallmark and Breast-related genesets (Table S4). Terms enriched in cluster 1 in all three tumors are shown (one-sided hypergeometric test, FDR-adjusted P < 0.05). (i) Pseudu-bulk H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 genome-browser tracks from basal-like clusters (pink) or equal numbers of cells sampled from all other clusters (green) at representative genomic regions.

(a,b) H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 reads per cell versus negative ER-signaling score in tumor 15 (a) or positive ER-signaling score in tumor 18 (b). Points represent cells; r is Pearson’s correlation coefficient. (c) H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag UMAPs from tumors 15 and 18 (Fig. 3e), colored by CyTOF-derived labels (top), with predicted-label composition per snCUT&Tag cluster (middle) and UCell scores for the ‘Down in Luminal vs. Basal (Charafe)’ signature (bottom). (d) Cells were classified as luminal or basal-like by CyTOF label transfer as in c. Differences in mean UCell scores for the indicated signatures between basal-like and luminal cells are shown across three tumors. EMT and basal-like-associated gene signatures show higher H3K4me1 deposition in the CyTOF-predicted basal-like group. (e) K5High and K5Low sorted cell populations from the luminal PDX model or MCF7 cells were subjected to H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. Peaks unique to each population were assigned to genes and compared to the indicated gene signatures. Shown is the difference in the GeneRatio (overlap count divided by the total number of peak-associated genes in that population) for each population, with positive values indicating increased overlap in K5High (basal-like) cells, whereas negative values indicate increased overlap in K5Low (luminal) cells. (f) Tumor 8 H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag UMAP from a 20kb-bin matrix, clustered by Leiden clustering (left). Stroma percentages per cluster, based on the H3K4me1-trained classifier, are shown on the right. (g) Following removal of the stromal compartment described in f, a normalized promoter-proximal H3K9me2 occupancy matrix was generated, and Leiden clustering was applied (n = 4,419 cells, see Methods). (h) Percentage of basal-like cells (cluster 2 in Fig. 3e) within each cluster in g, based on the H3K4me1-trained classifier. (i) Left: Differentially H3K9me2-bound genes in cluster 4, shown in g (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2FC > 0.6, adjusted p-value < 0.01), were tested against MSigDB Hallmark and Breast-related signatures. Shown are the top 5 terms significantly enriched (nominal p-value < 0.05) for genes with upregulation of H3K9me2 on their promoters. Right: UMAP as in g colored according to UCell gene-signature scores for the indicated gene sets. Cluster 4 shows elevated H3K9me2 occupancy over luminal-associated genes. (j) Read count per cell (nCount) by cluster (panel g). Violin plots show the distribution of individual cells, with the median denoted by a white dot and n indicated for each cluster. Cluster 4 shows the highest number of reads per cell, possibly corresponding to higher global levels of this mark in basal-like cells.

(a,b) Classifier performance in an independently processed, batch-corrected cohort of healthy individuals (n = 19) and luminal BC patients (n = 30), using the model trained on the original cohort in Fig. 4f. (a) ROC curve (AUC = 0.98; shading, 95% CI). (b) Confusion matrix with specificity set to 0.9. (c,d) ROC curve discriminating healthy individuals (n = 32) from luminal BC patients, diagnosed at the SHEBA medical center, Israel (c, n = 16, AUC = 0.96) or Kaplan medical center, Israel (d, n = 14, AUC = 0.99). Shading indicates the 95% CI. (e) ROC curve discriminating healthy individuals (n = 32) and triple-negative BC patients (n = 22, AUC = 0.98, shading indicates the 95% CI). (f) Healthy (n = 51) and luminal BC samples from three medical centers (n = 137) were pooled and stratified into 75% training cohort and a 25% test cohort. ROC curves are shown for training (left, n = 38 healthy vs. 103 luminal BC samples, AUC = 0.96) and the test cohort (right, n = 13 healthy vs. 34 luminal BC patients, AUC = 0.94). Shading indicates the 95% CI. (g) AUC estimates for discrimination of healthy individuals (n = 51) from luminal A (n = 98), luminal B (n = 31), or all luminal BC patients (n = 137) across the three medical centers. Points and lines indicate AUCs and 95% CIs, respectively.

(a-f) Selected EPINUC features in disease-free versus recurrent-disease groups within clinically defined subsets (see Fig. 5a): >50% ER-positive (a, n = 39 vs. 28), >50% PR-positive (b, n = 33 vs. 18), luminal A BC (c, n = 35 vs. 23), T1-T2 staged tumors (d, n = 43 vs. 20), grade 1-2 tumors (e, n = 36 vs. 18), and no LVI at diagnosis (f, n = 34 vs. 14). Two-sided Wilcoxon tests. (g) Distribution of 29 EPINUC features across luminal BC patients stratified by histological grade (grade 1, n = 29; grade 2, n = 67; grade 3, n = 36). Points represent individual patients. Kruskal-Wallis p-values were Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected across the 29 features. (h) Spearman correlations between mean histone PTM levels measured by CyTOF in tumor cells and EPINUC measurements in matched plasma (n = 10). Correlations with r > 0.2 are pink; P < 0.05 is bold (two-sided Spearman correlation test). H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 scatter plots are shown below, with Theil-Sen fits and 95% CIs. (i) Individual PPS analysis distinguishing disease-free (DF) from relapse (R, left column), or between healthy individuals (H) and each of the luminal outcome group. Color indicates PPS, reflecting predictive power of each individual feature. (j) OncotypeDX scores for patients in cohorts MAYO-1 and MAYO-2 with available measurements (disease-free, n = 40; relapse, n = 9, n.s., non-significant, two-sided Wilcoxon test). In a–g,j, boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend to the largest/smallest value within 1.5×IQR.

#1349. Man United's appointment of Mauricio Pochettino feels like the Glazers are back calling the shots at Old Trafford - with Jim Ratcliffe's henchmen Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking like irrelevant also-rans, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 12:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EST, 12 November 2026

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada once cited a line from the John Lennon song Beautiful Boy, when relating how an intended 12-month attachment at Barcelona had ended up with him staying there for 13 years. ‘Life is what happens to you while you’re busy making other plans.’

Lennon’s lyric seems far more appropriate to what Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment tells us about Berrada and his dubious grip on United, today.

While Berrada and his director of football Jason Wilcox have been busy making plans for United’s world domination – ‘to create the new history,’ as he described it to the journalist and broadcaster Andy Mitten just five months ago – it seems clear a Glazer family petrified by the shocking descent of their Premier League asset have stepped in to get Pochettino installed.

If it had been left to Berrada and Wilcox, we may have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse in the next few days. It’s been widely known and reported that Howe was Wilcox’s preference, while Christopher Vivell, director of recruitment, wanted Julian Nagelsmann.

Sources have told us that the Glazers wanted Pochettino and ordered Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men to fall in line with that. They point to a connection between the Glazers, Pochettino and US billionaire hedge fund owner Ken Griffin.

Griffin was the main financial contributor to the salary which saw Pochettino hired by US Soccer in 2024 and again to that contract extension he signed in August. It was also Griffin, the then youthful founder of Citadel, who provided substantial funds for the Glazers’ takeover of United in 2005. Manchester United deny this, insisting that Pochettino is not a Glazer appointee.

Should Berrada and Wilcox both survive the latest embarrassment – and it would be a travesty if they do, as United pay US Soccer £7.5million in compensation for Pochettino, who would have been out of contract if they’d moved for him in August – then both will be a virtual irrelevance now. Also-rans, bypassed by the latest executive dice roll for United.

Perhaps the TV cameras will pan to them celebrating in the executive seats during some United upturn under Pochettino, weeks or months from now. If so, let it be remembered that it took the influence of others to bend things United’s way.

If Jason Wilcox (left) and Omar Berrada (right) had got their way, we would seemingly have been treated to the sight of Eddie Howe wandering into the Old Trafford madhouse

Instead the Glazers insisted that Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) would have the keys and Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his men fell in line with that

Let us not pretend there’s been any visionary executive oversight from the Glazers. They’ve already rejected Pochettino twice, in favour of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2018 and Erik ten Hag four years later.

But sources close to Joel and Avram Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in their British sports asset, have indicated the brothers have been pushing to get him installed for some weeks.

The Glazers’ connection with US billionaire hedge fund owner Ken Griffin seems significant. Griffin was the main financial contributor to the salary which saw Pochettino hired by US Soccer in 2024 and again to that contract extension he signed in August.

It was also Griffin, the then youthful founder of Citadel, who provided substantial funds for the Glazers’ takeover of United in 2005.

It seems that the Old Trafford hierarchy, like so much about the club, will be skewed from now on. Pochettino does not answer to Berrada and Wilcox in the same way that Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have.

He transcends the structure imposed by Ratcliffe, the so-called controller of football operations, and becomes the most powerful man at Old Trafford. The individual on whose vision the futures of Berrada and Wilcox now rest. Should they stay, this is the last chance saloon for them.

United's slump in form this season has been so severe, the club have been forced to dispense with Michael Carrick just six months after giving him a two-year deal

Sources close to Avram (left) and Joel Glazer, the members of the dynasty who take some interest in United, indicate they have been pushing for Pochettino for some weeks

There should be optimism. Pochettino, more than Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, Unai Emery, Antonio Conte and all other available candidates, has the faculty, charisma and fundamental toughness to instil some mettle into United and drag the club from what Ratcliffe and Co have reduced it to. To instil the identity and culture missing for so long.

Time will only tell if he can actually make a go of the most complicated and challenging job in world football, which Ratcliffe has rendered so much harder, by stripping away so many good, essential people from the Old Trafford payroll. That really is a monumental ‘If’.

One United insider spoke for many today when observing: ‘I haven’t got a clue who can make a go of it with the people above them.’

Pochettino will find United no longer command the same spending power, for transfers and wages, as other top clubs, though their name still carries a cachet, if only they can be nimbler and smarter.

He will discover that one of the most godforsaken parts of the operation is the interminable decision-making process: multiple individuals sitting around the table whose opinions must be sought in rule by committee. Some of those who have been shown the door by Ratcliffe consider themselves well out of all that.

The individual United most need now is actually David Gill, the stellar chief executive who left in the same summer as Sir Alex Ferguson, 13 years ago.

Gill would bring a command and intellect way beyond the remotest comprehension of Berrada. He probably wouldn’t want the association with Ineos but nevertheless, United do need to find a proven, world-class chief executive officer. And a sporting director befitting the biggest club in the world.

In that interview with Mitten back in June, Berrada seemed very pleased with himself – sitting on a large sofa in a United meeting room with immaculately bright white adidas trainers and declaring that United had travelled a long way in 12 months.

‘I’m naturally optimistic by nature, although my wife says I should smile more,’ he said. ‘We’ve made some very difficult decisions, but they have put us where we are today.’

It was his 'aspiration’ to ‘make United great again’, he declared. He is a footnote to another unhappy chapter in the modern history of Manchester United, now. The monumental task lies at Pochettino’s door.

#1348. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

Buendia chips a pass through for Alysson to chase. Hornicek dashes out of his box to head it away and Alysson accidentally bumps into him. The home crowd scream for a card, with Alysson already on a yellow, but there’s absolutely nothing in the challenge, with VAR checking it very quickly.

All pretty one dimensional from Newcastle so far with nothing to really hurt Aston Villa in their attacking play, but the VAR check for a red card on Sven Botman has woken the crowd up. The Villa coaching staff and players were appealing for a red which incensed Newcastle and their supporters. You guessed it, there’s another yellow card. This time, Alysson is booked for simulation as he runs into traffic. It’s a very theatrical dive. There was no contact from Joelinton.

Joao Gomes is the next player to go into the book after he pulls Fernandez-Pardo’s shirt. The decision is met by ironic cheers from the home crowd. The Villa midfielder tries to protest against the decision and Buendia has to push him away to stop him from talking his way into a second yellow.

It’s been a feisty game so far. Newcastle fans are unhappy with the number of fouls given against them. The hosts are being very aggressive with their press as Gonzalez dispossesses Kamara to force a corner, but nothing comes from the set piece.

Newcastle fans can breathe a huge sigh of relief as Botman’s card stays as a yellow. The defender is a very lucky man.

Referee Gillett shows two yellow cards in incredibly quick succession as Joelinton and Botman both fly into forceful challenges on Manzambi and Jackson respectively. The crowd furiously boo both decisions. Botman’s tackle on Jackson was wild and over the top of the ball, with VAR checking for a possible red card.

Villa are finding holes in Newcastle’s defence as Manzambi plays in Cash, who fires into the side netting from a tight angle. Emery and his players are convinced they should of had a corner.

Once again, Villa hit Newcastle on the counter. This time, Jackson turns provider and tries to thread a pass into Alysson’s path. However, Hall is on high alert and defends diligently to intercept and clear.

Huge chance for Villa! Out of nowhere, Villa counter from a Newcastle corner. It’s excellent play from Alysson, who powers past his marker before slipping a pass to the onrushing Jackson. The striker is through and chops inside of Botman, before shooting straight at Hornicek with the outside of his boot. Given the ruthless form he’s been in, you’d expect more from Jackson there.

Villa are penned in at the moment, with Newcastle having made a fast start in these early stages. Suzuki has the ball and he’s put under tremendous pressure from Wissa. The goalkeeper is calmness personified as he coolly passes to Cash.

Fernandez-Pardo drives at Wan-Bissaka and tries to find Willock with a low delivery. The cross is intercepted by Lindelof, but it’s positive play from Newcastle’s summer recruit, who is lining up in his preferred position out wide.

Early signs reveal that Fernandez-Pardo is playing on the right wing, with Wissa operating as the central striker and Willock pushed up as the most advanced midfielder. Barnes is on the left.

Villa get us under way at St James’ Park.

Both line-ups are out on the pitch. St James’ Park is absolutely buzzing as the Premier League anthem rings around the stadium after a modified edition of Blaydon Races, with kick-off minutes away.

There is a new version of the Blaydon Races, reworked by Newcastle United in order to become their club’s official pre-match anthem. It is slower than the original and lacks a bit of oomph. But, you know what, I wanted to hate it and it was actually okay. Once supporters get used to the new pace of the song they should start joining in with the singing. I have to constantly have to remind myself at this age that just because something is new and different doesn’t mean it is bad.

Newcastle will be relieved that this game is at St James’ Park, with the club having lost their previous two away fixtures 4-1 against both Coventry and Leeds.

Summer signing Nicolas Jackson has five goals in his previous six games for Aston Villa in all competitions and looks to be brimming with confidence as he leads the line for Unai Emery. The striker dispatched both finishes for his brace against Fenerbahce with unerring composure and will target more goals at St James’ Park.

One of the interesting subplots to this evening’s game will be watching Johan Manzambi playing for Aston Villa.

The Switzerland international’s decision to reject Newcastle in order to sign for Villa helped convince Eddie Howe to quit in the summer.

Having already missed out on Victor Munoz, who decided to join Liverpool at the last moment, losing Manzambi - their first-choice target across the position board - was a blow Howe did not feel he could recover from.

In short, he was not convinced the alternatives would give him the tools to do the job this season. Aladji Bamba, who was signed instead, has not started a game for Newcastle this season and appears to be well down the pecking order in the centre midfield under Howe’s successor Matthias Jaissle.

Manzambi had a slow start to his Villa career because of injury but he was hugely impressive at the World Cup for Switzerland and is expected to become one of the best midfield players in Europe over the next few years. Nobody can say with any degree of confidence that will be the same for Bamba.

#1346. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

“I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler said while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”

The presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. All that remained was for the Paraguayan international to hurtle towards the corner flag, engulfed by his ecstatic team-mates. For the Brighton fans, soaked by showers at the Amex, rain can never have felt so sweet.

Gómez’s goal will earn comparisons with David Beckham’s lob from the halfway line at Wimbledon. The advancements in pressing and conditioning in the 30 years since, with space ever more congested, makes such a strike even harder today. Not since Wayne Rooney in 2017 has a player scored a Premier League goal from further out than Gómez’s 56 yards.

Gómez may well attempt an encore. He shot from even further out at the Stadium of Light a week ago. When October ends, three of the last four Premier League goal-of-the-month winners will be Brighton players. Alongside his meticulous emphasis on set-pieces, Hürzeler empowers flair in open play.

I think we are able to do it, we did it in Leeds, now we are in this situation.

“We are aware of what’s happened in these two games [against Forest and Lyon], one was a good result, one was a bad result, but in each game, when we are 100 per cent on what we have to do in our gameplan, I think we are able to do really wonderful things. When we are not like this, it is another story.”

Brighton have played against 10 men twice this season but were consigned to that very fate last weekend at the Stadium of Light.

Having gone ahead through De Cuyper, Struijk was given his marching orders (a decision that has since been overturned on appeal) and the visitors were made to show a different side to their character, battling in a deep block and frustrating Sunderland before adding a second.

"Today it's up to us" Marco Rose is hoping for Bournemouth's first league win of the season 🍒 https://t.co/VoNR9VfCOd

Pascal Gross may be 35 years old, but he is enjoying one of the finest seasons of his career, creating the most chances in the Premier League. Of his midfield talisman, Hurzeler said: “It started in pre-season. During pre-season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours doing nothing…

“He really suffered in pre-season. In pre-season you really build a foundation for the whole season, you build a physical foundation, a resilience, you build also the mindset… How he came back after this break was impressive. He looked so fit, so sharp, so ready… We saw a different face from him already and then it’s just a progression for him on the pitch…

“Of course no one expected it would be that good, but shows that he still has all this capacity in his body.”

Neither Brobbey nor Isidor make the match-day squad, so it will be up to 21-year-old Tutyerov to lead the line for Sunderland.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

Crystal Palace have reportedly run into some issues delaying their move to hire Thomas Frank as their new manager after the sacking of Pierre Sage.

Palace are struggling so far this season and look in need of a change, with Frank seeming like an ideal appointment due to his experience in the Premier League with Brentford and Tottenham.

The Danish tactician did superb work at Brentford, suggesting he could be a good option to help Palace out of trouble, even if he had less good fortune during his stint in charge of Spurs.

Still, according to Football Insider, there have been some delays as Palace look to hire Frank due to also needing to reach agreements with his sizeable number of backroom staff.

The Eagles will hope this can be resolved quickly, but talks with Frank have taken place and the report still suggests he should end up finalising a deal to take over at Selhurst Park.

Palace are currently bottom of the Premier League table with just seven points from their first ten games, so it’s not looking good for them so far in their fight for survival.

Still, it’s perhaps not too surprising that they’ve inevitably gone backwards after losing a lot of star players in recent times, as well as their hugely successful former manager Oliver Glasner.

Sage did a poor job when he took over this summer, but Palace can perhaps be a bit more optimistic about the future if they bring in Frank.

The 53-year-old turned Brentford into a solid mid-table side and he could surely do the same with this Palace squad, where there’s still a decent amount of talent not currently fulfilling its full potential.

#1344. Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive new patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

The heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

We generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs showed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

a,b, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice (aged 10 weeks) were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 1 week at 24 °C. Representative images of BAT IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) (a), and quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both (b). n = 6 per group. c,d, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline chow diet for 3 days or 1 week at 6 °C. c, Representative images of IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red) and DAPI (blue) in iWAT. d, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs positive for GFP+(UCP1+) only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 4 per group. e, Representative IF staining for UCP1 (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue) in human supraclavicular BAT. f, Quantification of the relative percentage of BAs that are positive for UCP1+ only, H6PD+ only or both. n = 5 per group. g, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs from WT mice were reverse-transfected with H6pd Dicer-substrate small interfering RNAs (dsiRNAs) or control dsiRNAs and collected after 2 days. RT–qPCR analysis of H6pd, Rgs2, Hsd11b1 and Ucp1 mRNA levels. n = 3 per group. h–j, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice were injected with lentivirus overexpressing H6PD or mCherry as a control into BAT. h, After 2 weeks, H6PD and β-actin protein levels were analysed using western blotting (WB). i, Representative IF staining of BAT for GFP (green), perilipin (red) and DAPI (blue). j, Quantification of the BA-H cell percentage. For j, n = 5 (mCherry) and n = 4 (H6PD). Statistics were computed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (b, d and f), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (g (H6pd and Hsd11b1)) or unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (g (Rgs2 and Ucp1) and j); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. For b, d, f, g and j, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 25 μm (a (right), c (bottom)), 50 μm (a (left), c (top) and e) and 100 μm (i).

To enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes showed selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

We next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further showed TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently showed that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

We next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.

a–c, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs of WT mice were treated with NA ± 11-DHC for 24 h (a) or pretreated with vehicle or 11-DHC for 24 h, followed by NA (b) or forskolin (c) treatment for 24 h. UCP1 and β-actin immunoblots and quantification. n = 3 independent cultures. Co-treat, co-treatment; pretreat, pretreatment. d–f, BAs were pretreated with vehicle or 11-DHC for 48 h, followed by NA (d), forskolin (e) or 8-BrcAMP (f) treatment for 30 min. Immunoblots and quantification of phosphorylated PKA substrates and β-actin are shown. n = 3 independent cultures. g, BAs were pretreated with vehicle or RU-486 for 1 h, followed by NA with or without DEX treatment for 24 h. Immunoblots and quantification of UCP1 and β-actin are shown. n = 4 independent cultures. h, Male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice (aged 10 weeks) were on a doxycycline chow diet for 1 week at 24 °C. BAT IF staining for GFP (green), RGS2 (red), perilipin (white) and DAPI (blue), and quantification of single- or double-positive BAs are shown. n = 4 per group. i, BAs were treated with vehicle or DEX for 2 h and subjected to ChIP using anti-GR antibody or control IgG. ChIP–qPCR analysis of Rgs2 promoter (−92 bp to +53 bp), presented as the percentage of input DNA. n = 4 per group. j, RT–qPCR analysis of Rgs2 in three-dimensionally cultured primary BAs, treated with vehicle, DEX, CL-316,243 or DEX + CL-316,243 for 24 h. n = 3 per group. k–m, BAs were reverse-transfected with Rgs2 or control dsiRNAs. k, Rgs2 mRNA was analysed 2 days after. Cells were then pretreated with 11-DHC for 24 h and stimulated with NA for 30 min. l,m, Immunoblots (l) and quantification (m) of phosphorylated PKA substrates and β-actin. n = 3 per group (k) and n = 4 per group (m). Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (a–h, j and m), unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-tests (i (GR) and k) and unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (i (IgG)); ***P < 0.001. NS, not significant. For a–g, i–k and m, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bar, 50 μm (h).

Forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase (AC) to generate cAMP26. 11-DHC pretreatment also blocked forskolin-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2c), suggesting inhibition of AC activity or downstream cAMP signalling. To determine where GR signalling acts within the canonical β-adrenergic receptor–cAMP–PKA pathway that controls UCP1 expression27, we measured PKA activity in in vitro-differentiated BAs after 24 h of 11-DHC pretreatment, followed by NA, forskolin or 8-BrcAMP (a cAMP derivative). 11-DHC pretreatment markedly reduced NA- or forskolin-induced PKA activity (Fig. 2d,e), but not the response to 8-BrcAMP (Fig. 2f), indicating that downstream cAMP signalling is not affected by GR activation. Thus, GR signalling potentially suppresses UCP1 expression by inhibiting AC-mediated cAMP production.

Whereas 11-DHC requires conversion to active glucocorticoids, dexamethasone (DEX) directly activates GR. In contrast to the delayed effect of 11-DHC, DEX suppressed NA-induced UCP1 expression after co-treatment (Fig. 2g), an effect that was abrogated by the GR antagonist mifepristone (RU-486) (Fig. 2g). Similarly, in the in vitro-differentiated BAs, CL-316,243 increased Ucp1 expression about 3-fold, whereas DEX pretreatment reduced this induction to about 1.6-fold (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Together, these data support the conclusion that GR activation maintains BA-L cells in a low-UCP1-expressing state by suppressing cAMP production.

We next investigated how GR signalling regulates BA heterogeneity. DEX is commonly used in adipogenic differentiation cocktails; its withdrawal increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.8-fold in BAs differentiated from BAT SVF of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Conversely, 11-DHC and the active glucocorticoid corticosterone decreased the BA-H/BA-L ratio compared with in the DEX-free control, independent of differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In WT mice, DEX induced BAT whitening and reduced the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 74% (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Thus, manipulating GR signalling alters BA heterogeneity both in vitro and in vivo.

To determine how GR signalling inhibits cAMP production, we examined other BA-L-enriched genes. Rgs2 was highly expressed in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f). RGS2 binds to the C1 domain of AC III, V and VI, attenuating Gαs-dependent cAMP accumulation28. IF staining confirmed selective RGS2 expression in BA-L cells, with 40% of BAs being UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2−, 55% UCP1−(GFP−)RGS2+ and 5% UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2+ (Fig. 2h). RGS2 was also selectively expressed in GFP− BA-L cells in in vitro-differentiated BAs (brown and beige) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Analysis of published GR chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by sequencing datasets29 identified GR occupancy within the promoter and intronic regions of Rgs2 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in in vitro-differentiated BAs confirmed GR binding at the Rgs2 promoter, which was enhanced by DEX (Fig. 2i). Lastly, DEX increased Rgs2 mRNA 2.2-fold in freshly isolated BAs (Fig. 2j), supporting Rgs2 as a GR target. Thus, RGS2 is a GR target in the BAs that inhibits cAMP production. Knocking down Rgs2 in in vitro-differentiated BAs (Fig. 2k) did not affect PKA activity in response to NA alone (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k). However, Rgs2 knockdown abrogated the inhibitory effect of 11-DHC pretreatment on NA-induced PKA substrate phosphorylation (Fig. 2l,m). Rgs2 is therefore a GR target in BAs that suppresses Ucp1 expression by inhibiting AC activity, and BA-L cells are stabilized in the low-thermogenic state through the GR–RGS2–AC signalling axis.

H6PD protein levels in BAT changed inversely with UCP1 across environmental temperatures, while GR protein was only slightly elevated at thermoneutrality (30 °C) (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cold exposure reduced H6PD protein by 1.8-fold in iWAT, but not in gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c), suggesting thermogenic-depot-specific regulation. CL-316,243 similarly decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). H6pd mRNA decreased rather than increased with rising temperature in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6e), indicating post-transcriptional regulation. Thus, H6PD protein levels, but not mRNA levels, change dynamically in BAT in response to fluctuating environmental temperatures, which may be essential for altering the BA-H/BA-L ratio in response to thermogenic demand.

Sympathetic neurons secrete NA to activate BA thermogenesis. We next tested whether sympathetic innervation mediates cold-induced H6PD protein reduction using unilateral BAT denervation, validated by reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) protein (Fig. 3a). Cold exposure increased BA-H cells from 31.1% to 85.6% (Fig. 3b), as previously reported6. Denervation prevented the cold-induced reduction of H6PD (Fig. 3a), and although there was an increase in the BA-H/BA-L ratio, the proportion of BA-H cells was 66% lower than the sham group during cold exposure (29.1% versus 85.6%) (Fig. 3b). The low BA-H/BA-L ratio was accompanied by BA whitening (Extended Data Fig. 6f), a feature associated with impaired thermogenesis30. Notably, H6PD consistently labelled BA-L cells regardless of the variable BA-H/BA-L ratio at different environmental temperatures (Fig. 3b). Thus, sympathetic innervation is required to reduce H6PD protein and raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio after cold exposure.

a,b, Male WT (a) or Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG (b) mice (aged 8 weeks) underwent sham (S) or unilateral BAT denervation (D). After 2 weeks of recovery, the mice were housed at 24 °C or 6 °C for 1 week (Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice received a doxycycline diet). a, Immunoblots and quantification of H6PD, TH, UCP1 and β-actin in BAT. b, BAT IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red) and DAPI (blue), and BA-H quantification. n = 3 per group (a) and n = 4 per group (b). c, Male WT mice (aged 10 weeks) were housed at 6 °C for 1 week, with or without subsequent housing at 30 °C for 1 week. Immunoblots and quantification of UCP1, H6PD, GR and β-actin are shown. n = 3 per group. d–k, After doxycycline (dox) diet feeding, Ucp1-Nr3c1flox/flox (Ucp1-rtTA;TRE-cre;Nr3c1flox/flox) mice become Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− (Ucp1-rtTA;TRE-cre;Nr3c1−/−), with Nr3c1 deleted in BA-H cells. TRE-Cre-negative littermates were used as controls. d, Male mice (aged 9 weeks (w)) were housed at 6 °C for 1 week, then fed a doxycycline diet at 6 °C for 1 week and then returned to 24 °C with continued feeding on a doxycycline diet. e, BAT IF staining for perilipin (green), GR (red) and DAPI (blue). Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− BAT exhibits a higher density and sinks. h, Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of BAT and iWAT. i, BAT IF staining for perilipin (green), UCP1 (red) and DAPI (blue). j,k, Energy expenditure (j) and body weight (k). n = 3 per group (f) and n = 7 per group (j and k). Statistics were computed using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (a and b), unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (c, f, j (average) and k) and two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple-comparison test (j (time-course curves and day–night)). For a–c, f, j and k, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bars, 50 μm (b, e, h (left) and i) and 1.2 mm (h (right)).

Cold exposure also downregulated GR target genes, including Rasd1, Fkbp5, Pik3r1, Tsc22d3 and Rgs2 in BAT, whereas denervation blunted these effects (Extended Data Fig. 6g), supporting the involvement of GR signalling in raising the BA-H/BA-L ratio. We next tested whether the opposite occurred when shifting mice from cold to thermoneutrality. H6PD protein increased 2.1-fold in BAT, while GR protein remained unchanged (Fig. 3c). Transitioning cold-exposed mice to 30 °C also restored GR target gene expression in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6h), indicating that H6PD and GR signalling dynamically respond to temperature fluctuations to regulate BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether blocking GR during the transition from cold to warmer temperatures prevents BA-H cells from switching to BA-L cells. We generated a BA-H-specific, inducible Nr3c1-knockout model by crossing Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Nr3c1flox/flox mice (Fig. 3d). Mice were first exposed to 6 °C for 1 week to raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio, followed by 1 week of doxycycline diet under cold conditions to induce Nr3c1 deletion in BA-H cells (Ucp1-Nr3c1flox/flox turning into Ucp1-Nr3c1−/−), and were then returned to room temperature with the doxycycline diet for another week. One week is long enough for the mice to reduce thermogenesis according to the rise in environmental temperature. IF staining confirmed Nr3c1 deletion in most BAs (Fig. 3e), consistent with 86% of BAs being BA-H cells during cold exposure (Fig. 3b), and western blotting showed reduced GR and RGS2 in isolated BAs (Fig. 3f). We previously showed that BA-H cells contain smaller lipid droplets and therefore have higher density, whereas BA-L cells have larger lipid droplets, lower density and float after mild centrifugation (like white adipocytes)6. Notably, BAT from Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice sank in PBS, whereas control BAT floated (Fig. 3g), suggesting a higher density and a higher BA-H/BA-L ratio. Consistently, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed browner BAT with smaller lipid droplets, increased iWAT beiging (Fig. 3h) and a higher proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 3i). Metabolic cage studies further showed increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption in Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice, without changes in body weight (Fig. 3j,k and Extended Data Fig. 6i), body composition, food intake, respiratory exchange ratio or locomotor activity (Extended Data Fig. 6j–n). As the controls were metabolically healthy young adults, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed no further improvements in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). These data highlight stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirements for GR signalling to regulate bistable BA states and thermogenesis. Inhibition of GR reactivation during the transition from cold to room temperature preserved a high BA-H/BA-L ratio and persistent thermogenesis despite reduced environmental thermogenic demand. These data not only confirm that we can block the BA-H-to-BA-L switch by inhibiting GR signalling, but also indicate that manipulating BA heterogeneity can increase thermogenesis and significantly boost whole-body energy expenditure.

To elucidate the sympathetic regulation of H6PD protein, we treated in vitro-differentiated BAs with NA but observed no change in H6PD protein (Fig. 4a), suggesting that other cell types and factors are involved in sympathetic regulation of H6PD. We next assessed cytokine expression in BAT and found that Il1b exhibited the greatest reduction (by 53%) after cold exposure (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), and the greatest induction (by 3.3-fold) when mice were shifted from cold to thermoneutrality (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7b). Cold-induced Il1b suppression was blunted by BAT sympathetic denervation (Fig. 4b), while NA reduced Il1b expression in BAT explants (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Il1b was predominantly expressed in SVFs rather than in mature adipocytes (Fig. 4d) and its expression changed with environmental temperature (Fig. 4d). qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) analysis further confirmed the predominant expression of Il1b in CD45+ SVFs (Fig. 4e), indicating an immune cell source. By contrast, systemic IL-1β levels remained unchanged across environmental temperatures, suggesting local regulation of IL-1β levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 7d).
