Notably, IF staining revealed that BA-L cells clustered around IL-1β puncta, whereas BA-H cells formed clusters further away (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 7e), a pattern that was observed across room temperature, during cold exposure and after denervation (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Quantification indicated that IL-1β puncta and GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) show a significant negative Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC = −0.5 ± 0.1), suggesting a mutually exclusive pattern between these two factors at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 7f). During cold exposure, this pattern persisted but was weaker (PCC = −0.2 ± 0.1), as fewer IL-1β puncta were available for quantification (Extended Data Fig. 7f). BAT denervation prevented the reduction in IL-1β puncta, maintained a low BA-H/BA-L ratio and preserved a strong negative correlation with GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) (PCC = −0.45 ± 0.1). Thus, across all three conditions, BA-L cells were consistently close to IL-1β puncta, indicating a strong correlation between IL-1β and BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether IL-1β regulates H6PD protein levels in BAs. Among the proinflammatory cytokines tested, TNF and IL-1β increased H6PD protein levels by 1.8- and 3.5-fold, respectively (Fig. 4g), without increasing H6pd mRNA (Extended Data Fig. 7g), confirming a post-transcriptional regulation of H6PD. Combined IL-1β, TNF and IFNγ treatment did not further increase H6PD protein beyond the effect of IL-1β alone (Fig. 4g). IL-1β increased H6PD protein in a time-dependent manner (Fig. 4h). During cycloheximide (CHX) treatment, H6PD abundance decreased by 30% and 50% at 6 and 12 h, respectively, whereas IL-1β prevented this decline (Fig. 4i), indicating increased H6PD protein stability from degradation. IL-1β is known to activate multiple downstream pathways, including JNK, MEK–ERK, p38–MAPK and IKK–NF-κB. Among inhibitors targeting these pathways, only the MEK and ERK inhibitor U0126 attenuated IL-1β-induced H6PD upregulation (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i), indicating that MEK–ERK mediates IL-1β-induced H6PD stability.

We next examined whether IL-1β regulates UCP1 expression. IL-1β did not alter UCP1 expression in the in vitro-differentiated BAs in the absence of 11-DHC, but reduced UCP1 protein levels by 53% in the presence of 11-DHC (Extended Data Fig. 7j,k), indicating that IL-1β suppresses UCP1 through GR signalling.

Adipose-tissue-resident immune cells can regulate sympathetic innervation31,32,33. However, TH and synaptophysin staining showed similar sympathetic innervation of BA-H cells and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m), indicating that IL-1β regulates BA heterogeneity independently of differential sympathetic innervation.

To identify the immune cells that secrete IL-1β in BAT, we integrated multiple published BAT scRNA-seq datasets14,34,35,36,37 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). β-Adrenergic receptors were expressed in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), suggesting potential sympathetic regulation. Subclustering analysis revealed that Il1b was enriched in neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−CXCR2+), monocytes (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−Ly6C+), and macrophages (CD45+CD11b+F4/80+) (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). Flow cytometry confirmed that IL-1β was mainly produced by CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b), with IL-1β+ cells predominantly comprising neutrophils and macrophages, but not monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 9c–e). IL-1β+ cells represented 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages, indicating that IL-1β production is restricted to specific subsets (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Despite the low frequency, the greater abundance of macrophages resulted in substantial numbers of IL-1β+ macrophages, with IL-1β+ neutrophils only 1.7-fold more abundant (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that both cell types are major IL-1β sources. IF staining further confirmed IL-1β colocalization with subsets of CXCR2+ neutrophils and F4/80+ macrophages in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g).

Depletion of CD45+ immune cells from BAT SVFs increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.7-fold without affecting overall differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j), supporting a role for immune cells in regulating BA heterogeneity. To further confirm the role of local IL-1β in thermogenic regulation, we injected lentivirus encoding Il1rn (encoding IL-1RA), a naturally occurring inhibitor of IL-1 receptor signalling, or an mCherry control directly into BAT (Extended Data Fig. 10a). IL-1RA increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio twofold in mice housed at room temperature (Fig. 4j,k). In in vitro-differentiated BAs, Il1r knockdown attenuated IL-1β-mediated suppression of UCP1 expression, indicating a direct effect of IL-1β on BAs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Moreover, in vivo pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β production using the caspase-1 inhibitor VX-765 increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.2-fold (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d), further demonstrating a functional role for IL-1β in regulating BA heterogeneity.

We next investigated how temperature fluctuations regulate IL-1β in BAT. Il1b expression in primary BAT SVFs was temperature-dependent (Fig. 4d), whereas IL-1β+ immune cell numbers remained unchanged across housing temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 10e–h), indicating regulation independent of immune cell recruitment. NA directly suppressed Il1b expression in BAT-derived CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 10i), suggesting adrenergic regulation of IL-1β production. Consistent with adrenergic receptor expression in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), scRNA-seq analysis showed selective expression of Adrb1 and Adrb2, but not α-adrenergic receptor genes, in Il1b-expressing immune cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 11a). We further examined adrenergic regulation of Il1b using bone marrow-derived neutrophils. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced Il1b expression dose dependently (Extended Data Fig. 11b), whereas NA pretreatment suppressed this induction in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). This effect was reversed by the non-selective β-adrenergic receptor antagonist propranolol, but not by the non-selective α-adrenergic receptor antagonist phenoxybenzamine (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Consistently, propranolol administration, but not phenoxybenzamine, increased Il1b expression in BAT in vivo (Extended Data Fig. 11g,h), supporting β-adrenergic suppression of IL-1β production.

Decreased BA thermogenesis has been reported with obesity38 and ageing3. However, high fat diet- (HFD)-induced obese mice were completely cold-tolerant, with 100% survival after 7 days of cold exposure (Fig. 5a,b). HFD feeding decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels (Fig. 5c), indicating preserved BAT thermogenic potential. By contrast, aged mice exhibited cold intolerance, with reduced body temperature and a 25% mortality within the first 2 days (Fig. 5d,e), suggesting impaired thermogenesis. Aged mice showed a 2.3-fold increase in H6PD and a 40% decrease in UCP1 (Fig. 5f), suggesting a reduced BA-H/BA-L ratio. GR was modestly reduced by HFD feeding but unchanged with ageing. These differences suggest that cold-induced thermogenesis is more severely impaired with ageing than with obesity at a young age, and that the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying impaired thermogenesis may differ substantially.

In young Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice, BA-H cells increased from 28.8% at 24 °C to 61.7% and 89.7% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively. In aged mice, the baseline BA-H/BA-L ratio at 24 °C was extremely low (0.31%), and BA-H cells increased to 15% and 50.9% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively (Fig. 5g,h), suggesting delayed BA bistable regulation in response to cold stimulation. H6PD progressively decreased during cold exposure in both young and aged mice (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 11i), but its level at cold exposure in aged mice was comparable to that in young mice at 24 °C (Extended Data Fig. 11i). UCP1 was also reduced in aged mice, consistent with the lower BA-H/BA-L ratio (Extended Data Fig. 11i). Despite increased BA-L abundance, cold-induced TNAP expression was also blunted with age, although TNAP remained enriched in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 11j), suggesting impaired futile creatine cycle activation. Aged mice also exhibited a 1.8-fold increase in BAT corticosterone (the active form of glucocorticoid in mice) in BAT, but not serum corticosterone (Extended Data Fig. 11k,l), and a sixfold increase in BAT Il1b expression arising from SVFs (Extended Data Fig. 11m,n). Together, these results suggest that elevated local IL-1β and H6PD-mediated overactivation of the GR–RGS2–AC axis lower the BA-H/BA-L ratio, therefore impairing cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice.

Lastly, we investigated whether GR inhibition could restore BA bistable regulation and thermogenesis in aged mice. One week of RU-486 treatment increased the proportion of BA-H cells in aged mice from 0.5% to 8.3% at room temperature and from 10.6% to 32.8% after 1 day of cold exposure (Fig. 5j–m). RU-486 also reduced lipid droplet accumulation within BAs and improved BAT whitening (Fig. 5n), increased rectal temperature during the cold tolerance test and reduced body weight in the first few days of cold exposure (Extended Data Fig. 11o,p). Metabolic cage studies revealed that RU-486 treatment increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption across the day–night cycle, without changes in respiratory exchange ratio, locomotor activity or food intake (Extended Data Fig. 11q–u). Thus, GR antagonism increases energy expenditure in aged mice, potentially due to elevated UCP1-dependent thermogenesis in BAT.

We found that the two BA subtypes are spatially organized and tightly regulated. IL-1β stabilizes surrounding BAs in the low-thermogenic state (BA-L cells) by extending H6PD protein half-life. H6PD facilitates active glucocorticoid production, which suppresses UCP1 expression through the GR–RGS2–AC axis (Extended Data Fig. 12a). BAs further from IL-1β puncta are stabilized in the high-thermogenic state (BA-H cells) with low H6PD protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 12b). During cold stimulation, activated sympathetic neurons secrete NA, which suppresses IL-1β production by immune cells. Low IL-1β levels promote H6PD degradation and switch BA-L cells into BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). After cold stimulation, this process is reversed, restoring a lower BA-H/BA-L ratio. Age impairs the flexibility to alter BA heterogeneity due to IL-1β overload in BAT, which significantly contributes to the age-related decline in thermogenesis (Extended Data Fig. 12b).

The advantages of this spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity are multifaceted. First, it enables a dual-layered response: an immediate, acute response through readily active BA-H cells, and a longer-term, chronic response that involves shifting cellular heterogeneity. Second, it facilitates communication between different cell types through spatial proximity, thereby integrating stimuli from multiple systems, combining environmental and internal cues, and enabling precise regulation of cell states. Third, shifting between BA-H and BA-L states preserves BAs from oxidative damage associated with sustained high thermogenesis.

Although this study primarily focused on UCP1-dependent thermogenesis, UCP1-independent mechanisms are also critical for thermogenic adipose tissue function and whole-body metabolic homeostasis39,40,41. We observed that TNAP, a key component of the futile creatine cycle, is enriched in BA-L cells. Cold exposure increased the proportion of BA-H cells while inducing CKB and TNAP expression in BAT42, reflecting enhanced futile creatine cycle activity either specifically in BA-L cells or across all BAs, with BA-L cells retaining higher activity. Importantly, cold-induced TNAP expression was compromised with age, while remaining enriched in BA-L cells. These results suggest that both UCP1- and futile creatine cycle-dependent thermogenesis are impaired with age.

BAT has long been recognized as a target organ for glucocorticoids, but their precise role remains unclear. Some studies indicate that glucocorticoids suppress UCP1 expression and/or BAT activity43,44,45,46, whereas others reach the opposite conclusions47,48,49. Glucocorticoids have also been implicated in warm-induced beige adipocyte whitening50. This study shows that GR signalling in BAT regulates BA heterogeneity by locking BAs in the BA-L state and reducing their responsiveness to NA. Active glucocorticoid levels are regulated locally, independent of systemic levels25. Thus, systemic glucocorticoid treatments may not alter active glucocorticoid levels in individual BAs, potentially explaining previous conflicting observations. Importantly, inducible GR deletion in BAs during the transition from cold to room temperature sustained the high BA-H/BA-L ratio and thermogenesis. The stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirement of GR signalling explains why Nr3c1-knockout mice do not exhibit altered BAT development or thermogenesis51,52, and indicates that targeting GR at selective timing could profoundly manipulate thermogenic activity.

Our study showed that BA heterogeneity is determined by communication from sympathetic neurons to immune cells, rather than by direct communication from sympathetic neurons to BAs. NA, the primary neurotransmitter from sympathetic nerves, has been shown to modulate immune cell response by regulating cytokine production by immune cells in the liver and adipose tissue53,54. We found that NA directly suppresses Il1b production in immune cells through β-adrenergic signalling, thereby modulating BA heterogeneity. Notably, a recent study showed that cold-induced β3-adrenergic activation transiently recruits neutrophils predominantly to white adipose tissue (WAT), particularly the visceral depot55. These infiltrating neutrophils produce IL-1β, which suppresses local lipolysis by attenuating cAMP-dependent signalling, thereby limiting excessive lipid mobilization. Based on our findings in BAT, IL-1β may similarly suppress lipolysis through the H6PD–GR–RGS2–AC axis in white adipocytes. Notably, Il1b expression in WAT exhibits transient kinetics, peaking at 12 h after stimulation and returning to basal levels at 24 h. Given that NA suppresses Il1b expression in BAT, it may similarly suppress Il1b expression in newly infiltrated neutrophils in WAT.

It remains unclear why in vitro-differentiated BAs exhibit heterogeneity. BAs may intrinsically differentiate into cells with varying UCP1 levels to preserve thermogenic flexibility or maintain metabolic balance. Cross-talk between BAs and IL-1β+ immune cells in vivo may further reinforce and spatially organize this heterogeneity. Alternatively, IL-1β+ immune cells in SVFs during differentiation may influence the local environment. Indeed, depletion of CD45+ immune cells from SVFs before differentiation substantially increased the proportion of BA-H cells, suggesting that SVF immune cells reduce the BA-H/BA-L ratio. Future efforts with cell type-specific receptor knockout mouse models will help to validate and further elucidate how sympathetic innervation regulates IL-1β secretion and how IL-1β regulates H6PD protein stability.

Decline of thermogenesis and age-related adiposity56 contribute to age-related metabolic disorders. Previous studies suggest that reduction in thermogenic activity may be due to impaired beige adipogenesis5,57, declined mitochondrial fuel oxidation3, reduced adrenergic receptors, altered other master regulators of thermogenesis58 and compromised sympathetic innervation due to infiltration of senescent immune cells59. Our study showed that Il1b is increased in aged BAT, consistent with previous studies reporting increased immune cell infiltration and upregulated cytokines in aged BAT59. Increased IL-1β stabilized large amounts of BAs in the BA-L state and suppressed thermogenesis in aged mice. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of GR signalling by a GR antagonist raised the BA-H/BA-L ratio and improved cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice, indicating that BA-specific GR signalling could be targeted to correct age-related cold intolerance and significantly increase basal metabolism. However, given the systemic effects of RU-486 (ref. 60), other tissues and cell types may also contribute. Future efforts will focus on the effects of targeted inhibition of GR signalling specifically in thermogenic cells.

All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of City of Hope (protocol 17014). Mice were maintained under a 12 h–12 h dark–light cycle in a temperature-controlled facility with ad libitum access to water and food. The diets included a standard chow diet (5053, Lab diet), an HFD (D12492, Research Diets) and a chow diet supplemented with 600 mg per kg doxycycline (S4107, Bio-Serv), as described for individual experiments. The Ucp1-rtTA mouse line was generated as previously described15,61. The Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mouse line was created by Biocytogen through microinjection of CRISPR components and a donor vector into C57BL/6J zygotes. The single guide RNA targeted the junction of the exon 6 coding region and 3′ untranslated region (UTR) (CTTCCTCCAAGTTGCTTATG + TGG) of the Ucp1 gene, and a P2A-mGFP cassette was inserted at the 5′ end of the 3′ UTR, immediately upstream of the Ucp1 gene stop codon. TRE-Cre (B6.Cg-Tg(tetO-cre)1Jaw/J, 006234), Rosa26-loxp-STOP-loxp-mT/mG (B6.129(Cg)-Gt (ROSA)26Sortm4(ACTB-tdTomato,-eGFP) Luo/J, 007676) and Nr3c1-floxed (B6.Cg-Nr3c1tm1.1Jda/J, 021021) mouse lines were purchased from the Jackson Laboratories. To generate mice lacking GR proteins selectively in BAs, Ucp1-rtTA and TRE-Cre mice were crossed with Nr3c1-floxed mice. Littermates lacking TRE-Cre were used as control mice. All mice were maintained on a pure C57BL/6J background. The sample sizes for animal experiments were determined based on previous studies. Experimental groups were randomly assigned. Investigators were blinded to group allocation during rectal temperature measurement, but blinding was not feasible for other experiments.

Unilateral denervation of BAT was performed as previously described62. In brief, 8-week-old male mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane and placed onto a warm surgical platform. The interscapular surgical region was shaved and sterilized with 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol and iodine. A 1 cm lateral incision was made from the scapula to the neck, and the interscapular BAT depot was carefully detached from the underlying muscle layer and retracted cranially over the head using toothed forceps. Five branches of the intercostal sympathetic nerve bundles innervating the left and right BAT lobes were exposed. Unilateral denervation was achieved by cutting the nerve bundles on the left side, while the right nerve bundles were exposed and touched as a sham-operated control. The BAT lobes were repositioned, and the incision was closed using absorbable 5.0 sutures. Mice were allowed to recover for 2 weeks before undergoing further experimental procedures.

To construct the H6pd-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse H6pd complementary DNA (cDNA) (NM_173371.4) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. To construct the Il1rn-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse Il1rn cDNA (NM_031167.5) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. The PCR products were cleaved with BamH I and Sal I and ligated into the pLenti-mCherry vector (36084, Addgene) to generate the pLenti-mH6pd lentiviral vector or pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral vector. Lentiviral particles were produced by co-transfecting HEK293T (ATCC) cells with the pLenti-mCherry, pLenti-mH6pd, or pLenti-mIl1rn transfer plasmids, along with the packaging psPAX2 (12260, Addgene) and envelope plasmids pMD2.G (12259, Addgene) at a 1:1:1 ratio, using PEI (1 μg DNA to 3 µl PEI). HEK293T cells were not independently authenticated but were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination, with negative results. After 72 h, the supernatant containing lentiviral particles was collected, filtered through a 0.45-μm PES filter and concentrated using the Lenti-X concentrator (631232, Takara Bio). The concentrated lentivirus was resuspended in PBS, stored at −80 °C and titrated using an RT-PCR Titration kit (631235, Takara Bio). Lentivirus administration in BAT was performed as described previously63. In brief, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP or Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane. A small lateral incision (~0.5–0.8 cm) was made in the interscapular area to expose BAT. Then 10–20 μl of either pLenti-mH6pd lentivirus, pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral or a negative control lentivirus (109 IFU ml−1) was directly injected at three distinct sites into each interscapular BAT lobe.

For three-dimensional fluorescence imaging of BAT, we used the Adipo-Clear method as described previously64. In brief, 8-week-old male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were fed a doxycycline diet for 3 days at 24 °C. Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with cold PBS containing 100 U ml−1 heparin (H3149, Sigma-Aldrich), followed by ice-cold 4% PFA. The BAT was then dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA at 4 °C overnight. After fixation, the tissue was washed with PBS, trimmed and delipidated using a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by 100% dichloromethane. After delipidation, the BAT was washed with a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by PTwH buffer. The sample was then incubated with primary rabbit anti-TH polyclonal antibody (1:200, ab152, Abcam) or rabbit anti-synaptophysin antibody (1:200, ab32127, Abcam) along with chicken anti-GFP antibody (1:200, ab13970, Abcam), diluted in PTxwH buffer at room temperature for 3 days. After incubation with primary antibodies, the sample was washed with PTxwH buffer and then incubated with secondary antibodies: Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research) secondary antibodies at room temperature for 3 days. The sample was dehydrated through a series of methanol and 100% dichloromethane and then cleared with dibenzyl ether. Three-dimensional imaging of the cleared BAT was performed using tile scanning with a confocal laser-scanning microscope (LSM 880, Zeiss) at ×10 and ×20 magnifications, with image acquisition and analysis conducted using the Zeiss Zen black software.

The SVF of BAT was isolated from the interscapular BAT of mice on postnatal day 7, while the SVF from iWAT was obtained from 5-week-old male mice. In brief, dissected BAT or iWAT was minced and digested for 45 min at 37 °C in a digestion buffer containing 1.5 mg ml−1 collagenase D (11088882001, Sigma-Aldrich) in an isolation buffer (0.123 M NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 1.3 mM CaCl2, 5 mM glucose, 100 mM HEPES and 4% BSA). The cell–tissue mixture was filtered through a 70-μm cell strainer (08-771-2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested fragments, then centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in growth medium (DMEM, 10566016 Life Technologies; 1% penicillin–streptomycin, SV30010 Hyclone; 0.1% gentamicin, 1855724 Life Technologies and 20 mM HEPES, Sigma-Aldrich, H3537) containing 20% FBS (16H328, Sigma-Aldrich) and filtered again through a 40-μm cell strainer (08-771-1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove clumps and adipocytes. The flow-through was centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C, and the SVF pellet was resuspended in SVF growth medium and plated onto a 12-well tissue culture plate for RNA and protein extraction or onto a 35 mm glass-bottom tissue culture dish for IF staining. For differentiation into brown and beige adipocytes, SVF cells were switched to fresh induction medium (DMEM plus DEX (1 μM), insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), isobutylmethylxanthine (0.5 mM), T3 (1 nM), indomethacin (0.125 mM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS on day 0 (2 days after reaching confluence). After 2 days, the medium was replaced with maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS, and this maintenance medium was changed every 2 days until further use.

For glucocorticoid treatment, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described. During differentiation, cells were treated with or without 1 μM corticosterone (16063, Cayman Chemical), 1 μM DEX (D4902, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM 11-DHC (32907, Cayman Chemical) in the induction medium. On differentiation day 6, the density of GFP fluorescence was assessed under a microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence) to quantify the BA-H/BA-L ratio. For the PKA activity assay, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs differentiated were pretreated with 1 μM 11-DHC or vehicle for 48 h, followed by incubation with 1 μM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM forskolin (F6886, Sigma-Aldrich) or 500 μM 8-Br-cAMP (B7880, Sigma-Aldrich) for 30 min. PKA activity was measured by western blot analysis using antibodies specific to phosphorylated PKA substrates. For the H6PD half-life assay, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs were pretreated with 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β (401-ML-005, R&D Systems) or vehicle for 4 h, followed by exposure to 50 µg ml−1 CHX (C1988, Sigma-Aldrich) with IL-1β or saline for various timepoints (0, 3, 6 and 12 h) at 37 °C, with H6PD quantified by western blot analysis. For cytokine treatment, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β, 20 ng ml−1 TNF (410-MT-010, R&D Systems) and 10 ng ml−1 IFNγ (485-MI-100, R&D Systems) alone or in combination for 48 h. For IL-1β signalling inhibition, BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β or IL-1β in combination with 10 μM p38 kinase inhibitor SB203580 (559395, Sigma-Aldrich), 5 μM NF-κB inhibitor BAY11-7082 (196871, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM JNK inhibitor SP600125 (420119, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM ERK inhibitor U0126 (662005, Sigma-Aldrich) or 5 mM IKKβ inhibitor aspirin (A5376, Sigma-Aldrich) for 48 h, with inhibitors administered 1 h before IL-1β treatment. To test the effect of IL-1β on UCP1 expression, BAs on day 6 were switched to culture medium containing charcoal-stripped FBS and then treated with vehicle or 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β for 48 h in the absence or presence of 1 μM 11-DHC. For DEX and RU-486 treatment, the BAs on day 6 were pretreated with vehicle or 10 μM RU-486 for 1 h, followed by treatment with 1 μM NA in the presence or absence of 1 μM DEX for 24 h. The concentrations of UCP1, H6PD and β-actin were quantified by western blot analysis. To assess the effect of immune cells on BAs heterogeneity, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described, with or without CD45+ immune cells. CD45+ immune cells were depleted from SVFs using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies).

Mature BAs from the interscapular BAT of 10-week-old male mice were obtained as described before. In brief, BATs were dissected, cleaned of contaminating muscle and WAT, minced into small pieces, and digested in collagenase-dispase buffer (17703034, Gibco) for 1 h at 37 °C with shaking at 110 r.p.m. The cell suspension was filtered through 100-μm cell strainers (08-771-19, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested tissues, washed with 3 volumes of DMEM/F12 medium (10565018, Life Technologies) containing 10% FBS and centrifuged at 100g for 5 min at room temperature. The floating BAs were transferred and resuspended in PBS wash buffer three times. After quantification, 5 × 105 BAs were suspended in Matrigel (Corning, CB-40234C) at a 1:1 volume ratio and seeded into 6-well tissue culture dishes. The plates were incubated at 37 °C for 15 min to induce gel formation. Maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS was then added to the wells with either vehicle, 1 μM DEX, 10 μM CL-316,243 (C5976, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM DEX combined with 10 μM CL-316,243 for 24 h. For the separation of BA-H and BA-L cells, we modified our previous protocol6 by adding additional steps to further deplete contaminating SVFs in BA-L cells. In brief, floating BAs were collected as BA-L cells, and the pellet containing BA-H cells and SVF was further separated using the EasyPlate magnet-based method. The cell suspension was incubated with PE-conjugated antibodies against immune cells (PE-anti-CD45, 103106, BioLegend), endothelial cells (PE-anti-CD31, 102408, BioLegend), fibroblasts (PE-anti-CD140a, 135905, BioLegend) and pericytes (PE-anti-CD146, 134704, BioLegend) and processed using EasySep reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Freshly isolated BA-H and BA-L cells (1 × 105 per condition) were incubated in tracing medium (D5030, Sigma-Aldrich) containing either 5 mM [U-13C]glucose or 0.5 mM [U-13C]palmitate for 2 h and 6 h. After incubation, cells were washed with NaCl and collected with cold 50% methanol as before22,23. Metabolites were extracted and analysed by GC–MS.

Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with PBS, followed by 10% formalin fixative buffer. The interscapular BAT, iWAT and gWAT were carefully dissected and post-fixed in 10% formalin buffer overnight at 4 °C. After dehydration, paraffin embedding and sectioning, tissue sections were stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E).

For human samples, adipose tissue was collected during thyroid surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. Supraclavicular adipose tissue was removed as waste biological material from subjects undergoing surgery at the General Hospital (AOU; Ancona, Italy) for thyroid diseases. Ethical approval was obtained from the specific Commission within the Azienda Ospedaliero Universitaria delle Marche (University Hospital of the Marche Region). The ethical approval protocol code is 208156. Immediately after removal, tissue pieces were fixed overnight at 4 °C by immersion in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). They were then dehydrated, cleared and paraffin embedded. Sections from three levels (100 μm apart) were stained with H&E to assess morphology and BAT presence for UCP1-immunohistochemistry.

For IF staining of mouse and human tissues, paraffin-embedded sections of Ucp1-mGFP and Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice and human BAT slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated using a graded ethanol series to double-distilled H2O. The slides were immersed in 10 mM sodium citrate buffer (C9999, Sigma-Aldrich) and boiled for 30 min for antigen retrieval, then blocked in PBST containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% BSA. Primary antibodies used were as follows: perilipin (1:500, NB100-60554, Novus and ab61682, Abcam), UCP1 (1:200, ab23841, Abcam and MAB6158, R&D Systems), GFP (1:200, ab13970, Abcam; and 2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), mCherry (1:200, ab167453, Abcam), H6PD (1:200, ab170895, Abcam; and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), TNAP (1:200, AF2910, R&D Systems), GR (1:200, 12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), RGS2 (1:200, NBP1-32284, Novus), IL-1RA (1:100, MA5-35068, Thermo Fisher Scientific), IL-1β (1:50, AF-401-NA, R&D Systems), F4/80 (1:100, ab6640, Abcam) and CXCR2 (1:100, 20634-1-AP, Proteintech). Secondary antibodies (1:200 dilution) used were Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (A31571, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31572, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A32814, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rat IgG (H+L) (A48270, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A21447, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research). Slides were counterstained with 1 μg ml−1 DAPI (D9542, Sigma-Aldrich) and mounted with prolonged Anti-Fade mounting medium (P36931, Invitrogen). Bright-field and fluorescence images were acquired using an inverted fluorescence phase-contrast microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence).

Fluorescence microscopy images were acquired for three experimental conditions: room temperature, cold exposure and cold exposure with denervation. For each condition, dual-channel fluorescence images were collected with UCP1 labelled in the green channel and IL-1β labelled in the magenta channel, along with corresponding autofluorescence reference images for cellular region identification. All image analysis was performed using custom Python scripts using the tifffile, numpy, scipy and pandas libraries. To restrict analysis to cellular regions and exclude background artifacts, autofluorescence images were Gaussian-smoothed and used to generate binary masks with a threshold of 50 arbitrary units applied to autofluorescence intensity values65, ensuring that correlation analysis was performed exclusively on biologically relevant areas. To eliminate low-intensity noise and focus analysis on meaningful fluorescence signals, intensity-based thresholds were applied to both channels: UCP1 (green channel) at 70 arbitrary units and IL-1β (magenta channel) at 20 arbitrary units. Pixels were retained for analysis if they exceeded the threshold in either channel, using a logical OR to preserve regions with specific labelling while maintaining sensitivity to differential expression patterns. Co-localization between UCP1 and IL-1β was quantified using the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), calculated pixel-wise across filtered cellular regions66. After masking and thresholding, images were vectorized by flattening two-dimensional pixel arrays into one-dimensional arrays. The PCC was computed using scipy.stats, providing both the correlation coefficient and associated P value for each image pair. Statistical comparisons between experimental conditions were performed using Welch’s t-tests for independent samples with unequal variances. This approach accounts for potential differences in variance between experimental groups while providing robust statistical inference. Results were compiled into structured data frames and visualized using bar plots with error bars.

Total RNA was extracted from tissues or cultured cells using either TRIzol reagent (15596026, Thermo Fisher Scientific) or RNAqueous-Micro Total RNA Isolation Kit (AM1931, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The first-strand cDNA was synthesized using the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (1708891, Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR was performed using the SYBR Green PCR system (A25742, Applied Biosystems) with Tbp as the internal control. A list of all of the primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Adipose tissues, cultured adipocytes and isolated mature BAs were collected and lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (20-188, Sigma-Aldrich) containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (P5726, P0044, Sigma-Aldrich). The extracted protein samples were loaded onto and separated on a 4–15% gradient SDS–PAGE TGX stain-free gel (4568086, Bio-Rad) and transferred to a PVDF membrane (1620177, Bio-Rad). The membranes were incubated with specific primary antibodies against H6PD (ab170895, Abcam and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), UCP1 (ab23841, Abcam), GFP (2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), phosphorylated PKA substrates (RRXS*/T*) (9624S, Cell Signaling Technology), TH (ab152, Abcam), TNAP (AF2910, R&D Systems), CKB (18713-1-AP, Proteintech), GR (12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), IL-1R1 (PA5-97866, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and β-actin (4970 and 58169, Cell Signaling Technology). HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1706515, Bio-Rad) and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1706516, Bio-Rad) were used as secondary antibodies. The immunoreactive signals were detected using the Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (32209, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent substrate (34577, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

Mature BAs were reverse-transfected with dsiRNA as described previously67. In brief, on differentiation day 5, BAT-derived primary BAs were trypsinized using 0.25% trypsin (25200, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min. The cells were then resuspended in culture medium and seeded onto gelatin-coated cell culture plates that had been pre-incubated with a pool of 50 nM H6pd dsiRNAs, 50 nM Rgs2 dsiRNAs, 50 nM Il1r1 dsiRNAs or relevant control dsiRNAs (Integrated DNA Technologies), mixed with 5 μl ml−1 of Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (13778075, Thermo Fisher Scientific) diluted in Opti-MEM medium (31985070, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The final density of BAs was 2.5 × 105 cells per cm2 of culture plate. Mature BAs were treated or collected 2 days after transfection. A list of all of the dsiRNA sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Mice were housed individually in temperature- and light-controlled rodent incubators (Powers Scientific) set to either thermoneutrality (30 °C) or cold (6 °C), with ad libitum access to food and water. For the β3-adrenoceptor agonist treatment experiment, mice were maintained at thermoneutrality for 1 week, followed by daily intraperitoneal injections of CL-316,243 in PBS at 1 mg per kg body weight for an additional 7 days. For adrenoceptor antagonist treatment, mice were exposed at 6 °C for 16 h, followed by intraperitoneal injections of propranolol (10 mg per kg; P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or phenoxybenzamine hydrochloride (5 mg per kg; HY-B043A, MedChemExpress) in PBS for 4 h.

For flow cytometry analysis, SVF cells were blocked with anti-mouse-CD16/32 (1:500, 101302, BioLegend) for 10 min, and then stained with anti-mouse-CD45-BV605 (1:400, 103155, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD11b-APC (1:100, 101212, BioLegend), anti-mouse-F4/80-488 (1:100, 123120, BioLegend), anti-mouse-Ly6C-PE/Cy7 (1:400, 128018, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CXCR2-PE (1:20, 149304, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD3-488 (1:100, 100210, BioLegend) and anti-mouse-CD19-PE (1:200, 152408, BioLegend) for individual experiments for 20 min on ice. After antibody incubation, the cells were washed once with 2% FBS–PBS. For intracellular staining, cells were stained with LIVE–DEAD fixable dead cell stain (65-0868-14, Invitrogen) for 30 min on ice. After washing with PBS, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a fixation/permeabilization kit (554714, BD bioscience) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, cells were fixed with fixation–permeabilization solution for 15 min on ice, followed by a wash with PBS and 1× perm–wash buffer. Cells were stained with anti-mouse-IL-1β-APC/eFluor 780 (1:80, 47-7114-82, Invitrogen) in 1× perm–wash buffer for 30 min on ice. After staining, cells were washed once with 1× perm–wash buffer and analysed by BD Fortessa cytometer. The flow plots were analysed by FlowJo (v.10).

Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were subcutaneously (s.c.) injected with either vehicle or 5 mg per kg per day water-soluble DEX (D2915, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in PBS for 2 weeks. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were maintained on doxycycline chow diet and administered vehicle or VX-765 (HY-13205, MedChemExpress, 50 mg per kg per day), dissolved in 20% (v/v) Cremophor EL, through daily intraperitoneal injection for 1 week. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG or WT mice aged 70–75 weeks were injected s.c. with 60 mg per kg mifepristone (RU-486) (HY-13683, MedChemExpress) dissolved in DMSO–corn oil or with DMSO–corn oil alone daily as controls for 1 week. Body temperature was recorded daily throughout the treatment period. After the final RU-486 or vehicle injection, mice were individually housed and exposed to a cold environment (6 °C). Rectal temperatures were measured at the indicated timepoints using a rodent thermometer (Bioseb, TK8851). For metabolic phenotyping, 72-week-old male WT mice were s.c. injected with either vehicle or RU-486 (60 mg per kg per day) for 1 week, followed by metabolic phenotyping with continuing daily vehicle or RU-486 injection for an additional 3 days. During the metabolic cage study, energy expenditure, oxygen consumption, RER, locomotor activity and food intake were recorded. At the end point, the mice were perfused with PBS and 10% formalin and processed for H&E and IF staining as described above.

Male Ucp1-rtTA;TRE-cre;Nr3c1flox/flox or control littermates aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline diet at 6 °C for 1 week, then continued for an additional week after being moved back to 24 °C, followed by glucose tolerance tests and insulin tolerance tests. For the glucose tolerance test, mice were fasted for 12 h before intraperitoneal injection of glucose (2 g per kg body weight). For the insulin tolerance test, mice were fasted for 6 h before intraperitoneal injection of insulin (0.75 U kg−1, Eli Lilly). Tail vein blood samples were collected at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after injection, and blood glucose levels were measured using a Contour glucometer (Bayer).

BAT depots were dissected from the interscapular BAT of male C57BL/6J mice exposed to 30 °C for 1 week and minced into 1–2 mm3 explants. The explants were washed three times with PBS and transferred to a six-well plate containing DMEM with 10% FBS. BAT SVFs were isolated as described above, and CD45+ immune cells were enriched using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Explants were incubated in saline or 10 mM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 h and CD45+ immune cells were treated with saline or NA (1 μM) for 4 h. After incubation, explants and CD45+ cells were collected for RNA extraction.

Bone marrow neutrophils were isolated from 10-week-old male WT mice. In brief, femurs and tibias were flushed with PBS containing 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS using a 23-gauge needle, and the cell suspension was filtered through a 70-μm strainer. Cells were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min, and the pellet was resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (R7757, Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 min at room temperature, followed by neutralization with PBS containing 2% FBS. Neutrophils were enriched using PE-anti-Ly6G antibody (127608, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Neutrophils were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 2% FBS. Neutrophils were stimulated with LPS (0–1,000 ng ml−1; L4391, Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h or pretreated with NA (0–10 μM) for 30 min before 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For time-dependent experiments, neutrophils were treated with LPS with or without 1 μM NA pretreatment for 1–9 h. For adrenergic blockade experiments, neutrophils were pretreated with 1 μM propranolol (P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM phenoxybenzamine (HY-B0431A, MedChemExpress) for 60 min, followed by 1 μM NA and 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For IL-1β measurement, 10 μM nigericin (HY-100381, MedChemExpress) was added 30 min before sample collection. Neutrophils were collected for RNA extraction, and the supernatants were collected for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis.

Blood samples were collected between 08:00 and 10:00, then centrifuged at 2,000g and 4 °C for 20 min to separate the serum. BAT was homogenized in a TissueLyser with 1 ml of 80% methanol on ice. The samples were then subjected to 3–5 freeze–thaw cycles and centrifuged at 4 °C and 13,000 r.p.m. for 15 min. The supernatant, which contains sterols, was collected, evaporated and dissolved in an assay buffer. Serum and tissue corticosterone levels were measured using a corticosterone ELISA kit (ADI-900-097, Enzo Biochem). Serum IL-1β levels were measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (ab197742, Abcam). Neutrophil supernatant IL-1β was measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (MLB00C-1, R&D Systems).

scRNA-seq data from the non-adipocyte fraction of BAT of C57BL/6J mice maintained at room temperature were obtained and selected from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accessions GSE207707, GSE177635, GSE160585 and GSE161447. Data processing and analysis were conducted using Seurat v.4.0.6 in R v.4.1.2. Each dataset was imported, converted to Seurat objects, normalized and then variable features were identified. Integration anchors were computed to merge the datasets into a unified Seurat object. Quality control involved filtering out cells with fewer than 200 detected features and those with mitochondrial gene content exceeding 10%. The integrated data were scaled, and principal component analysis was performed. Clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm with a resolution of 1.0. For visualization, t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding was used to depict cell clusters. Identification of each cell type was determined by comparing cell cluster-specific marker genes with known cell type-specific markers from the literature. Immune cell clusters were further identified and subclustered based on the expression of Ptprc, and non-immune cell types, including erythrocytes (Hba-a1 and Hba-a2), capillary endothelial cells (Pecam1 and Gpibp1), smooth muscle cells (Acta2) and adipose progenitor cells (Pdgfra and Col3a1), were excluded from the analysis.

To identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and enriched pathways between BA-L and BA-H cells, scRNA-seq data deposited in the NCBI GEO database under accession number GSE125269 were analysed. Adipocyte clusters were selected based on Plin1 expression, while contaminating endothelial cells (Pecam1) were excluded from the analysis. BA-L and BA-H cell populations were identified as described previously6. These populations were further compared to identify DEGs using the FindMarker function, which applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a log-transformed fold change threshold of 0.25 and a minimum detection fraction (min.pct) of 25%. To control the false discovery rate, P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and genes with an adjusted P of <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Visualization of the top 50 upregulated DEGs in both BA-L and BA-H cells was generated using the DoHeatmap function. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed on the top 75 upregulated and downregulated DEGs in BA-L cells using Gene Ontology Biological Processes. The analysis used Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P values to identify significantly enriched pathways. Pathways with an adjusted P of <0.05 and containing at least three enriched genes were considered significantly enriched. The top 20 enriched pathways were determined based on adjusted P values. Dot plots of these pathways were generated to visualize the enrichment results, with specific pathways of interest highlighted for enhanced interpretability.

After the vehicle and DEX treatment, in vitro-differentiated BAs were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde (15714-S, Electron Microscopy Sciences) for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with 125 mM glycine for 10 min. Cells were then incubated with ice-cold nucleus preparation buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, 250 mM sucrose, 0.1% NP-40, 0.2 mM DTT, protease inhibitor cocktails) and homogenized using a KIMBLE Dounce tissue grinder (D8938, Sigma-Aldrich). The nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 1,000g for 10 min, washed with PBS containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and then resuspended in 250 μl nuclear lysis buffer (10 mM Tris, pH 8, 1 mM EDTA and 0.1% SDS). The chromatin was fragmented using the Bioruptor sonicator (Diagenode) for 30 cycles, 30 s on–30 s off with the maximum power setting to generate DNA fragments of 200–500 bp. The sheared chromatin was centrifuged at 13,000 r.p.m. for 10 min at 4 °C to remove debris and diluted tenfold with ChIP dilution buffer (16.7 mM Tris (pH 8), 1.2 mM EDTA, 167 mM NaCl, 1.1% Triton X-100, 0.01% SDS, protease inhibitor cocktail), with 10 μg chromatin for each ChIP. An aliquot of 10% was used for the input control. Then, 5 μg anti-GR antibody (NBP2-42221, Novus Biologicals) or normal rabbit IgG (2729S, Cell Signaling Technology) was added for overnight rocking at 4 °C. Next, 40 μl protein A/G Dynabeads (26162, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to the ChIP samples and rotated for 2 h at 4 °C. The Dynabeads were washed in low-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), high-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris (pH 8), 2 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), LiCl wash buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 250 mM LiCl) and TE buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA) twice at each step. The antibody–chromatin complex was eluted and reverse-cross-linked in 200 μl elution buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 50 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 300 mM NaCl, 0.8 mg ml−1 proteinase K and 10 μg ml−1 RNase A) by incubating at 50 °C for 2 h and subsequently at 65 °C for 8 h. The immunoprecipitated DNA fragments were purified using the MiniElute PCR Purification Kit (28004, Qiagen). ChIP–qPCR was performed using the primers listed in Supplementary Table 1. ChIP enrichments were calculated relative to the input DNA control.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v.10. Results are presented as mean ± s.e.m. All measurements were obtained from individual samples. For each two-group comparison, equality of variances was first assessed using the F test. An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used when the F test indicated equal variances, whereas Welch’s t-tests were used when the assumption of equal variances was not met. For one-way ANOVA, Tukey’s multiple-comparison test was used when variances were equal, whereas Dunnett’s T3 multiple-comparison test was used when variances were unequal. For two-way ANOVA, Tukey’s or Šídák’s multiple-comparison test was selected according to the experimental design. The statistical tests used are specified in the corresponding figure legends. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Exact P values for all statistical comparisons are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Integration of scRNA-seq datasets of the non-adipocyte fraction of BAT was obtained and selected from the NCBI GEO database under accessions GSE207707, GSE177635, GSE160585 and GSE161447. DEGs and enriched pathways between BA-L and BA-H cells were obtained from the publicly available GEO database (GSE125269). Source data are provided with this paper.

a, Heatmap of genes differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells in BAT, with H6pd, Rgs2, and Ucp1 highlighted with a red asterisk. Data were obtained from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (accession GSE125269). b, Heatmap of genes related to thermogenesis and GR signalling that are differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells, with Ucp1 and H6pd highlighted in red. c, Top pathway enrichment analysis for BA-L cells compared with BA-H cells, including upregulated and downregulated biological processes, with glucocorticoid-related pathways highlighted in red. The “Gene Ratio” represents the ratio of the number of input (differentially expressed) genes associated with a given pathway to the total number of input genes. p-values are shown in standard scientific notation; dot colour indicates the adjusted p-values (the brighter red indicating greater significance), and the dot size reflects the number of enriched genes. d, UMAP plots of the adipocyte fraction from BAT of WT mice maintained at room temperature. e, Distribution of the expression of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1 within UMAP plots. f, Violin plots showing the expression and distribution of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1.

a, The Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mouse model is generated by crossing Ucp1-rtTA transgenic mice with TRE-Cre and Rosa26-loxP-STOP-loxP-mT/mG transgenic mice. In Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mice, all cells express tdTomato. When mice are put on a doxycycline diet, UCP1-high-expressing cells will start rtTA expression; rtTA will then bind to the TRE promoter, inducing Cre expression. Cre will specifically excise the floxed membrane-localizing Tomato (mTomato) sequence, initiating expression of membrane-localizing GFP (mGFP). b, BA-L cells and BA-H cells were freshly isolated from the BAT of WT mice. H6PD and UCP1 immunoblots and quantification normalized to Ponceau S staining. Representative Ponceau S-stained membrane as shown as loading controls. n = 4 per group. c, SVFs and BAs were freshly isolated from the BAT of WT mice. PDGFRα, UCP1, H6PD, and β-actin immunoblots and quantification. n = 4 per group. d, Ucp1-mGFP knock-in (KI) generation strategy: A P2A-mGFP cassette was inserted into the 5′ end of 3′UTR, immediately upstream of the STOP codon of Ucp1 gene. e, Representative GFP fluorescent images of whole BAT from 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP (left) and WT (right) littermates, demonstrating GFP expression exclusively in Ucp1-mGFP mice. f, GFP, UCP1, and β-actin immunoblots and quantification in whole BAT from 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice and WT littermates. n = 6 per group. g, IF staining showing the pattern of GFP (green) expression in the BAT of 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice. h, IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white), and DAPI (blue) in vitro-differentiated brown adipocytes and beige adipocytes derived from Ucp1-mGFP mice BAT SVFs and iWAT SVFs. Statistics were computed by unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test [b, f (UCP1)] or unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-test [c, f (GFP)]. **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001. For b, c, and f, data are mean ± s.e.m.

a, Molecular mechanism for the maintenance of the BA-L state. BA has two stable states, low and high thermogenesis, based on UCP1 expression. BA states are governed by their spatial proximity to IL-1β+ immune cells (mainly neutrophils and macrophages), which integrate signals from sympathetic neurons and immune cells to determine whether H6PD protein levels should be stabilized or degraded. Green arrows illustrate how BA-L cells are stabilized in a low-thermogenic state: IL-1β enhances the protein stability of H6PD in thermogenic adipocytes, thereby boosting the production of active glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid activates the expression of its target RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and reduces cAMP production, thereby reducing UCP1 expression. Red arrows illustrate how BA-L cells switch into BA-H cells upon cold exposure: cold stimulation activates sympathetic neurons, which decrease local BAT IL-1β levels; lower IL-1β levels lead to H6PD protein degradation, turning BA-L into BA-H. The purple arrow illustrates that in aged individuals, IL-1β is elevated in BAT. High IL-1β levels persistently prevent H6PD degradation, desensitizing BAs’ cold response by locking them in BA-L states. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/basqx8x (2026). b, Bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner governs thermogenic activity. We report that IL-1β-secreting immune cells, mainly neutrophils and macrophages, stabilize the surrounding BAs in a low-thermogenic state by preventing H6PD degradation; BAs farther from IL-1β+ cells are stabilized in a high-thermogenic state. Specifically, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells and boosts the production of active GC. GC then activates the expression of its target, RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP production and, in turn, UCP1 expression. This bistable regulation dynamically and precisely controls cellular heterogeneity in response to signalling from sympathetic nerves and the immune system, managing thermogenesis at the tissue level. Increased IL-1β levels in the BAT of aged individuals lock BAs in a low-thermogenic state, thereby lowering thermogenic activity and leading to cold intolerance. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/mj195m9 (2026).

Leeds United are reportedly expected to be one of the clubs in the mix to sign in-form Middlesbrough striker Will Lankshear.

The talented 21-year-old has enjoyed a prolific start to the season, scoring 15 goals in 16 games in all competitions so far, including a perfect record of 13 in 13 in the Championship.

It seems inevitable that a Premier League club will soon move to snap up Lankshear, who was previously on the books at Tottenham as a youngster, but without getting much in the way of first-team opportunities.

Now the England Under-21 international is flourishing, though, having done well to gain experience on loan at Oxford United last season before his permanent transfer to Middlesbrough.

According to Football Insider, links with Leeds could now be one to watch, in what would be a smart bit of business by the Yorkshire outfit.

Leeds would do well to strengthen their attack for January, with Lankshear looking like he clearly has the potential to be a difference-maker in the top flight.

The former Spurs attacker might not be in a big rush to leave Boro due to their promotion hopes, but he could also be a key addition to help Daniel Farke’s side secure their status in the Premier League.

For now, Leeds look to be in a good position after a solid start, but it’s early days yet, and they won’t want to be dragged too close to the relegation zone.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

If Lankshear can continue scoring at such a prolific rate then he could surely be a valuable asset for LUFC or other Premier League clubs.

“Will Lankshear is obviously going to have a lot of Premier League clubs looking at him,” former Premier League scout Mick Brown told Football Insider.

“He’s proving already he’s a top-class striker, it’s not like he’s just come out of nowehere, he’s somebody these clubs have been aware of even when he was at Tottenham.”

He added: “Leeds, for example, will be watching him closely because everybody knows how badly they want to sign a new striker and he would tick a number of boxes for them.”

#1342. Archie Gray and Hayden Hackney on Scotland's radar as Sebastien Pocognoli looks to tempt stars away from England

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:44 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 17:53 EST, 12 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has revealed that Scotland are stepping up their efforts to persuade players who are eligible for England to wear Dark Blue.

While the Belgian is content with the group of players at his disposal, he admits he and the SFA are in dialogue with certain individuals who, potentially, could improve the squad.

It’s understood that Tottenham’s Archie Gray and Everton’s Hayden Hackney are among the names with whom there are ongoing discussions ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifiers next year.

Both players have represented England – the country in which they were born – at Under-21 level yet could still switch to Scotland through family connections.

‘I have had direct contact or indirect contact,’ the Belgian admitted when asked about similarly eligible players. ‘When I go to the direct contact, it’s because I feel it’s a first positive approach.

‘Yeah, I’ve done it with many players. I’ll do my best to bring them.’

Scotland boss Pocognoli is keen to add to his options and has spoken to potential new recruits

Under Steve Clarke, Scotland tried to persuade Harvey Barnes to switch allegiance only for the Newcastle player to confirm that he felt English.

Prepared to take each case on its merits, Pocognoli explained: ‘With Barnes it was different. The two other lads (Gray and Hackney) are young lads. It’s a long way. But if you wait too long, it might not be the right moment.

‘In a year’s time, we will see. Right now, we have players in the squad who are performing well.

‘It will always be up to them (current players) to be the priority because we’ve built things and we’ve had time with the ones who are here right now.’

While Pocognoli has previously made it clear that he won’t beg any player to pull on a Scotland shirt, he feels it’s incumbent on him and the SFA to gauge the feelings of players down south who could help his side.

‘We are on it,’ he stressed. ‘We are always proactive in all of these situations.

‘What is very exciting about those two names is that they are young players. That’s interesting.

Archie Gray's dad Andy, uncle Eddie and grandfather Frank all represented Scotland

‘We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.

‘The best way to convince players is to show good football, show them they can come to us, enjoy it and be successful. They have to feel when they leave a top club that they arrive here into top conditions and a top environment.

‘That’s the best publicity we can offer, to show good football. In the end, it’s a human decision, a feeling.

‘I didn’t have that case. With my Italian blood, maybe I wasn’t that good! But I can understand the feeling of what it’s like to have to choose a country, with your background, family, football education and social circle.

‘So, it’s not easy. But it’s always a feeling from inside and I need to feel it. When I feel it, I’ll try to be on it.’

Hayden Hackney has impressed for Everton this season and has played for Scotland Under-21s

Meanwhile, Pocognoli believes a fully fit Kieran Tierney can have a major role to play in his new-look side.

While the preferred systems of his predecessors meant accommodating the Celtic man and Andy Robertson could be a conundrum, the 3-4-3 which the Belgian deploys seems better suited to fielding the pair at the same time.

With Tierney back in contention to face North Macedonia after pulling out of the last squad through injury, the manager said: ‘He will bring a different profile. He has a fantastic left foot and is an experienced player who knows the squad and knows what it means to play for Scotland. It is a big plus. He trained very well this week and is very focused.

‘He can play different positions. He can play left-back, he can play in the back three, as he has in the past. He plays left-back for Celtic, but in some games he has inverted. He can also bring some offensive attributes in the back three. We are lucky to have someone with that profile.

‘It is always a challenge to try to make all the players shine in the best shape possible. We have strong competition on the left side.

‘We have quality players. I will try to find the best balance and make everybody shine. If we can play Kieran and Andy in the same team if they are fit, it is a plus for the team.’

Kieran Tierney has been tipped to have a big impact for Scotland under Pocognoli

Pocognoli is desperate to secure his first victory at Hampden this evening having tasted defeat in his first two home games with Switzerland and Slovenia.

‘I haven’t really experienced Hampden yet and I’d like to,’ he said. ‘I was frustrated in the first game (against the Swiss) because I thought we started quite good in the first 10 minutes.

‘Then we know what happened (red card for Jack Hendry). In the last game, it was just disappointment.

‘It’s important that we play a consistent game and combine a good result with good football. If we play average and win, I’ll be happy with three points.

‘But the process is to play good football as well. It’s important that we excite the fans and we have the players for that. I hope that we deliver what we’ve worked on in the last four days.’

Manchester United star Bruno Fernandes has reportedly rejected another contract offer from the club to throw his future into further doubt.

This is said to be the second new deal Man Utd have offered Fernandes, who is currently due to be out of contract at the end of the season.

However, the Red Devils have the option to trigger a one-year extension, so in theory could keep the Portugal international until summer 2028.

That’s according to BBC Sport, who state that United have once again tried to tie Fernandes down to a longer-term contract, but it seems he’s turned their offer down.

This certainly seems far from ideal, with MUFC in need of some stability from their club captain as they prepare to change manager once again.

Still, as argued here in the Daily Briefing, the obvious solution to this problem could be to reunite incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino with Chelsea playmaker Cole Palmer.

The England international played arguably the best football of his career under Pochettino in their single season together at Stamford Bridge, and a reunion could work out well for all parties.

While Palmer would not come cheap, he’s suffered a bit of a dip in form for Chelsea in recent times, and that could mean the right offer would tempt the Blues into cashing in.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Pochettino, meanwhile, would surely relish the chance to make this statement signing to help kick-start his reign at Old Trafford.

It would undoubtedly be a blow to lose a legendary figure like Fernandes, but the 32-year-old may now be getting to the point in his career where his influence at the very top level begins to wane anyway.

Palmer, meanwhile, is still only 24 and likely still has his best years ahead of him. He’s also a Manchester lad and known to be a United fan. It just all makes sense.

#1340. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.
