#1338. Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 372–377 (2026) Cite this article

Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

The increasing integration of renewable energy calls for sustainable electrochemical energy storage systems beyond lithium-ion batteries1. Aqueous metal–iodine batteries offer a promising platform for large-scale energy storage by combining earth-abundant electrode materials, aqueous electrolytes and conversion-type iodine chemistry2,3. Unlike intercalation-type positive electrodes, iodine positive electrodes store charge by reversible valence-state changes, offering access to multi-electron redox chemistry with increased capacity and redox potential4. Most studies have focused on the two-electron I−/I0 redox couple, with a theoretical capacity of 211 mAh g−1 at a redox potential of 0.54 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode10. Extending iodine conversion to the successive I−/I0/I+ redox couples doubles the theoretical capacity to 422 mAh g−1 while introducing the I0/I+ redox process at a higher redox potential of 1.07 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode11. However, despite this potential, achieving reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge3,7.

The crux of iodine conversion chemistry lies in interfacial reactions, where electrolyte composition and interfacial microenvironment govern reaction pathways. Electron-deficient I+ is strongly electrophilic and susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water, resulting in hydrolysis and poor reversibility in aqueous environments9,12. Previous studies have achieved four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries by stabilizing reactive I+ through interhalogen complexes (for example, ICl2 or IBr2) in highly concentrated chloride- or bromide-containing electrolytes5,6,13. In these systems, electrophilic I+ coordinates with two nucleophilic halide ions (Cl− or Br−) through non-covalent interactions8,14. However, at water-enriched interfaces, hydration of nucleophilic species (Nuc) competes with these interactions and destabilizes I+ complexes (Fig. 1a). Highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes mitigate this competition by reducing water activity and increasing halide availability, but their high salt contents and corrosivity constrain broader implementation (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), necessitating new electrolyte chemistry and a mechanistic framework that move beyond reliance on halogen-containing electrolytes and conventional interhalogen stabilization5,8.

a, The mechanism of the competition between halogen bond and hydrogen bond. b, The conventional interhalogen stabilization mechanism in highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes. c, The KA–PA–Nuc framework levering anionic chemistry and halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free electrolytes. IHP, inner Helmholtz plane; OHP, outer Helmholtz plane.

Given the competition between I+ stabilization and hydration at water-enriched interfaces, overcoming this challenge requires simultaneous regulation of the interfacial environment and water–Nuc interactions. Anionic chemistry offers a powerful lever to coordinate these interfacial and molecular interactions15,16,17,18. Herein we establish a kosmotropic anion (KA)–polar anion (PA)–Nuc electrolyte framework for reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes (Fig. 1c). Systematic experiments and theoretical calculations reveal how the synergistic effects of PAs and KAs coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, thereby stabilizing interfacial electrochemical behaviour and promoting reversible four-electron iodine conversion. The applicability of this electrolyte framework is demonstrated across four halogen-free Nuc (urea, acetamide, pyridine and nicotinamide) and in both aqueous Zn–I2 and Al–I2 batteries (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Beyond establishing a halogen-free electrolyte chemistry, this work reveals how electrolyte chemistry governs iodine conversion across interfacial, molecular and electrochemical scales, providing a mechanistic basis for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

Stabilizing I+ against hydrolysis is essential for reversible four-electron iodine conversion in aqueous electrolytes. Previous studies have relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes for interhalogen stabilization19,20, whereas more recent studies have explored specific additive-halogen nucleophilic substitution reactions21,22. These approaches primarily address I+ stabilization through specific molecular interactions, whereas how electrolyte chemistry collectively regulates the interfacial microenvironment, molecular stabilization and the resulting iodine conversion pathways remains less understood. This work establishes a mechanistic framework that integrates anionic chemistry with halogen-bond stabilization in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, strong PAs establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interface, whereas KAs weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding to facilitate halogen-bond stabilization of I+. These complementary effects underpin the halogen-free KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, whose composition was subsequently optimized (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4) and exhibits sufficient electrochemical stability (Supplementary Fig. 5) for four-electron iodine conversion.

a, Molecular interplay governed by anionic chemistry and halogen bonding. b, Cyclic voltammetry profiles of iodine conversion reaction using urea as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. c, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using acetamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. d, Cyclic voltammetry profiles using nicotinamide as Nuc at 0.6 mV s−1. e–g, Corresponding GCD profiles for b–d at 1 A g−1, respectively. All electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework was validated in aqueous Zn–I2 batteries across four different Nuc (Supplementary Fig. 6). Electron-deficient I+ can interact with two electron-rich Nuc molecules to form linear Nuc–I+–Nuc halogen bonds. These halogen bonds provide the molecular basis for I+ stabilization, as supported by Nuc-free controls, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and theoretical calculations23 (Supplementary Figs. 7–11). Using urea (U) as a representative Nuc, KA–U exhibits only the I−/I0 redox process, whereas PA–U enables further I0/I+ oxidation but with poor reversibility (Fig. 2b,e). The excessive capacity at the second charge plateau is attributed to irreversible iodine oxidation coupled with parasitic water oxidation (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Combining KA and PA in KA–PA–U produces two reversible redox peaks and corresponding charge–discharge plateaus, demonstrating their synergistic role in enabling reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion (Supplementary Fig. 14). Replacing U with acetamide (AE), nicotinamide (NA) or pyridine (PD) shows the same phenomenon, with reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion achieved only in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes, including under identical ionic strength conditions, indicating the broad applicability of this electrolyte framework (Fig. 2c,d,f,g and Supplementary Figs. 15–18).

To isolate the role of PAs in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework, SO42− was maintained as the KA, whereas structurally related CF3SO3−, CF3COO− or CH3COO− was introduced as the second anion. Density-functional-theory calculations reveal a polarity sequence of CH3COO− > CF3COO− > CF3SO3− (Supplementary Fig. 19), providing a basis for examining how anion polarity influences interfacial behaviours24,25. Molecular-dynamics simulations show similar water-enriched bulk environments across the three electrolytes (Supplementary Figs. 20–22), but distinct interfacial structures (Fig. 3d). CH3COO− reduces the interfacial water density while increasing anion enrichment, whereas CF3COO− and CF3SO3− retain high interfacial water intensity (Fig. 3e,f). In situ attenuated total reflection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy further supports this interfacial redistribution. The δ-HOH vibration at 1,640 cm−1 remains pronounced with CF3SO3− or CF3COO− (Fig. 3g,h and Supplementary Fig. 23), but is suppressed with CH3COO− alongside pronounced anion-associated signals26,27,28,29 (Fig. 3i). Notably, highly concentrated ZnCl2 retains a water-enriched interface despite its water-deficient bulk environment (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Differential capacitance measurements indicate stronger interfacial adsorption of CH3COO− than of CF3COO− and CF3SO3− (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 27), linking preferential adsorption of strongly PAs to the formation of a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment30.

a, Cyclic voltammetry profiles in electrolytes with different anions. b, GCD profiles in electrolytes with different anions. The rising and falling voltage curves correspond to charging and discharging processes, respectively. c, Cycling stability in electrolytes with different anions, with upper and lower curves representing Coulombic efficiency and specific capacity, respectively. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, Schematic snapshot of the interfacial structure in the electrolyte with CH3COO−. e, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of H2O in electrolytes with different anions, with the grey shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. f, Corresponding interfacial cumulated density profiles of anions in electrolytes with different anions, with the pink shaded region highlighting interfacial variations. g–i, In situ ATR-IR spectra in the electrolytes with CF3SO3− (g), CF3COO− (h) and CH3COO− (i).

These polarity-dependent interfacial structures lead to distinct iodine conversion behaviour. CF3SO3− shows a negligible I0/I+ process, whereas CF3COO− enables I0/I+ oxidation but with limited reversibility. By contrast, CH3COO− supports reversible I−/I0/I+ conversion with improved stability and capacity (Fig. 3a–c and Supplementary Fig. 28). In situ ultraviolet–visible spectra and micro-computed-tomography analyses further link these differences to iodine species distribution, showing that CH3COO− confines iodine species within the electrode and suppresses their migration into the bulk electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Together, these results establish a mechanistic relationship between anion polarity and the resulting water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment that governs the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Building on the understanding of PAs, the critical role of KAs in the KA–PA–Nuc framework was further explored. Nuc stabilize I+ through electron-rich nitrogen or oxygen centres, which also interact with water through hydrogen bonding and therefore compete with halogen-bond formation (Supplementary Fig. 31). Inspired by anion-specific effects on water–solute interactions, SO42−, CH3COO−, NO3−, CF3SO3− and ClO4− were compared in the same PA–Nuc baseline31,32,33,34 (Supplementary Fig. 32). Although these anions have little effect on the initial capacity, they produce different cycling stability (Supplementary Fig. 33). SO42− maintains nearly overlapping galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) profiles, whereas CH3COO− and CF3SO3− show intermediate cycling stability and ClO4− undergoes rapid deterioration (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 34), giving a stability sequence of SO42− > CH3COO− > CF3SO3− > ClO4−. NO3− deviates from this sequence owing to its limited electrochemical stability within the applied voltage range35 (Supplementary Fig. 35a,b).

a, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing SO42− at different cycles. b, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing CF3SO3− at different cycles. c, GCD profiles in the electrolyte containing ClO4− at different cycles. Electrochemical measurements were performed in Zn–I2 coin cells with an iodine mass loading of 2.2 mg cm−2. d, 2H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. e, 1H NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. f, 13C NMR spectra of electrolytes containing different anions. g, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing SO42−. h, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing CF3SO3−. i, Two-dimensional 1H–15N HMBC NMR spectrum of the electrolyte containing ClO4−.

NMR spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations reveal the molecular origin of these electrochemical differences. The 2H chemical shift follows SO42− > CH3COO− > NO3− > CF3SO3− > ClO4− (Fig. 4d), indicating progressively stronger anion-induced water polarization and restructuring of the aqueous hydrogen-bond network36,37. These differences in water–anion coordination translate into distinct water–Nuc interactions. The corresponding 15N chemical shifts, together with the inverse trends observed in 1H and 13C chemical shifts, indicate that KAs such as SO42− polarize hydration water and thereby weaken Nuc–water hydrogen bonding, whereas chaotropic anions such as ClO4− interact directly with the Nuc backbone and facilitate Nuc hydration32 (Fig. 4e,f, and Supplementary Figs. 32 and 36–38). Nuc solubility measurements, two-dimensional 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) NMR spectra, and calculated Nuc–water distances and hydrogen-bond populations further support this interpretation (Fig. 4g–i, and Supplementary Figs. 35c, 39 and 40). By weakening Nuc–water interactions, SO42− increases the availability of Nuc for halogen-bond stabilization of I+, thereby promoting reversible iodine conversion. These results reveal how anionic chemistry regulates molecular water–Nuc interactions to govern the reversibility of four-electron iodine conversion.

Having established the complementary roles of PA and KA in interfacial and molecular regulation, we next examined how these effects manifest in the electrochemical processes governing iodine conversion. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) combined with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis was used to decouple the complex impedance response and identify individual electrochemical processes38,39,40 (Supplementary Figs. 41–43). In the absence of either KA or PA, the DRT responses evolve distinctly with additional competing interfacial processes, whereas their combined presence maintains stable interfacial electrochemical behaviour throughout iodine conversion41,42 (Extended Data Fig. 1). Rate-dependent analysis identifies charge transfer, rather than ion transport, as the dominant kinetic contribution to iodine conversion in the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte (Supplementary Figs. 44–50). In situ Raman spectroscopy further links these electrochemical processes to iodine chemistry, revealing the reversible evolution of the Nuc–I+–Nuc species during cycling (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52).

The KA–PA–Nuc framework supports four-electron iodine conversion across different operating conditions and cell configurations. Zn–I2 cells retain 96% of their capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g−1 and 94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g−1, while sustaining four-electron conversion at iodine loadings up to 12.2 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. 53–55, 58a and 59). This electrolyte framework is also compatible with different current collectors and pouch-cell configurations and extends to aqueous Al–I2 cells using Al–Zn alloy negative electrodes (Supplementary Figs. 56–58b,c, 60 and 61). A techno-economic analysis under standardized modelling assumptions further illustrates its theoretical cost-reduction potential by avoiding highly concentrated, halogen-containing electrolytes and costly current collectors (Supplementary Fig. 58d–f and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Mechanistic and post-mortem analyses further reveal that the apparent low Coulombic efficiency and capacity fading involve coupled reversible and irreversible iodine inventory loss, with the latter becoming more pronounced at increased iodine loading (Supplementary Figs. 62–67 and Extended Data Figs. 2–4). Together, these results clarify the iodine conversion pathways while defining the applicability and remaining limitations of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, showing that sustained reversible four-electron iodine conversion requires not only stabilization of hypervalent iodine species but also broader management of the entire iodine inventory.

All chemicals were used as received without further purification unless otherwise stated. The manufacturer and purity of each material are specified at its first occurrence in Methods and are not repeated thereafter unless a different source or purity was used.

The KA–PA–Nuc electrolytes were prepared by dissolving KA, PA and Nuc into deionized water at room temperature. For aqueous Zn–I2 batteries, KA and PA were 1.5 M ZnSO4 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M Zn (CH3COO)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich), respectively. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc framework, various Nuc were used, including 2 M urea (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich), 2 M acetamide (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.2 M pyridine (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) or 0.4 M nicotinamide (>99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). To explore the role of PAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 1.5 M ZnSO4 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. Zn(CH3COO)2, Zn(CF3COO)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) or Zn(CF3SO3)2 (>98%, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 0.5 M to obtain electrolytes containing different PAs. To evaluate the role of KAs, a baseline electrolyte containing 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide was prepared. ZnSO4, Zn(NO3)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), Zn(CF3SO3)2 or Zn(ClO4)2 (purity not specified, Sigma-Aldrich) was then added at a concentration of 1.5 M for comparative analysis. To compare electrolytes performance under a standardized ionic strength condition, the ionic strength of each electrolyte was calculated according to the equation:

where Ci and Zi represent the molar concentration and charge number of ion i, respectively. For aqueous Al–I2 batteries, the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 1.5 M Al2(SO4)3 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 Mg (CH3COO)2 (>99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 M nicotinamide into deionized water.

Iodine-activated carbon (I2–AC) composites were prepared using an evaporation–adsorption method. In brief, 0.5 g iodine (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) and 0.5 g activated carbon (AC; YP-80F, purity not specified, Kuraray) were manually ground in an agate mortar with a pestle for 10 min under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was sealed in a Teflon reactor and heated at 120 °C for 6 h. For the preparation of iodine positive electrodes using titanium (80 mesh, >99.5%, Hebei Conway Metal Products) or stainless steel mesh (80 mesh, 316L, Hebei Conway Metal Products) as the current collector, I2–AC, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, 60 wt% dispersion H2O, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P (purity not specified, Canrd) were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 40 mg I2–AC, 5 mg Super P and 5 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle under ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using a roller press (Etelux) and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The areal iodine loading was controlled by adjusting the thickness of the composite film. The dried film was then pressed onto the titanium or stainless steel mesh using the roller press. The resulting electrodes were punched into 12 mm disks using a manual disk punch (T07, ‌Hefei Kejing Material Technology).

For iodine positive electrodes using carbon paper (TGP-H-060, Toray) as the current collector, I2–AC, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, weight-average molecular weight, Mw ≈ 534,000 g mol−1 by gel permeation chromatography, powder, Sigma-Aldrich) and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg I2–AC, 20 mg PVDF and 20 mg Super P were manually mixed with N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (>99.5%, Thermo Scientific Acros) using an agate mortar and pestle in ambient conditions. The resulting slurry was manually and uniformly spread onto the carbon paper using a laboratory spatula. The coated electrodes were dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 8 h and subsequently cut into 12-mm disks using the manual disk punch. Commercial Zn foils (70 µm, >99.99%, ‌Qinghe Haoxuan Metal Materials) were used as negative electrodes as received.

To assess the potential of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, a Ag/AgCl electrode in saturated KCl (Beijing Jingke Instrument Science Instrument) was used as the reference, and AC electrodes were prepared as the counter electrode. The measured potentials are reported directly versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode. For the preparation of AC electrodes, AC, PTFE and Super P were combined at a mass ratio of 8:1:1. For each batch, 160 mg AC, 20 mg Super P and 20 mg PTFE (calculated on a dry-PTFE basis) were manually mixed with deionized water using an agate mortar and pestle at ambient conditions. The resulting mixture was rolled into a self-standing film using the roller press and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 3 h in air. The dried film was then pressed onto titanium mesh using the roller press. By adjusting the electrode thickness, the capacity of the AC electrode was controlled to be much higher than that of the iodine working electrode, ensuring its capability as the counter electrode for evaluating the electrochemical performance of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte. To further validate the applicability of the KA–PA–Nuc electrolyte framework in multi-electron aqueous Al–I2 batteries, Al–Zn alloys were fabricated as negative electrodes following a previous study43. In brief, symmetric cells were assembled using Zn foils (70 µm, 16 mm in diameter) as electrodes and 2 M Al (CF3SO3)3 (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) as the electrolyte. During charging, Al3+ in the electrolyte deposited on and reacted with the metal Zn substrate, forming the Zn-supported Al–Zn alloys.

Halogen-bond complexes were synthesized via a cation-exchange reaction using corresponding silver analogues, following a previously reported procedure with some modifications44. All operations were carried out under a standard Schlenk line. In a typical synthesis, 0.94 mmol of the corresponding silver salt (Ag2SO4, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCH3COO, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3COO, >98%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgCF3SO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; AgNO3, >99%, Sigma-Aldrich; or AgClO4, >97%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a 20-ml vial equipped with a stir bar. The vial was sealed with a rubber septum and evacuated. Subsequently, 6.0 ml dry CH2Cl2 (purity not specified, VWR Chemicals) and 1.90 mmol pyridine (3.80 mmol for Ag2SO4) were added at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was stirred for 10 min to form the Ag(I)–pyridine bis-coordination complex. Next, 2.00 mmol of iodine (4.00 mmol for Ag2SO4) was added, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for an additional 20 min under continuous stirring. The supernatant was then carefully transferred to another vial via cannula filtration, followed by the addition of 15 ml dry n-hexane (>99%, Macron Fine Chemicals) to induce precipitation of the halogen-bond complex. The mixture was stored at −20 °C overnight to complete precipitation. Afterwards, the supernatant was removed using a syringe, and the resulting solid was washed with 20 ml dry n-hexane to remove any residual I2. Finally, the product was dried under vacuum on the Schlenk line.

In situ ATR-IR spectra were recorded by a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. Gold-coated silicon plates were used as working electrodes, with Zn foils (70 µm, 10 mm in diameter) and glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter, Whatman) used as reference electrodes and separators, respectively. To assess the critical role of the PA in the interfacial environment, 1.5 M KA electrolyte was maintained as the baseline, and 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2, 0.5 M Zn(CF3COO)2 or 0.5 M Zn(CF3SO3)2 was separately added. An electrolyte volume of 500 μl was used for each measurement. During tests, the assembled batteries were connected to a Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat to run a cyclic voltammetry programme at a scan rate of 0.2 mV s−1 for a full charge and discharge cycle. All spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm−1, with 50 scans per measurement. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

Raman spectra were recorded using a Bruker Senterra II Raman spectrometer with a 532-nm excitation wavelength. The in situ Zn–I2 cell comprised an iodine positive electrode (12 mm in diameter, iodine mass loading 2.2 mg cm−2), a Zn negative electrode (70 µm, 12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre (GF/D, 12 mm in diameter). An electrolyte volume of 200 μl was used. Raman spectra were collected during GCD cycling using an external Gamry Interface 1000 potentiostat. Measurements were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C.

FTIR spectra of various electrolytes were obtained using an ATR-FTIR spectrometer (BRUKER, Platinum-ATR). Scanning electron microscopy characterization of electrodes was performed using a JEOL 7600 microscope. Ultraviolet–visible measurements were conducted on a Shimadzu UV-3600i Plus spectrophotometer. For in situ ultraviolet–visible measurements, a two-electrode Zn–I2 cuvette cell was connected to a Neware battery test system for GCD cycling. NMR analyses, including 1H, 13C and 1H–15N HMBC spectra, were carried out on a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 500). 15N spectra were collected using a Bruker NMR instrument (Avance Neo 700). Deuterium oxide (>99.9%, Fluorochem) was used as the solvent for electrolyte characterization, and dideuteromethylenechloride (>99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the solvent for characterizing halogen-bond complexes. Micro-computed-tomography imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Xradia 620 Versa system with a ×4 objective, operating at a tube voltage of 80 kV and an exposure time of 8 s, achieving a voxel resolution of 0.8 μm. For each sample, a disk with a diameter of 2 mm was prepared to balance X-ray attenuation and representative sampling volume. The acquired computed-tomography datasets were subsequently processed and analysed using Avizo software.

Electrochemical studies of halogen-free electrolytes were performed using CR2025 coin cells, whereas those of halogen-containing electrolytes were performed using Swagelok cells. For CR2025 Zn–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode, Zn negative electrode (70 µm) and separator (GF/D) had diameters of 12 mm, 16 mm and 19 mm, respectively. For Swagelok Zn–I2 cells, corresponding electrodes and separators had the same diameter of 12 mm. For CR2025 Al–I2 coin cells, the iodine positive electrode had a diameter of 12 mm, the Al–Zn alloy negative electrode had a diameter of 16 mm, and a GF/D separator with a diameter of 19 mm was used. An electrolyte volume of 100 μl was used for each cell. Coin cells were mechanically crimped at 50 kg cm−2 using a hydraulic crimping machine (MSK-110, Hefei Kejing Material Technology) during assembly. Swagelok cells were manually tightened during assembly.

For the 1.1-Ah pouch cell, 2 double-side coated iodine positive electrodes (10 × 15 cm), and 3 Zn negative electrodes (70 µm, 10 × 15 cm) were stacked alternately. The areal iodine loading of positive electrodes is controlled at 10 mg cm−2. Four glass fibre separators (GF/D, 10.1 × 15.1 cm) were utilized, and 1.5 ml electrolyte was added to each separator. The electrolyte consisted of 1.5 M ZnSO4, 0.5 M Zn(CH3COO)2 and 0.4 M nicotinamide. Titanium foils were connected to electrodes as tabs. After lamination, the assembled battery was encapsulated in an aluminium–plastic film and mechanically constrained using a customized model during electrochemical measurements. The applied pressure was not specifically quantified.

GCD tests were conducted using a Neware battery test system in a room maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 25–28 °C. All other electrochemical measurements described below were performed at an ambient laboratory temperature of approximately 18–25 °C. Cyclic voltammetry, linear sweep voltammetry and EIS measurements were performed using a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat. For the electrochemical stability window analysis, linear sweep voltammetry measurements were performed using a three-electrode configuration consisting of a titanium mesh working electrode (1 × 2 cm), an AC counter electrode (1 × 2 cm) and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode at a scan rate of 2 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to an exposed geometric area of 1 cm², and the potentials are reported directly versus Ag/AgCl. The polarization measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti CR2025 coin cells using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter), titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter) at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1. The measured current was normalized to the geometric area of the titanium electrode. For in situ EIS tests, a thin Zn wire was inserted into the coin cell as an additional reference electrode to establish a three-electrode configuration. This reference electrode was placed between the positive electrode and negative electrode, separated by two layers of separators (GF/A, Whatman). For measurements of the individual iodine positive electrode, the potential is reported versus the Zn reference electrode as potential (V versus Zn/Zn²+), whereas the full-cell and Zn negative electrode responses are reported as voltage (V) owing to the voltage was applied on full cell. For peak assignment, the assembled cells were connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat to perform staircase potentio EIS with a potential range of approximately 0.6–1.8 V. For rate-step identification, the assembled cells simultaneously connected to a Biologic VMP-3 potentiostat and a Neware battery test system to conduct potentio EIS and GCD cycling, respectively. All Nyquist plots were fitted using EC-Lab software based on the equivalent circuit (R1 + Q2/R2 + Q3/R3 + W4). DRT data were calculated from EIS data using MatlabR2019 with the DRT tool developed by Francesco Ciucci’s research group. The differential capacitance was calculated using the following equation:

where C is the differential capacitance, ω is the angular frequency and Zim is the imaginary component of the impedance. In this work, a specific frequency of 1,000 Hz was used. Measurements were performed in asymmetric Zn–Ti cells assembled in CR2025 coin-cell configuration, using Zn foil (16 mm in diameter) and titanium foil (12 mm in diameter) as the two electrodes and a glass fibre separator (19 mm in diameter). The potential was varied from 1.0 V to 1.7 V versus Zn/Zn2+. No ohmic-drop (iR) correction was applied to the potentials or voltages reported in this work.

All molecular-dynamics simulations were performed using the LAMMPS package45 to investigate the bulk solvation structure of various aqueous electrolytes. The initial configurations were constructed using Packmol46, which randomly packed electrolyte components into a periodic cubic box according to the target molar ratios, ensuring no initial atomic overlaps. The simulation cell was then relaxed by energy minimization before subsequent equilibration. Force-field parameters for organic molecules were taken from the OPLS-AA family47,48, whereas others were adopted from validated aqueous zinc salt parameter sets in the literature. To partially account for polarization effects in concentrated electrolytes, the atomic charges were uniformly scaled (scaling factor 0.8)49. Interaction of water was represented by TIP3P50, and all X–H bonds were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm51. Each system was first energy-minimized and equilibrated in the isothermal–isobaric ensemble (300 K, 1 atm) using a Nosé–Hoover thermostat until both the density and potential energy were stable. Subsequently, production runs were performed in the canonical ensemble for 5 ns (5,000 ps) with a 1-fs integration step to ensure complete equilibration while avoiding structural drift.

Radial distribution functions gij(r) were computed to analyse ion pairing and solvation structure. Coordination numbers were obtained by integrating gij(r) up to their first minimum. Both radial distribution functions and hydrogen bonds were identified using the hydrogen-bond analysis tools implemented in VMD52. Average hydrogen-bond numbers and distributions were determined over the equilibrated trajectories to characterize the reorganization of the hydrogen-bond network by different anions.

To probe field-induced ion and molecular redistribution, an additional set of simulations was conducted in the canonical ensemble with a uniform static electric field applied along the z axis. The field strength corresponded to the experimentally estimated potential gradient.

Density-functional-theory calculations were performed using the Gaussian16 program package, using the M06-2X exchange-correlation functional53. Geometry optimizations were conducted using a mixed basis-set approach: the 6-311+G(d,p) basis set was applied to all elements excluding iodine54. Iodine was described using an effective core potential from the Stuttgart/Dresden group55. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model, with water selected as the solvent56.

The data that support the findings of this study are available within this article and its Supplementary Information. Further data are available from the corresponding author upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Manchester United are reportedly monitoring Como star Nico Paz as a potential transfer target amid uncertainty over Bruno Fernandes’ future.

Man Utd should soon announce that they’ve hired Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager, and it could be that his fellow Argentine will be brought in for that key role in attacking midfield.

BBC Sport have reported on Fernandes snubbing a new contract offer from the Red Devils, and we’ve posted on the Daily Briefing about why Chelsea’s Cole Palmer could be the ideal choice to replace him.

Alternatively, however, there could also be some interest in signing Paz from Como in that position, according to a report from the Sun.

Paz recently dismantled United in the Champions League and very much looks like the game’s next superstar, so this would be a hugely exciting signing.

At this moment in time, however, it perhaps seems unlikely Paz would choose MUFC over the long list of other top clubs likely to be in for him.

As noted by the Sun, Real Madrid also have the option to buy the 21-year-old back, so that complicates matters further.

United undoubtedly need a game-changing signing like this, but perhaps the Manchester-born Palmer is more realistic at this moment in time.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

It will be interesting to see, however, if Pochettino’s presence could change things for United, and perhaps give them more of a pull factor in the transfer market again.

Paz may well be tempted to link up with his fellow countryman, who also has a great record when it comes to improving and developing young players.

Pochettino actually did a great job with Palmer as a youngster at Chelsea, so that’s another connection surely worth exploring.

#1336. Arsenal late show keeps heat on Man City

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

Eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

“We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta said. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

“The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

“I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO

Yet Madueke provided the crucial contribution, driving a right-footed shot towards goal which took a heavy deflection off Forest defender Jair Cunha to beat Matz Sels.

Madueke has struggled for consistency and minutes since his £52m move from Chelsea, so this felt like a big moment for the winger.

“If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke said. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We showed grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”

Forest’s problems at home are increasing and Oliver Glasner is now the club’s fifth manager in a year to experience such problems. His team have now gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters. They have only recorded two home wins in the league over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

They did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

Liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Murillo had Forest’s best opportunity two minutes into injury time after cutting inside the penalty area but could not find the top corner.

"That was magic!" What a goal this would have been from Murillo?! 😩 https://t.co/D07lB7hN47

Another defeat will only add to their concerns and Glasner needs to quickly find a solution or face another relegation battle.

It does not promise to get easier immediately, either, with Manchester City, Chelsea and Brighton up next in the league at home, but there were encouraging signs here, despite the club sitting in the bottom three.

Glasner said: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

“It feels unfair but I don’t want to be complaining as we are the only ones who can change it.

“It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

“We are playing better right now but we also concede how competitive the Premier League is because every mistake you get punished.”

We knew the margins would be really small. They are extremely well coached and organised. The longer the game goes on they gain more belief. We had to be so patient - and clinical when we got the chance. The way they were defending, they were more comfortable. But we have players with different qualities and can adapt to what the game is delivering.

We have another three big chances that should be goals. That is the difference, you have to be clinical. If we keep generating them, they will come.

Let’s enjoy the win, because it was a very tough one. And then, on Wednesday, we have an incredible game against Bayern Munich away [in the Champions League].

When you see their goal it’s deflected otherwise, it’s straight to the gloves of Matz Sels. You have periods in football where you feel everything going against you and then there are periods when things are on your side.

Now it is how we deal with the situation and react as a team and just how we can change this is by staying positive, sticking together and working hard.

And having this coolness, not to worry too much because I can see good performances and not good results. The results will come if the performances stay good.

Noni [Madueke], Jurrien [Timber], Mikel [Merino] was brilliant when he came on and Viktor [Gyokeres] really changed the game - all of them did and that’s what we need. Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that’s the difference.

Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn’t have a shot on target and that’s something we discussed. We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it’s in.

Great reaction [after scoring goal], to have the will to defend a really open and difficult and stressful situation.

We knew it would be a tough game, it always is against Arsenal. They have a good team. But we feel we can change the result, maybe a draw, maybe a win. Now we have to put it in the past and focus on the next match.

We have a good manager and I think we are still getting his ideas. We changed everything in our system this season. It is difficult but after three or four months we keep improving and I think we are close to reaching our best.

If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd so we know that we’re going to start some and finish some and for me it’s the same mentality every time I just want to create or score.

Amazing feeling [to score] but I feel better about the win.

We have elite players, all 20-something players are elite and of the highest level. Great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench you’re ready to have an impact.

32 - Since Mikel Arteta became Arsenal manager in December 2019, they have had the joint-most 1-0 wins in the Premier League of any side (32, level with Everton). Stereotype. https://t.co/nD7C3j7Xjw

Arsenal dig out a very ugly victory, and one they probably did not warrant. A draw would have been the fairest outcome from a game that was low on quality, but Arsenal’s bench makes a difference again with Noni Madueke scoring the winning goal. Forest can take positives from their performance, primarily the solidity of their defending and a more threatening Delap performance.

Forest with another late moment of danger! Delap peeled in behind the Arsenal defence, and he was found by a glorious pass, but Konsa made a fantastic last-ditch challenge to surely preserve the points from Arsenal.

What a goal that would have been from Murillo! The burly defender did so well to skip between Konsa and Saka, before sending Rice the wrong way in the box with a roll of the studs. Murillo tired for the curler into the top corner with his weaker right foot, and he was not far away. Great effort.

"That was magic!" What a goal this would have been from Murillo?! 😩 https://t.co/D07lB7hN47

Arsenal have a throw in the Forest half after some grafting by Gyokeres and there are just three added minutes to play.

Was that Forest’s chance?! Quick thinking from Liam Delap on the halfway line caught Arsenal out, launching a quick throw into the path of Hudson-Odoi with Timber ahead of the ball. Hudson-Odoi carried the ball to the edge of the box and picked out Wood with a pass, but the big striker wanted too much time and Rice recovered to block.

Anything can happen when there is a one-goal margin, but Arsenal have been in complete control since scoring. Forest have lost some of their structure as they chase the game and they are more open as a result. Merino wins a free-kick, and then Gabriel ushers the ball out for a throw in.

Forest cling on by their fingernails with Arsenal flooding forward, but Merino’s pass to Saka in the box was underhit. Chris Wood and Hudson-Odoi are now on for Forest as they chase an equaliser. Cunha and McAtee the Forest players to depart.

Arsenal have kept a grip of the game since the goal, Gyokeres with some willing running to ensure the game remains in Forest’s half.

The Arsenal winger was helped by a deflection, but after Forest’s defence beckoned him to cut inside on his right foot he took up the invitation. It was a clean strike from Madueke, but the flick off Cunha’s thigh was crucial and the ball flew past Sels into the roof of the net.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC

Saka floats in a teasing cross which bounces through to Sels, but that was a better Arsenal delivery. One or two signs that Timber, and his combination with Saka and Odegaard, might be the route to a goal.

Odegaard with a week free-kick from a good crossing position after Saka won a foul, before Raya’s long ball towards Gyokeres is too strong and Forest have a goal kick. Arsenal still to muster a shot on target from 73 per cent possession.

Ndoye are Dominguez are the Forest players coming off in a double change, replaced by Kalimuendo and Sangare. Forest will be worth a point if the game continues this way.

Declan Rice with a shank out for a throw when he was looking for Saka. Kalimuendo is ready to come for Forest, so Glasner is introducing another forward.

Good chance for Rice but he blasts over! Arsenal’s best move of the game with Saka, Odegaard and Timber working as a triangle to get in behind the Forest defence, and Timber’s pull-back was accurate. Rice was always leaning back though as he tried to sweep the ball into the far corner.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO

Delap with a tame shot from distance, before Timber instigates a more dangerous Arsenal attack with a reverse pass into Odegaard. The ball is worked to Madueke and his deflected cross is headed away. Saka wants a throw but the linesman has other ideas. Still no goal despite more endeavour in this half.

Arsenal building some pressure, and they have another corner. Arteta signalling that he wants to make the change before the corner is taken and here come the changes: White for Timber, Havertz for Gyokeres and Merino on for Bruno Guimaraes.

Gabriel meets Rice’s delivery, but he fails to direct his header on target.

Excellent defending from Gabriel up against Ndoye in the right channel, but it was another promising moment for Forest in this second half. Madueke then isolates his man one-on-one, and wins another corner.

Timber, Merino and Gyokeres are all ready to come on for Arsenal.

The game is see-sawing, Arsenal have a corner after Calafiori fed Madueke down the left and his cross was blocked. Sels punches away, and then Odegaard loses some patience and tries to find Calafiori with a pass that is not on.

Saka and Rice lose duels when fishing for fouls and Forest have another corner. Arsenal’s performance level has certainly not improved since half-time.

Arsenal clear, but Odegaard blocks a cross and Forest win a second corner in quick succession. Excellent goalkeeping from Raya to claim, and he bowls the ball forward quickly, but Forest snuff out the danger against Madueke.

The first half was an attack against defence session for long periods but Arsenal know they are in an arm wrestle now. Forest far more aggressive, and the crowd are more involved. But that could open up avenues of space. White with a really poor pass towards Saka which is astray.

Arsenal have a corner of their own after breaking from Raya’s gloves. Much more open game so far.

Forest deal with Saka’s delivery, and there was a very brief VAR check for a handball penalty. Nothing doing.

Madueke looking dangerous, receiving a Gabriel ball over the top and dashing inside but his shot was blocked.

The winger then tried to make amends, but he gave away a free-kick at the expense of a booking.

Delap’s shot from a tight angle is then deflected wide. Forest corner, from which Murillo’s header loops into Raya’s gloves. Forest showing more attacking ambition.

Liam Delap is producing a very decent centre-forward performance.

The £50m record signing is proving a real threat with his power and running.

Madueke and Rice not one the same wavelength, before Delap does well to win a shoulder to shoulder with Gabriel only to slice his cross behind for an Arsenal goal kick. Sums up the lack of attacking quality in the game.

Forest have another free-kick in a shooting position after Havertz is penalised for blocking a long shot with his hand. McAtee’s effort from the free-kick is scooped miles over the bar.

Both teams looking livelier in the early exchanges of the half, but Forest’s counter-attack was the more dangerous, with Liam Delap doing well to hold on to the ball and whipping a cross into the box that was just ahead of Williams.

Noni Madueke replaces Eberechi Eze, so a more natural wide player on his stronger foot on Arsenal’s left flank.

Frustrating first half for Arsenal and Mikel Arteta will be demanding more from his attacking players.

Arsenal have not registered a shot on target so far and their delivery from set-pieces has been poor.

Forest look relatively comfortable and had the best chance of the half with a shot from Dan Ndoye which was saved by David Raya.

Are we heading for a hat-trick of 0-0 draws at the City Ground between these two teams?

A very uneventful 45 minutes which has been played at the pace of a pre-season game at times. Similarities with the last two fixtures between these teams at the City Ground, and Arsenal’s games against Leeds and Lille this week. They put their foot on the pedal after half-time in both games, and they need to do the same here.

Guimaraes is off the pitch, and there will be more than two minutes added now as a result of his treatment. Forest win a corner, but Havertz heads away at the near post.

Just the two minutes of added time to play.

Liam Delap wins a free-kick in a shooting position for Forest after Arsenal were caught with numbers forward. Big moment for the home team, this. Calafiori was caught on the ball again, he has not had the best of games.

Williams and McAtee are over the free keek, which is around 25 yards out, left of centre.

Williams blasts the ball into Bruno Guimaraes, who goes down and stays down after taking the shot flush in the face.

More incisive from Arsenal, with Rice punching the ball into Odegaard and then on to Havertz but the angle was always against him and the German could only shoot into the side-netting. Forest have defended very well, overall. Although they have been deep for the most part, they have jumped and pushed out at the right times to stop Arsenal accessing the box.

Glasner and Arteta dish out some instruction while there is a stoppage in play to deal with a hand in the face that troubled Schlager. Can either side find a breakthrough before the break?

David Raya claimed that Forest corner with ease and the game has now resumed its pattern. Forest retreating into their shape, and Arsenal passing in front of them. Schlager penalised for a foul on Saka, the home fans not happy with the decision, I think because Saka was going away from goal.

Rice clips in a menacing delivery, but Havertz skewed his header wide from seven or eight yards. Good chance, Arsenal’s best so far.

More Arsenal probing but the small details are letting them down: Eze’s return to Odegaard forced his team-mate to check, and then Odegaard’s touch was heavy after a wall pass from Guimaraes.

Delap does well to make a nuisance of himself at the other end, and his long-range shot deflects behind for a corner.

Strong from Konsa to win the ball, drive out of defence and win a foul. Rice with a well-weighted scoop over the Forest defence for the run of Ben White, but he skewed his cross behind for a goal kick.

Arsenal with another corner. No doubt they have been the game’s dominant force when it comes to possession and territory, but there has been a lack of cutting edge so far. Saka goes for the near post again but Forest deal with it. The home crowd groan at Sels for not releasing the ball quickly in search of a break.

Arsenal work the ball across their midfield with Guimaraes, Rice and Odegaard all involved, and a dangerous Saka cross is headed behind for a corner.

Scramble! The near-post flick on caused chaos and Konsa’s goal-bound backheel was blocked, but the ball would not quite drop for Ben White to score a tap-in.

After two successive goalless draws here between the two clubs, this is following a similar script so far.

It’s a very tight affair with Arsenal enjoying more of the possession but Forest seemingly happy with that and content to them on the break.

Bruno Guimaraes has made a bright start for the visitors.

Forest’s best attacking moment of the game and it comes from an Arsenal mistake.

Calafiori just had to play a five-yard pass back to Gabriel but scuffed it, and Munoz pounced. Running at the Arsenal penalty area, Munoz’s cross was deflected to the back post and the ball found it’s way to Ndoye. Decent reverse shot through legs, but Raya had it covered and tipped around the post.

From the corner, Forest are penalised for a foul.

Arsenal continue to have Forest penned in their own half, very difficult for the home team to play through the midfield or over Konsa and Gabriel so far.

Saka produces his first successful dribble to beat Williams, and the left wing-back trips him at the expense of a free-kick and a booking. Rice’s delivery from the right was uncharacteristically poor.

Munoz tries to drag Forest up the pitch to apply some pressure on Arsenal but he is penalised for a shirt pull on Gabriel. The atmosphere sounds pretty sleepy, a result of some tepid Arsenal possession and Forest’s bad home record.

Forest making sure they have numbers around Saka whenever Arsenal funnel attacks down their right, which is almost always their preferred side.

Neat from Guimaraes in midfield to turn and find Saka with some earlier service, and Sels tips his cross away from danger.

Delap and Ndoye waiting for a slip-up or counter-attack but they are feeding on scraps at the moment. Arsenal yet to carve out a proper chance, though.

It’s already pretty clear that one of the key duels today will be between Gabriel and Liam Delap.

Forest’s record signing Delap has already let Gabriel know he’s in the game with his physicality.

Cute pass from Bruno Guimaraes to break the Forest midfield line and find Odegaard, but strangely the Arsenal captain could not sort his feet out to control the ball and back a clean pass. Then Williams defends well against Saka from an Arsenal attacking transition.

Pretty subdued start from Forest. The crowd’s spirits were raised there by Delap chasing down Konsa who had the deal with the sun his eyes, but the Forest striker pushed him in the back.

Arsenal enjoying all of the possession so far, and most of it has come in Forest’s half. One or two players on Arsenal’s right/Forest’s left struggling with the low evening sun. Havertz did get in behind but his cross into the middle was too strong.

Arsenal get the game under way, and play short from kick-off.

There will be a degree of pressure on birthday boy James McAtee today to make an impression.

With Morgan Gibbs-White injured, McAtee is likely to take the No 10 position and continue his redemption arc.

McAtee has been revitalised since the arrival of Oliver Glasner and this is a big afternoon for the former England under 21 international.

In honour of nine-year-old Forest fan James Kerry, who died earlier this month of cancer.

We'll wear black armbands this afternoon, as we join our hosts in remembering nine-year-old Nottingham Forest supporter, James Kerry, who passed away earlier this month following a brave battle with cancer. Rest in peace, James ❤️ https://t.co/YFIXnCfJJX

Surely we cannot have another 0-0 in this fixture? Looking at the talent in Arsenal’s front third, and the fact they are playing their two most offensive full-backs, this might be more open than assummed.

Arsenal can cut Manchester City’s lead to three points with a win today but does it all matter?

Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict is threatening to run into next year and this title race feels fake and damaged.

It is a sham of a season with the prospect of asterisks all over the Premier League campaign.

Arsenal can only carry on as normal as they defend their title but this is an unsatisfactory mess.

The margins are really small and it’s a team and a manager that we know really well, extraordinary manager, really well organised.

They are dangerous in many areas, a very well set-up team and you need to be very tight, very neat, very efficient in everything that you do. You have to insist and insist, and then there’s a lot of volume of actions.

[On coming from behind] Yes, and it’s part of the game, your capacity when something doesn’t go as planned to react and still win the game, and we know the challenge that we have here. In the last two years, we haven’t been able to win here and that’s an opportunity as well to show what we are made of.

Another reason Arsenal will be feeling confident today is Forest’s abysmal home form in the Premier League.

It may surprise neutrals outside of Nottingham but results at the City Ground have been poor for some time.

Indeed, it is just two league wins in 11 months in front of their own supporters which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Before this game, Forest’s head coach Oliver Glasner said: “We have to change it. I spoke to one or two experienced lads who know Forest better than I do and talked about the situation. But if you always talk about the problem it makes it bigger and bigger.

“We haven’t scored a goal at home yet or won a game at home, and that is what we have to change.”

Trips to the City Ground have seldom been easy for Mikel Arteta, with two successive 0-0 draws in the Premier League.

An FA Cup defeat in Jan 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparked a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

Yet Arsenal have secured two wins in a row since that defeat at Brighton, without being truly at their fluent best, and will be confident against a Forest team without injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White.

Dominguez and Schlager are the preferred midfield pair in the 3-4-2-1 with Sangare on the bench. McAtee and Ndoye will support Liam Delap in attack. Much attacking responsibility on Munoz at right wing-back, who also has the cavalier Calafiori on his side of the pitch, which could prove fireworks.

No surprise that Havertz, Odegaard, Saka and Calafiori are restored to Arsenal’s Premier League starting XI having started on the bench in mid-week. Eze over Madueke and Guimaraes over Lewis-Skelly were closer calls for Arteta. Ben White comes in for Timber, with Arsenal managing the minutes of both right-backs.

🟡 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🔵 Your Sunday starters 👊 🤝 Presented by @deel

Fascinating stuff from Sam Dean this morning, who has profiled a member of Mikel Arteta’s inner circle who is not listed on Arsenal’s website. Germán Castaños, an expert in innovation who has written multiple books on alternative thinking, has become a key member of the team. Things started with a phone call with Nicolas Jover, then a meeting with Arteta and now he splits his time between Argentina and London. Find out more about Arsenal’s mystery man and his methods here.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Manchester United have officially confirmed an agreement to hire Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager to replace Michael Carrick.

Carrick’s sacking was announced yesterday, and now Man Utd have provided a further update by confirming that Pochettino will be their new manager with immediate effect.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager is leaving his role as head coach of the United States Men’s National Team to take over at Old Trafford, and the club praised him in their official statement.

“The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players,” United said on their website.

“Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues. He began his coaching career with Espanyol in 2009 before joining Southampton and achieving a club-record Premier League points tally in 2014.

“During five full seasons at Tottenham Hotspur, Pochettino established the club as regular UEFA Champions League contenders, securing qualification in four consecutive seasons and leading the club to its first final in the competition in 2019.

“In 2021, he joined Paris Saint-Germain, where he won the Ligue 1 title, the Coupe de France and the Trophée des Champions before joining Chelsea in 2023.”

Pochettino’s work at Spurs really stands out in his career so far, where he managed to make the club more competitive than they’ve ever been in the modern era.

The 54-year-old also achieved that without requiring huge amounts of money to spend, instead working with top young talents and helping them develop into superstars, most notably Harry Kane and Son Heung-min.

It will be interesting to see if Pochettino can now have better luck at turning things around for MUFC after a bit of a dismal recent period.

#1334. NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease. A prototypical example of such a disconnect is the NLRP3 inflammasome, which mediates inflammation in diverse settings of disease and protective immunity1,2. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro requires two signals: (1) priming by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides and (2) activation by molecules that disrupt cellular homeostasis1,3. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome in vivo is activated by lipopolysaccharide alone. The mechanisms that underlie the difference between in vitro and in vivo activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome are undefined. Here we report that extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness is a determinant of NLRP3 activities and that in vitro systems using physiological ECM stiffness enable one-signal in vivo-like NLRP3 activities to occur in human and mouse phagocytes. Physiological ECM stiffness induced expression of the transcription factor NRF2, which was found to be necessary for one-signal NLRP3 activation. Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Macrophages derived from the stiff matrix of the bone—osteoclasts—had reduced NRF2 levels and impaired NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. These findings indicate that NRF2 may be a transcriptional checkpoint that controls NLRP3 inflammasome activity.

Inflammasomes are cytoplasmic organelles that mediate inflammatory responses to infection and injury, primarily through the cleavage and release of the interleukin-1 (IL-1) family of cytokines3. Diverse proteins can seed inflammasome assembly, with NLRP3 being the best characterized and most commonly associated with human disease. NLRP3 activation in vitro requires two signals1. Signal 1 is provided by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which sensitizes (that is, primes) the NLRP3 pathway for responsiveness to subsequent stimuli. Signal 2 can be provided by a diverse set of stimuli, all of which induce interactions between NLRP3 and the protein ASC, which leads to the recruitment and activation of caspase-1 (refs. 1,4). The NLRP3–ASC–caspase-1 complex represents the minimal components of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Activated caspase-1 in the inflammasome cleaves pro-IL-1β and the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD), which leads to the release of bioactive IL-1β (IL-1β p17) and pyroptosis5,6,7,8.

Although this two-signal model holds true for NLRP3 activation in vitro, LPS alone is sufficient to activate NLRP3 in vivo9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16. An explanation for the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo NLRP3 activation remains elusive and was investigated herein.

We investigated the kinetics of NLRP3 activation in vivo after intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of LPS into mice. LPS injection induced the NLRP3-dependent accumulation of IL-1β in the serum within 3 h (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Caspase-11 is a regulator of LPS-induced IL-1β production in vivo. Caspase-11 was dispensable for IL-1β accumulation in the serum 3 h after LPS injection but was required for IL-1β production 6 h after LPS injection (Extended Data Fig. 1c). These data indicate that LPS can activate NLRP3 rapidly and independently of caspase-11. Within 1 h of LPS injection, cleaved IL-1β was detected in the peritoneal fluid (Fig. 1a,b). Nlrp3−/− mice did not accumulate IL-1β in the peritoneal fluid after LPS injection (Extended Data Fig. 1d). The speed of IL-1β p17 production observed in the peritoneal fluid suggested that a pool of resident cells is responsible. We depleted peritoneal macrophages using clodronate liposomes17, which led to the loss of 99.8% of these cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Under these conditions, i.p. LPS injections induced minimal production of IL-1β (Fig. 1c). However, ex vivo LPS stimulations of isolated resident peritoneal macrophages did not induce IL-1β production from these cells (Extended Data Fig. 1f). By contrast, LPS induced the secretion of TNF from ex vivo cultured peritoneal macrophages (Extended Data Fig. 1g). These data suggest that peritoneal macrophages secrete IL-1β in vivo in response to LPS treatment but lose this capability ex vivo.

One distinction between the experimental methodologies used in vitro and in vivo is the ECM. Normal tissue has a stiffness of 1–10 kilopascals (kPa), whereas plastic Petri dishes have a stiffness of 3,000,000 kPa18,19,20. Macrophages have the ability to sense and adapt to ECM stiffness21,22,23,24,25,26. To determine the effect of ECM stiffness on NLRP3 inflammasome activities, we varied the ECM stiffness on which macrophages are cultured. We selected plastic Petri dishes overlaid with polydimethylsiloxane to model the stiffness of normal tissue (soft plates, 2 kPa) and fibrotic tissue (stiff plates, 32 kPa), and used plastic Petri dishes as a control (plastic plates, 3,000,000 kPa)19,27. Plates were functionalized through the adsorption of fibronectin onto the surface. Isolated resident peritoneal macrophages cultured on surfaces mimicking normal tissue stiffness displayed the in vivo-like ability to release cleaved IL-1β in response to LPS alone (Fig. 1d). This ability to produce IL-1β was reduced as ECM stiffness increased (Fig. 1d). Similar findings were observed with mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). BMDMs cultured on soft plates (but not plastic) induced NLRP3-dependent IL-1β release (Fig. 1e,f). No effect of ECM stiffness was observed on NLRP3 protein abundance or on the LPS-stimulated activation of MAP kinase pathways (Fig. 1g,h). There was an increase in phosphorylation of NF-κB p65 in BMDMs grown on both soft and stiff ECM compared with plastic, but this result did not correlate with IL-1β secretion (Fig. 1e,g).

In BMDMs cultured on soft ECM, LPS was sufficient to stimulate the production and cleavage of pro-IL-1β, the cleavage of caspase-1 and the cleavage and oligomerization of GSDMD (Fig. 1i,j). With the exception of pro-IL-1β production (which proceeds via TLR4), all these inflammasome-associated activities were reduced or non-existent as the stiffness of the ECM was increased to that of plastic. LPS-induced IL-1β release on soft ECM required NLRP3 but not caspase-11 (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1h). These data highlight the selective sensitivity of the NLRP3 pathway to changes in ECM stiffness.

Similar assays were performed using human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs). Human MDMs cultured on soft ECM produced cleaved IL-1β in response to LPS (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 1i). Inhibition of NLRP3 using the chemical MCC950 (ref. 28) prevented the production of cleaved IL-1β (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 1j). In human monocytes, LPS can promote IL-1β production via NLRP3 through a process that is insensitive to potassium efflux inhibition29. LPS stimulations were performed in the presence of high concentrations of extracellular potassium, a method to prevent potassium efflux30. Under these conditions, LPS-induced IL-1β production was inhibited (Extended Data Fig. 1k). The means by which macrophages link soft ECM to NLRP3 activation is therefore distinct from the behaviours of human monocytes.

We determined how long macrophages must adapt to ECM stiffness before LPS-induced IL-1β production is observed. LPS stimulation of BMDMs cultured on soft ECM for 16 h induced IL-1β production (Fig. 1e,f), whereas stimulation of BMDMs cultured on soft ECM for 2 h did not (Extended Data Fig. 2a). To determine whether macrophages require integrin-mediated interactions, we cultured BMDMs on soft ECM coated with either fibronectin (to facilitate integrin interactions) or poly-l-lysine (to facilitate charge-based interactions). Macrophages cultured on poly-l-lysine did not produce IL-1β when stimulated with LPS, despite secreting IL-6 (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). To determine whether adhesion is required, we cultured BMDMs in suspension and compared them to cells adhered to plastic plates. Cells in suspension did not secrete IL-1β when stimulated with LPS but maintained their responsiveness to LPS + ATP (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Macrophages may therefore require hours-long, integrin-mediated adhesion to adapt to ECM stiffness.

We performed RNA sequencing of BMDMs cultured on ECM of variable stiffness for 2 h or overnight (16 h). BMDMs cultured for 2 h were transcriptionally similar regardless of ECM stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 2e). BMDMs cultured overnight demonstrated stiffness-dependent differences in gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Differential gene expression analyses of BMDMs cultured overnight revealed several hundred genes induced on soft ECM and suppressed on plastic (Fig. 2a). Ingenuity pathway analysis of genes induced only on soft ECM identified the NRF2-mediated stress response pathway as a top hit (Fig. 2b,c).
