#1332. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Florian Wirtz has scored or assisted in three consecutive games for the first time in his Liverpool career: 🅰️ vs LASK 🅰️ vs Brentford ⚽️ vs Villarreal https://t.co/woLWk2SGGL

It was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

It’s up there with one of the best I’ve played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot.

Whenever I get the ball and there’s an opportunity to go one v one or two v one, I believe in myself. I’ll just keep going and be ruthless.

Rio Ngumoha talking to Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime: “Definitely one of the best games I played. I enjoyed it.  Whenever I get the ball and go one v one, the more it makes the opposition worried.”

When he was reminded that he was the youngest Englishman to provide an assist in the Champions League, he said: “Records are amazing to break.”

And on playing on the right instead of the left wing: “It’s helped me a lot in training. Slowly I’m getting better on the right.”

And to hear the crowd chanting his name: “This stadium, we have the best fans. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.”

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

On the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Just the three minutes of added time to play, and Liverpool are probably grateful for that.

Could Liverpool be in for a nervous finish? Their defence is caught square again after a run in behind from Ayoze Perez, and Oluwaseyi was totally unmarked at the back post to apply a simple finish at silence Anfield.

Cody Gakpo threatens to score Liverpool’s fifth with an overhead free-kick, teed up by McConnell’s chipped cross to the back post, but he could not keep the attempt down.

The game is meandering towards its conclusion now, though a Villarreal goal would make things interesting.

Another Liverpool youngster enjoys a taste of first-team actions: James McConnell is on for Nyoni.

2 - Rio Ngumoha (18y 52d) is the third-youngest player to provide multiple assists in a UEFA Champions League game behind Warren Zaïre-Emery v Milan (17y 231d) and Theo Walcott v Hamburger SV (17y 250d). Flying. https://t.co/CUbbleRhEJ

Perez hits the post for Villarreal with only Alisson to beat, but the flag is raised for offside. I think that would have stood had he found the net, Van Dijk may have been playing him just onside.

Ngumoha receives his standing ovation, lovely moment for him. He has strong claims to be in Liverpool’s best XI. Bradley Barcola replaces him, not the player Villarreal’s tired defenders needed to see.

That is surely game over now, Liverpool heading for three Champions League wins from three. Former Newcastle United forward Ayoze Perez is now on for Villarreal. Ngumoha will be replaced by Barcola shortly and I’m sure he will receive a standing ovation.

The game has been transformed, and Villarreal are falling to pieces. They were guilty of losing possession far too cheaply, but Wirtz deserves credit for finishing with an authority he has been accused of lacking. Well struck across the goalkeeper with his left foot, his first Liverpool goal since April.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Ngumoha has been Liverpool’s best player on the night, although Cardona sold himself all too easily near the touchline. Ngumoha makes the right decision to pick out Mac Allister with a low cross, and the midfielder converts with the simplest of finishes.

Isak then replaces Koumas immediately after the goal.

Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal but Anfield also singing about Rio Ngumoha. He went past two Villarreal defenders to create that one. He has been outstanding.

There will be time to talk more about Rio Ngumoha – this is his best performance in a Liverpool shirt, a coming-of-age night if you will – but it cannot be overlooked how Alexis Mac Allister has been transformed. He was unrecognisable last season but now he is every inch the man who was a major cog in the push for the title.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Tsimikas with a dangerous, driven cross from the left which is just beyond the reach of Koumas. Liverpool knocking on the door.

Nyoni’s standing foot was slipping, but he made a clean connection on his shot from range and it whistled just wide of the foot of the post. Ngumoha then has the crowd cooing again, with another drop of the shoulder to beat his man.

Gravenberch found himself sweeping up as Liverpool’s last man, there. The second half has had a more conventional feel, Liverpool making the running as they shoot towards the Kop and their opponents soaking up the pressure. A game of fewer chances since the break.

Always helps having knowledge in close vicinity: a quick discussion with Rafa Benitez about Liverpool’s set up for the second period. Ryan Gravenberch hasn’t been moved to play as a right-back, even though you might think that is the case. Liverpool, essentially, are playing man-against-man. It is going to ask players to be brave on the ball and composed when they are in possession, as the slightest slip will lead to problems. It is high risk and high reward.

Not enough power in Gakpo’s strike from the edge of the area and Gulasci saves. Ngumoha looking such a threat again, attracting the attention of three or four yellow shirts and winning Liverpool another corner. Former Spurs player Juan Foyth has just been introduced by Villarreal.

Liverpool more industrious when they lose possession early in the half. Nyoni then produces a silky turn away from pressure deep in his own half which elicits an “ooohh” from the home fans.

Gravenberch took the ball off Ngumoha’s toes in the box, and the Dutchman’s shot from a tight angle was saved by Gulasci at his near post. I think Ngumoha deserved to have the shot himself after more great skill to find a yard.

Wirtz replaces Araujo, which could mean Gravenberch at right-back.

Oluwaseyi, another of Villarreal’s Canadian cohort, is on too. He replaces Saliba.

Florian Wirtz has been readied for action and will soon enter the fray. You would think these will be the kind of conditions in which he will excel. He needs to. Liverpool are lucky to be level.

03:54 - Georges Mikautadze's opener for Villarreal (03:54) is the second-earliest goal Liverpool have conceded at home in major European competition behind only Elpídio Silva's strike in the 3rd minute for Boavista in the UEFA Champions League in September 2001. Cold. https://t.co/NvKmS5jLap

Dreadful first 30 minutes from Liverpool but they have woken up since, and now they are strong favourites to win the game from here. Iraola’s selection gamble backfired somewhat, but he may well get away with it.

From the second phase of a corner, Ngumoha did well to keep the ball alive and lift a cross to the back post. Cardona tried to usher the ball behind and made the fatal mistake of letting it bounce in his penalty area, and Araujo sneaked in to score from close range.

The goalscorer Cardona makes a mistake to let Ngumoha’s cross drift to the backpost. That’s Liverpool’s equaliser from Ronald Araujo. As soon as Liverpool have got their act together they have looked dangerous.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

The crowd were impatient with him early in the half, but Gakpo is looking more of a threat now, Cruyff-turning away and shooting in the box but Veiga was across to block. Just the one minute of added time to play.

Gakpo wins Liverpool a free-kick in a shooting position left of centre, tripped after Nyoni had carried the ball well through midfield. Too much air on the attempt from Mac Allister, who a couple of minutes earlier fired not too far wide from 25 yards.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Really slick interplay from Villarreal again, and Moleiro’s shot from 25 yards is pushed over the bar by Alisson. You can pick holes in Liverpool, but Villarreal’s play deserves plaudits too.

Alexis Mac Allister grabs a goal back for Liverpool 🔴 Game 🔛 https://t.co/Ml9OYgbNq6

Liverpool have scarcely merited a goal but they have one via a set-piece. Alexis Mac Allister was up early at the near post and he produced a well-directed glancing header into the far corner. That changes the complexion of the game.

Great finish from Mac Allister. The opportunity for Gakpo to cross from the left - that won the corner - was made by Koumas’ hold-up play. First time he has really got hold of it and pinned the defender.

Another run from deep causes Liverpool’s defence problems, but Mikautadze took a touch when a first-time pass could have released the runner through on goal. More groans from the crowd when Tsimikas is caught on the ball.

Then Gakpo flashes a better ball across the face of goal, and Veiga glances it behind for a Liverpool corner.

Villarreal want a corner, and they should have one after a shot deflects off Araujo’s back. Goal kick given though.

Gakpo and Koumas are on the wrong wavelength, and there are groans from the crowd at another misplaced pass.

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1331. When I overtook Jim Leighton, that was when I started to wind Kenny up about beating his cap tally... ANDY ROBERTSON on going level with Dalglish

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:28 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:04 EST, 12 November 2026

It's a story which extols the virtues of loyalty and leadership in the proper sense.

More than anything, though, Andy Robertson’s achievements in football are – and always will be – reminders of what’s possible when a talented individual takes rejection as their motivation to redefine themselves in the eyes of the world.

Even though it’s been told many times before, the tale of the full-back’s determination to bounce back from being shown the door as a teenager by Celtic will never grow old.

Without having the character to overcome such adversity, he would not have been caught in the safety net at Queen’s Park. There would have been no moves to Dundee United and Hull. No Champions League and title-winning medals from his time with Liverpool. No first cap for his country.

In terms of a life lesson for those aspiring footballers who may find themselves in a cul-de-sac in their own careers, it has few equals.

All being well, Robertson will make his 102nd appearance for Scotland against North Macedonia, equalling the record tally of his idol and great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Andy Robertson will go level with Kenny Dalglish as Scotland's record cap holder on Friday

Both men are proud Glaswegians and Scots who bonded throughout their time together at Anfield. Dalglish would be the first to admit, though, that their respective paths have been distinct.

With a God-given talent so bright it could blind you, Dalglish was a superstar in the making before he wore a Scotland jersey for the first time against Belgium in 1971.

Coming in a friendly in Poland in 2014, Robertson’s first appearance only arrived after those early struggles.

It took huge character for him to even get that far. To add a century more across a dozen years under four different managers is a gargantuan achievement.

Football has a funny habit of throwing up strange co-incidences. Yesterday happened to be 40 years to the day since Dalglish won the last of his caps in a 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Characteristically, before he took his own walk down memory lane, the man who’ll join him on that mark this evening was at pains to give the Anfield icon his rightful place.

‘It’s not really about me,’ Robertson insisted. ‘For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he (Dalglish) achieved in his career, for the person he is... tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest in Scotland.

Dalglish scored 30 goals in his 102 caps and is regarded as Scotland's greatest ever player

‘Obviously, in terms of the number, I will stand side by side with him. But I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.

‘Because, for me, he was arguably the best player in the world at one time and will always be the greatest in this country, no matter what happens in the future.

‘He’ll always be the first one to do X, Y and Z. I just think that shouldn’t be forgotten.

‘Tomorrow is definitely a reason to do that for Kenny.’

There is, though, still no understating what Robertson has achieved across 12 years. Playing for Scotland wasn’t always the joy that it’s been in more recent times.

‘We get looked after so well off the pitch,’ he offered. ‘That probably wasn’t always the case when I first came in.

‘Under Gordon (Strachan) in my first qualifying campaign, I think I was still young enough to not think too much about it. But then I also remember under Alex McLeish and then the start of Steve Clarke, there was a real disconnect between the country and the players.

‘There wasn’t too much love for the players. We were getting 10,000, 15,000 inside Hampden. That was the most difficult time, especially as captain and being at Liverpool as well.’

He stuck at it and never shirked responsibility. In time he was able to chalk up the numbers because the side steadily improved and broke through the glass ceiling.

Robertson shares a laugh with Nathan Patterson ahead of the visit of North Macedonia

‘Of course, I would be sitting here with a few less caps if we hadn’t been successful,’ he reflected. ‘The fact that we got to two Euros, a World Cup and all the warm-up games and things like that resulted in me having an extra maybe 15 caps.

‘What makes it more special to me is the fact that we’ve managed to achieve things.’

All of this was beyond his wildest dreams at the beginning. A late substitute for Barry Bannan in a friendly in Warsaw on March 5, 2014, he can still hear Gordon Strachan whispering in his ear.

‘He basically said, “Don’t be scared, don’t go into your shell”,’ he recalled. ‘He said, “The reason I’ve picked you is because you’re brave. I see you bombing up and down the pitch for Dundee United”. He said, “Go and be that player”.

‘I always remember the first ball came to me and the words were ringing in my ears. I think I carried it 30 yards forward. It gave me the confidence to just go and try and play exactly the way I was playing under Jackie McNamara.’

Four years later, by then a Liverpool player, Robertson was handed the armband by McLeish following Scott Brown’s retirement.

‘That made me grow up and made me realise what it took to become a leader,’ he reflected. ‘I kind of grew into it. I believe that I became the captain that I wanted to be.’

It was only when he equalled McLeish’s 77 appearances that the prospect of one day equalling or surpassing Dalglish entered his head.

‘I think everyone in the room and everyone who personally knows me well enough knows that personal achievements aren’t really what I focus on,’ he said. ‘But I would lie if I said this wasn’t one that I’ve chased.

Like Dalglish, Robertson is a Liverpool icon having made 378 appearances for the Anfield club

‘I think when I overtook Darren Fletcher (80 caps), when I was in the 80s, it felt like ages for me to get to Jim Leighton (91). Then I thought I’ve only got one more person to go.

‘That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen, started to wind Kenny up a bit more that it was going to happen.

‘I think that was maybe when I realised that this was maybe possible if I got lucky with injuries, if I kept playing for Liverpool.

‘Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of. My international career has been everything for me.’

To wear the armband at one international tournament would have been a laudable achievement in itself. To do so three times would have seemed an impossible feat in those difficult early days.

The hunger to repeat the trick at Euro 2028 is as strong as ever.

‘I’ve always kept pushing,’ he said. ‘We’re always trying something new. My wife asked me a similar question last week when we were talking about it. I was going to try and catch Gemma Fay (203 caps), but I think that might be a little bit too far from me...’

Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi has previously been a transfer target for Bayern Munich, but at the moment he’d be too expensive.

The Spain international has fallen down the pecking order in recent times, with Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta favouring Myles Lewis-Skelly at the end of last season and then signing Bruno Guimaraes in the summer.

Still, Zubimendi looks too expensive for Bayern at the moment, while there also doesn’t look to be room in Vincent Kompany’s squad for another midfielder right now, according to Christian Falk.

Writing in his latest CF Bayern Insider column, Falk said: “Bayern will not go for the Spaniard in the winter. What I can say is that he was on the list of Bayern Munich in the past before he got his move to the Premier League. Bayern Munich were scouting him and there were talks, but in the end, it wasn’t a match!

“Now, I don’t think it’s the right time to go for him. There just isn’t the space in the midfield department. He will also be very expensive, and FC Bayern are searching in other positions. Bayern admire Zubimendi but they won’t go for him in the January transfer window.”

Zubimendi started well at Arsenal and surely still has it in him to contribute something to Arteta’s squad over the course of a long season in which they’re sure to struggle with injuries and suspensions at some point.

The 27-year-old will perhaps be patient enough to wait for an opportunity, as it seems unlikely that Arteta will just continue to freeze him out after showing so much trust in him for large chunks of the previous campaign.

Still, talkSPORT have linked Zubimendi as a target for Atletico Madrid, and there’s every chance that big clubs like that could come in for him at some point and offer him a tempting opportunity.

Arsenal fans will be relieved, however, to hear that Zubimendi himself has played down talk of an imminent departure.

“I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season. As he does with all the players, he explained the plan to me,” Zubimendi said to Marca, as quoted and translated by the Metro.

“He warned me that there were new signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

“I understand because, for me, we’re among the five best teams in Europe. There are some fantastic players. New signings have arrived in my position, and there were already some very good players. I’m also part of that competition that makes it so difficult to get playing time.

“I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation. It’s something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too.

“I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side. I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.”

#1329. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. Manchester United’s players piled the pressure on Michael Carrick with a horror show against Cesc Fabregas’s Como. United’s worst start to a season for four decades plumbed new depths after their worst display of the campaign yet. Here, Telegraph Sport dissects their nightmare evening.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Manchester United’s trip to Como in the Champions League. Under normal circumstances, a visit to the idyllic Lombardy city would be a source of thrill and wonder, but Michael Carrick heads into the eye of a literal and proverbial storm at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia with his team desperately hoping to reverse their fortunes.

Absolutely tipping it down in Como, with 64mm of rain forecast before #MUFC kick-off here tomorrow ☔️ https://t.co/WvI3X8dilh

Two wins – against Ipswich Town and Sabah – in United’s first 10 matches of the season, a public outburst from Lisandro Martínez and accusations of a “toxic culture” at the club have piled pressure on Carrick. And an uninspiring draw at Elland Road on Sunday did little to settle the rising tide of discontent within the United fanbase.

When asked for his team news, the first words that came from the United head coach’s mouth were: “Right, bit of mixed bag to be honest.” That was not a great sign, and Carrick will be without Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu, who are injured, while Leny Yoro serves a suspension following his red card against Atlético Madrid.

Like United, the hosts are without a handful of key players, with Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao and Jesus Rodriguez missing from the match-day squad. The abundantly talented Argentine No 10 Nico Paz will feature, however, and he will be keen to showcase his talents in the Champions League.

Como have ascended from Serie B to Europe’s top table in three seasons (and from bankruptcy in nine) under Cesc Fàbregas’ watchful eye. The Spaniard is a minority owner and shareholder of the club, but as head coach he has introduced an incisive, possession-based style of play which contains hints of the managerial greats under whom he played: Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho, Vicente del Bosque, Antonio Conte etc.

#1328. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative condition. Recently, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting SOD1 and FUS have shown early promise in clinical trials9,10, but these approaches only benefit patients with SOD1 and FUS mutations—less than 3% of patients with ALS—leaving an urgent need for therapies for the remaining roughly 97% of patients with ALS. A common feature of all non-FUS and non-SOD1 ALS is the aggregation of TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) in neurons1,2, a finding also observed in roughly 50% of both frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease2,11. However, no therapies that directly target TDP-43 are available, leaving the underlying nuclear loss of function (LoF) unaddressed. TDP-43 is an RNA-binding protein that is normally located in the nucleus and has crucial roles in the regulation of RNA splicing12,13. Cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 induces a nuclear LoF resulting in cryptic exon inclusion, cryptic alternative polyadenylation and/or exon skipping in some mature messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts3. These events occur in hundreds of transcripts, including genes with crucial neuronal functions, such as STMN2, UNC13A and KCNQ2 (refs. 4,5,6,7,8). Whereas the impact of STMN2 mis-splicing on axonal regeneration and KCNQ2 exon skipping on intrinsic excitability has been studied, the direct impact of TDP-43 LoF on synaptic function has not been addressed.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have shown that single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within and proximal to a cryptic exon in UNC13A increase the risk of developing ALS and accelerate disease progression14,15,16. Under normal physiological conditions, these risk SNPs do not induce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, but after TDP-43 LoF, risk SNPs exacerbate cryptic exon inclusion leading to increased loss of functional RNA transcripts and protein6,7. UNC13A is a presynaptic protein that is required at the active zone to properly dock and prime synaptic vesicles for fusion with the plasma membrane17. Genetic deletion of Unc13a in mice leads to a roughly 90% reduction in spontaneous and evoked glutamatergic excitatory synaptic transmission18,19,20. Although the UNC13A genetic association strongly implicates this event in ALS pathogenesis, the contribution of TDP-43 LoF to synaptic dysfunction and the role of UNC13A cryptic splicing—particularly in the context of many mis-splicing events in other synaptic transcripts—is unaddressed. Resolving these outstanding questions is crucial for establishing whether correcting UNC13A splicing represents a viable therapeutic approach for restoring normal neuronal function.

Here we report that TDP-43 loss in mature human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell-derived neurons induces loss of presynaptic UNC13A and a notable reduction in AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptor-mediated synaptic transmission, leading to a loss of coordinated network activity. Despite the widespread roles of TDP-43 in RNA regulation, isolated genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon rescues these deficits, demonstrating that this single event is a key driver of synapse dysfunction in ALS. To this end, we developed splice-switching ASOs that can rescue UNC13A mRNA splicing, UNC13A protein levels and UNC13A presynaptic localization, and restore both spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ASO treatment rescues UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion in a humanized mouse model that recreates this human-specific mis-splicing event. Thus, ASOs targeting the UNC13A cryptic exon represent an innovative therapeutic strategy for treating ALS and FTD, and their use for treating sporadic ALS is supported by genetic evidence.

TDP-43 plays important roles in development and therefore, to avoid interfering with neuronal maturation by depleting TDP-43 from the iPS cell stage, we used CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to generate a cell line in which both endogenous copies of TDP-43 harbour a HaloTag to allow for proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC)-mediated21 knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d). TDP-43 is degraded by HaloPROTAC in a dose-dependent manner and in a process blocked by proteasome inhibition or the NEDD8 E1 inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 1e–g). HaloTag-TDP-43 iPS cells were differentiated into mature excitatory cortical-like neurons (HaloTDP iNeurons) that expressed the layer V excitatory cortical marker CTIP2 and lacked expression of the inhibitory marker NKX2.1 or the neuronal progenitor marker PAX6 (Extended Data Fig. 1h). TDP-43 was also found to be correctly localized to the nucleus (Fig. 1b). Tagging of TDP-43 can alter its function and, whereas the HaloTag partially affected TDP-43 function (Extended Data Fig. 1i), UNC13A cryptic splicing and mRNA downregulation were robustly detected only on HaloPROTAC knockdown of TDP-43 (Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2a), similar to CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-mediated knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Loss of UNC13A mRNA led to a time-dependent decrease in UNC13A protein whereby less than 5% of protein remained after 10 days of HaloPROTAC treatment (Fig. 1e,f). Immunofluorescence staining revealed a loss of synaptic UNC13A staining at synapsin-positive puncta (Fig. 1g,h). HaloPROTAC-mediated knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons did not lead to alterations in the RNA levels of N-methyl-d-aspartate and AMPA receptor subunits as assessed by reverse transcription–quantitative PCR (RT–qPCR) (Extended Data Fig. 2g).

Previous investigations of the physiological functions of UNC13A have been mainly conducted using primary rodent neurons with limited studies in human neurons18,19,20,22. We therefore sought to assess the impact of UNC13A loss in human iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Whole-cell patch clamp recordings showed that depletion of UNC13A through CRISPRi impaired synaptic transmission, as evidenced by a reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Fig. 1i), consistent with a presynaptic deficit and in line with previously published work19,20. HaloPROTAC-mediated TDP-43 depletion also reduced mEPSC frequency (Fig. 1j), mirroring the presynaptic deficit observed on UNC13A loss. Treatment with 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) blocked mEPSCs, confirming that synaptic events were mediated primarily by means of fast AMPA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Whereas UNC13A depletion had no effect on mEPSC amplitude, consistent with a purely presynaptic deficit (Extended Data Fig. 3b), TDP-43 depletion led to a modest reduction in amplitude (Extended Data Fig. 3c), suggesting extra postsynaptic deficits independent of UNC13A depletion. Passive membrane properties remained comparable between control and UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e).

To investigate the effect of UNC13A and TDP-43 loss on network activity, we carried out multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings. We found that either UNC13A or TDP-43 depletion induced a disordered and asynchronous pattern of network activity, measured by a reduction in the normalized electrode cross-correlations (Fig. 1k–m). This result indicates that UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons fail to support network-level activity. The number of active electrodes remained consistent (Extended Data Fig. 3g) and phase-contrast images showed comparable cell coverage between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3h), ruling out issues with electrode coverage as a confounding factor. CNQX treatment of control neurons confirmed network synchrony was highly dependent on fast AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Whereas extra MEA metrics were also affected by both TDP-43 and UNC13A loss, the network synchrony deficit was the largest and most consistently observed change (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Thus, we show that TDP-43 depletion substantially impairs fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission and synchronized network activity in human neurons, mirroring a comparable loss of synaptic function and network activity induced by direct UNC13A loss.

Knockdown of TDP-43 leads to cryptic exon inclusion within UNC13A intron 20 along with an independent downstream intron retention event at intron 31 and other lower-frequency splicing abnormalities throughout the UNC13A mRNA transcript6,7. To determine the degree to which protein loss is dependent on the UNC13A intron 20 cryptic exon, we performed CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing to remove the cryptic exon from the genome of SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Using two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) we made a homozygous deletion of 233 nucleotides (nt) that contain both splice acceptors and the common donor splice site of the cryptic exon. In wild-type (WT) cells containing the full UNC13A gene there was robust induction of UNC13A mis-splicing after TDP-43 depletion as assessed by reverse transcription–PCR (RT–PCR) (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d), whereas in cells with genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, no cryptic splicing was detected (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Cryptic exon deletion rescued correctly spliced levels of UNC13A mRNA, as determined by RT–qPCR, and led to roughly 75% rescue of UNC13A protein following TDP-43 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). We subsequently deleted the UNC13A cryptic exon in iPS cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a–e) and detected a similar rescue in UNC13A RNA and protein following CRISPRi-mediated knockdown of TDP-43, confirming the relevance of this event in iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5f–k). In the UNC13A cryptic exon deletion cell line, we performed further CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to add a HaloTag in the TARDBP gene to efficiently induce TDP-43 loss after differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 6). Similar to results in SH-SY5Y cells, genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in HaloTDP iNeurons rescued UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction and restored mRNA and presynaptic protein levels (Fig. 2a–h), demonstrating this splicing event is the main driver of TDP-43-dependent UNC13A loss.

TDP-43 knockdown yields synaptic transmission defects similar to those induced by direct depletion of UNC13A. However, TDP-43 has hundreds of validated RNA targets, regulating splicing, stability and transport of transcripts involved in virtually every aspect of neuronal function. Therefore, the reduction in synaptic transmission could reflect a multi-gene insult affecting pathways including synaptic vesicle trafficking, Ca2+ signalling and active zone organization. To determine the extent to which UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion contributes to impaired synaptic function following loss of TDP-43, we performed whole-cell patch clamping experiments in WT and cryptic exon deletion lines. Rescue of this single cryptic exon largely restored synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion with an 80% recovery in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 2i,j). mEPSC amplitude was still marginally (roughly 10%) reduced, supporting the conclusion that UNC13A cryptic exon deletion rescues specifically presynaptic function (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Passive membrane properties were similar between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7b). As mEPSC frequency is influenced by synapse number, we measured excitatory synapse density along the dendrites of iNeurons. We found that TDP-43-knockdown neurons had fewer synapses than controls, a feature that persisted even when the UNC13A cryptic exon was deleted (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d), suggesting a strong recovery in synapse function in the remaining synapses.

Despite the small reduction in synapse number, MEA recordings showed that deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in TDP-43-depleted neurons restored synchronous network activity, indicating effective neurotransmitter release and propagation of signalling across the network (Fig. 2k,l and Extended Data Fig. 7e). This represented the most robustly rescued MEA metric (Extended Data Fig. 7f). Taken together, these findings show that correction of a single cryptic exon splicing event (intron 20 UNC13A cryptic exon) is sufficient to restore synaptic transmission and rescue the asynchronous patterns of network activity caused by TDP-43 loss. Active electrodes and cell coverage were comparable across conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Likewise, analysis of neuronal survival confirmed that network-level changes were not attributable to changes in viability due to TDP-43 loss (Extended Data Fig. 7h) demonstrating that TDP-43 driven UNC13A loss drives a functional synaptic deficit in otherwise structurally intact, viable neurons.

The rescue of UNC13A levels and restoration of synaptic signalling conferred by deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in the context of TDP-43 knockdown highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting this event in patients. We therefore sought to identify ASOs that can induce splice switching similar to those successful in targeting splicing events in SMN2 and STMN2 (refs. 23,24). We first designed locked nucleic acid-modified ASOs that targeted regions covering the cryptic exon acceptor and donor splice sites (Extended Data Fig. 8a). We screened the ASOs by transfection in SK-N-BE(2) cells and assessed their ability to restore UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 8b) and found that 21-nt ASOs targeting the donor splice site could restore UNC13A splicing. We confirmed splicing rescue and ability to restore UNC13A RNA and UNC13A protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 8c–g). To improve therapeutic tolerance, we adapted the best performing ASOs to have full 2′-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) ribose-modified bases and tested their ability to rescue UNC13A splicing and restore protein levels in HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 8h). We found these could restore splicing to more than 90% and protein levels to 30–50% of normal levels. Treatment with the M21-4 MOE ASO led to increased presynaptic UNC13A protein expression at synapsin-positive puncta following TDP-43 depletion compared with treatment with the control scrambled ASO (Fig. 3d). To identify ASOs that could increase protein rescue above 50% of normal levels, we carried out a secondary screen by performing an ASO walk along the cryptic donor site with 18-nt MOE-based ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We evaluated the ability of the 18-nt ASOs to rescue splicing in SH-SY5Y cells by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 9b) and confirmed that the best performing 18-nt ASOs could rescue correct UNC13A mRNA splicing to more than 90%, and protein to more than 50% in SH-SY5Y cells and HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 9c–h). In addition, we performed amplicon sequencing, which confirmed the ability of ASOs to rescue both reference and risk alleles in our HaloTDP iNeurons (Extended Data Fig. 9i).

To validate the efficacy of UNC13A ASOs to rescue cryptic splicing in an in vivo model, we generated humanized UNC13A (hUNC13A) reporter mice, in which mouse intron 20 was replaced with human UNC13A intron 20 containing the cryptic exon. TDP-43 knockdown was performed by tail vein injection of an adeno-associated virus encoding a synthetic microRNA targeting the mouse Tardbp gene (Fig. 3g). On the same day, intracerebroventricular injections were performed in hUNC13A reporter mice with the M21-4 MOE ASO or artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Three weeks post-injection, spinal cords were dissected from the mice. RT–PCR analysis from spinal cord tissue following knockdown of TDP-43 showed no cryptic exon inclusion in WT mice and robust cryptic exon inclusion in hUNC13A reporter mice, which was partially rescued by administration of UNC13A splice-correcting ASO (Fig. 3h–k). Overall, these results show that ASOs can reduce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon on TDP-43 knockdown both in vitro and in vivo, and can rescue UNC13A protein expression to above 50% in cultured neurons.

Unc13a heterozygous knockout mice and individuals with heterozygous LoF UNC13A mutations are viable and do not present with abnormal neurophysiology18,25. Recovery of UNC13A expression to WT levels after TDP-43 LoF is probably not required to restore synapse function, in agreement with previous work in primary mouse cultures that showed that clear deficits in synapse function are only observed when expression of Unc13a falls below 30% of normal physiological levels20,25. Indeed, treatment with M18-17 ASO, which rescues UNC13A levels to more than 50% of control, was able to rescue synaptic transmission as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4a). We then tested our M21-4 ASO, which rescues UNC13A protein levels to roughly 30% of normal levels. Despite the lower level of protein rescue, treatment with M21-4 ASO also rescued synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4b). mEPSC amplitude and passive membrane properties were unaffected by treatment with ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 10a–d), suggesting that ASO treatment specifically rescues presynaptic deficits caused by the cryptic exon in UNC13A.
