#1306. Mancini: ‘Esposito brothers got confused, Italy always play to win’

Roberto Mancini confirms the Esposito brothers ‘got confused’ over who was meant to take a penalty in Italy’s 3-1 win over France. ‘We should always play with the idea of winning.’

The Azzurri had a rough start to the Nations League group when losing 2-0 to Belgium, but also a difficult start tonight at San Siro, going behind within 10 minutes when Michael Olise pounced on a Gianluigi Donnarumma howler.

Francesco Pio Esposito equalised, then Sebastiano Esposito fired a penalty off target, but Davide Frattesi and Pio Esposito managed to turn the game around anyway.

“I gave what I could give, but the players were the ones who received it quickly, even if we know there is a long road ahead of us,” said Mancini in his press conference.

“After going behind so early, we could’ve conceded another three or four if we’d let our heads drop, instead we did well to keep calm. We’ve got to improve in our courage, the young players must do things enough times that they become normal. It takes time, and I hope the older figures in the team can help the process.”

There was confusion on the touchline when Sebastiano Esposito stepped up to take the first penalty, but Pio claimed that both the brothers were on the list as potential spot-kick takers.

“Pio was the first on there, then Sebastiano, so maybe they got confused between brothers. Next time, they won’t get confused again,” replied Mancini.

Soon after the penalty miss, Sebastiano Esposito was substituted, and Italy scored another two goals.

“I am the coach, so I have to decide. We needed pace on the right, because Seba was a bit fatigued. Federico Dimarco could also have given us options from set plays, he is not a classic winger, but he can play that role.”

There had been some doubt on the starting 4-3-3 line-up, with Bologna winger Nicolò Cambiaghi impressing on the left, providing an assist and winning a penalty.

“Dimarco is a wing-back, but he can run and has a great foot. He might not always be able to play there, but there are games where he can.”

Pio Esposito is a remarkable talent, as this was his ninth goal in just 14 senior caps, having turned 21 over the summer.

“We hope he can score many more goals. Gigi Riva had 35 and it’s not so far away, so we hope he can get there. We need goals from Pio and everyone else, but he can certainly score many,” added Mancini.

Italy are now top of the Nations League group on 10 points, so a draw in Belgium would suffice to reach the quarter-finals, although the coach seems to have his sights set firmly on first place.

“Even if my team isn’t necessarily at the same level as the opponent, I still think we should always play with the idea of winning, because anything can happen in 90 minutes. You can lose or win, because this is football.”

Mancini had walked away from the Italy job and many doubted his return, so does he feel like this is making up for lost time?

“I am just happy to be here and help getting this team back where it belongs. We can only do that by playing football. I’m very happy trying to help Italy achieve certain objectives.”

Old school effective team performance! we are quick to criticize a bad match, we should be just as quick to praise a fantastic performance! I hope Esposito can reach Riva’s record, and maybe we have a successful brother pair into the future.

#1305. Why Cristiano Ronaldo Never Won the Golden Boy Award

Cristiano Ronaldo has enjoyed an illustrious career, winning over 30 major trophies, including five Champions League titles, making him one of the most decorated players in football history. Since his professional debut for Sporting Lisbon in 2002, the Portuguese forward has won five Ballon d'Or awards, which is only bettered by his great rival Lionel Messi, who has eight. He has also won other respected European awards, such as the UEFA Men's Player of the Year three times and the European Golden Shoe on four occasions.

Despite all this, the 39-year-old has never won the Golden Boy Award. He was only eligible to win it for three years and narrowly missed out on it each time. Here is why he never got his hands on the trophy and who won it instead of one of the greatest football players of all time.

The Golden Boy Award began in 2003 and is given to a player under the age of 21 who plays in the top flight of a European league. Tuttosport established the award, and since 2003, sports journalists from 11 newspapers across Europe have participated in the voting to decide the winner. Notable outlets included in the voting process are L'Equipe, The Times, and Bild.

Each newspaper ranks five players under the age of 21 in order of who they believe has performed well throughout the last calendar year. The best player receives 10 points, while the second, third, fourth, and fifth-ranked youngsters receive seven, five, three and one, respectively. At the end of this voting process, the player with the most points is awarded the prize of Golden Boy.

Who will be taking Pau Cubarsi's crown in 2027?

In the first three editions of the Golden Boy, Ronaldo was eligible to win it. At 18 years of age, the Portuguese teenager joined Manchester United for £12m after spending a couple of years at Sporting. In his first season at the club, he played 40 times in all competitions, scoring six times and registering eight assists. After his impressive year for the Red Devils, he narrowly missed out on the award to Rafael van der Vaart, who excelled at Ajax and was a couple of years older than Ronaldo.

The following year, Ronaldo missed out to his teammate Wayne Rooney. In the 2004/05 season, Rooney scored 17 goals in all competitions for United, establishing himself as one of the key players in the team. Meanwhile, Ronaldo's impact at the club was increasing, but he only managed nine goals in 50 appearances. In 2005, Lionel Messi won the award, which was the Portuguese forward's last year of eligibility to win the coveted prize. While the Argentinian was the centre of attention at the start of his career, it took Ronaldo a little bit longer to establish himself as one of the elite players in Europe. The 39-year-old has spoken about the importance of Sir Alex Ferguson to his development, especially in his first few years at United. He said:

"And it's difficult. Imagine at 18, you arrive from Sporting, you play with the stars – with Giggsy, Scholes, Roy Keane, Solskjaer – I was a little bit nervous. But he helped me a lot by the communication.

“He would call me to his office with the translator there. The most important thing was he told me things that helped me to grow up as a person, and as a player. And since day one, everything that he told me, he did. So I appreciated it a lot.

“I'm always saying it, but he was like a father figure to me in football. I appreciate everything he did for me, my family and especially for the club. He did an amazing job.”

Cristiano Ronaldo Stats From 2002 to 2005

Sergio Ramos, Gareth Bale and Wayne Rooney all feature in Cristiano Ronaldo's best XI of teammates from his incredible career.

Only one player out of the 24 has gone on to win the Ballon d'Or. That is, of course, Messi, who won the Golden Boy in 2005 before winning his first Ballon d'Or four years later. Since then, he went on to define the award alongside Ronaldo, with the two players, who both feature among the greatest athletes of all time, winning 13 between them, enjoying near-total dominance from 2008 until 2021.

Whether Bellingham, Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsi or the likes of Kylian Mbappe and Erling Haaland can break this record in the next few years remains to be seen. It doesn't look like it will be changing any time soon, though with the award being won by five different players in the past five years.

While some Golden Boy winners have blossomed, others have bombed...

#1304. Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Published: 05:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:21 EST, 13 November 2026

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Offered the chance to kick Australian cricket while it was down, England made humiliating contact with fresh air on the opening day of their eight-match white-ball trip.

Only hours after Pat Cummins had added a twist to the sandpaper saga by dismissing Usman Khawaja’s claims that the whole squad knew about the ball-tampering plans in South Africa eight years ago as ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Harry Brook’s side were blown away for 131 in the first ODI – having at one stage been 65 for eight.

Australia then romped home by seven wickets with more than 26 overs in hand to take a 1–0 lead into the second game of this three-match series in Adelaide on Sunday. For England, anyway, complete and utter nonsense felt about right.

It is not quite a year since they began their Ashes campaign here at the Optus Stadium by being bowled out in 32.5 overs in their first innings and 34.4 in their second – before stumbling to a 4–1 defeat.

Now, they obligingly split the difference, dismissed in 33.4 as Mahli Beardman, a 21-year-old fast bowler from Dunsborough, a couple of hours drive down the coast from Perth, picked up six for 34 – the best figures for Australia by an ODI debutant.

His first victim was Joe Root, caught behind for a painful 17 off 36 balls, and his second Brook, who had made only a single when he fidgeted fatally outside off stump.

That might have been enough to satisfy most newcomers, but Beardman had barely started. Jordan Cox made two before edging a poke, and Sam Curran top-edged a pull to fine leg for a duck.

When Liam Dawson, yet to score, squeezed a drive to backward point, Beardman had five wickets in 28 balls – not bad for a player whose only previous taste of international cricket had come in a T20 in Pakistan in January.

He then ended a lively last-wicket stand of 29 by removing Jofra Archer, who had just driven him down the ground for four. It was the only authentic boundary England managed off his bowling: the other, a streaky inside edge from Root, summed up the problems posed by his pace, bounce and accuracy. As bids for a place on next summer’s Ashes tour go, this was hard to ignore.

‘Laying in bed last night, that’s not what I had planned,’ said Beardman, who was taken under his wing by Australian fast-bowling legend Dennis Lillee after a mutual friend spotted him as a young teenager bowling at a bin down the side of a house. ‘It was an incredible game and it all happened so fast.’

If England had learned lessons from their collapses in the last year’s Test here, they showed little sign of being able to implement them. Players drove on the up, as they had so heedlessly a year earlier, and failed to cope with the Perth bounce.

England head coach Brendon McCullum was critical of his side's failure to adapt to the pitch, and called on them to learn from their mistakes going forward.

'It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline,' said McCullum. 'There are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away. We probably knew we were in for a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

'We're disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view.'

And all this after they had played a warm-up game at the WACA – a grievous omission before the Ashes – and trained with such intensity that white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen had declared it the best practice session he had seen from an England team.

In the event, their top-scorer was Gus Atkinson, who hit an unbeaten 29 from No 10, including England’s only six.

Mitchell Marsh, stroke-less in the previous day’s press conference, put that into perspective by clearing the ropes four times during a 29-ball half-century, while Cooper Connolly – dropped by Tom Banton at midwicket on five – hit two sixes himself.

England’s only consolation had come at the start of Australia’s reply, when Atkinson bowled Travis Head first ball off the inside edge. Head it was who had taken care of Australia’s fourth-innings chase here a year ago, thrashing a 69-ball century that knocked the stuffing out of Ben Stokes’s attack.

Instead, it was Marsh who went for his shots, stopped only when he flicked Jamie Overton to Ben Duckett at deep midwicket, by which time Australia were already halfway there. For a few hours, at least, no one was talking about sandpaper.

#1303. Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase1,2. Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability3,4,5,6. Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment4. In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress7,8,9,10, but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

DNA lesion bypass by leading-strand repriming was demonstrated for the core Escherichia coli replisome, in which primer synthesis is performed by the primase also responsible for lagging-strand replication12,13. By contrast, eukaryotic replisomes reconstituted from purified Saccharomyces cerevisiae proteins cannot efficiently resume synthesis downstream of leading-strand lesions1 because the Pol α–primase complex that is responsible for priming each Okazaki fragment is targeted to the lagging-strand template14. This targeting mechanism is conserved in the human replisome14, indicating that inefficient priming on the leading strand by Pol α–primase is a universal feature of eukaryotic replisomes.

Unlike S. cerevisiae, humans have an additional primase called PRIMPOL7,8,9. PRIMPOL is a 560-amino-acid (aa) monomeric enzyme comprising a 21-aa amino-terminal helix of unknown function, an archaeo-eukaryotic primase (AEP) domain, a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding zinc-finger (ZnF) and two C-terminal replication protein A (RPA) binding motifs (RBMs)6,15. Extensive evidence from human, mouse and chicken cell lines shows that PRIMPOL promotes replication fork progression under conditions that stall replicative DNA polymerases8,9,10 and that this requires PRIMPOL primase activity10,16,17,18, leading to the formation of daughter-strand gaps5,19. Current models indicate that PRIMPOL is recruited to replication forks through a direct interaction with RPA9,11,16. However, because RPA is constitutively associated with the lagging-strand template, it is unclear whether this mode of recruitment is sufficient for efficient PRIMPOL priming on the leading strand, or whether an additional mechanism directs PRIMPOL specifically to the leading-strand template to rescue stalled replication forks.

To investigate leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the replisome, we leveraged a system that we recently developed to assemble fast and efficient human replisomes from purified proteins20. In this approach, CMG is first loaded onto the forked end of a 9.7-kb DNA template before additional proteins are added to assemble replisomes that perform robust leading- and lagging-strand DNA replication (Fig. 1a). Pol ε performs the bulk of leading-strand synthesis, whereas Pol α–primase and Pol δ replicate the lagging strand. RFC and CTF18-RFC load the polymerase processivity factor PCNA onto the lagging and leading strands, respectively, and TIMELESS (TIM)–TIPIN, CLASPIN and AND1 associate with CMG to promote rapid replisome progression20. To monitor fork stalling and restart, a single cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD)—an important ultraviolet (UV)-induced DNA lesion and a potent block to replicative polymerases—was introduced to the leading-strand template 3.5 kb from the forked end1,20.

a, Schematic of the forked-DNA replication assay with a template containing a leading-strand CPD lesion. b, Time course of a replication assay on the leading-strand CPD template in the absence or presence of PRIMPOL. c, Two-dimensional gel analysis of a 30-min replication reaction in the presence of PRIMPOL.

Figure 1b shows that the CPD is a potent block to leading-strand DNA synthesis (3.5-kb stall lead product in denaturing gel), which causes replication forks to stall, as visualized by the slowly migrating species in the native gel (stalled fork). Similar replisome behaviour was observed when the CPD was substituted for a tetrahydrofuran abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Addition of PRIMPOL caused a reduction in the stalled fork population and the accumulation of full-length products in the native gel, concomitant with the appearance of an approximately 6.2-kb product in the denaturing gel (Fig. 1b, lanes 5–8, restart lead product). This result strongly indicated that PRIMPOL was promoting fork restart by leading-strand repriming. To confirm that the 6.2-kb products resulted from leading-strand repriming, products were analysed by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (Fig. 1c). This showed that the 6.2-kb products were exclusively associated with the full-length product in the native gel and were roughly twice as intense as the 3.5-kb stall leading-strand product, as expected for bona fide restart products. Moreover, replication of the CPD template in the presence of a primase-defective PRIMPOL mutant (ZnFD2A)10 generated only stalled leading strands and Okazaki fragments (Extended Data Fig. 1b). These data illustrate the successful reconstitution of replication fork restart by leading-strand repriming using purified human proteins.

Replication fork restart also occurred efficiently after polymerase stalling at an abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1c), suggesting that the mechanism of repriming is agnostic to the chemical nature of the initial blocking lesion. Restart also occurred independently of Pol δ (Extended Data Fig. 1d) and Pol α–primase (Extended Data Fig. 1c), illustrating that only Pol ε is required to extend the primer made by PRIMPOL in this system. Therefore, unless stated, Pol δ is omitted from subsequent experiments to avoid complications from strand-displacement synthesis.

Unlike Pol α–primase, which has a strong preference for rNTPs for primer synthesis21, following the 5′ rNTP, PRIMPOL incorporates dNTPs with a much higher efficiency than rNTPs owing to a sugar discrimination mechanism7,8,22. Consistent with these properties, omitting GTP, CTP and UTP did not compromise leading-strand restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e, compare lanes 7 and 8), indicating that ATP is sufficient for primer initiation in these assays. However, despite previous reports that manganese stimulates PRIMPOL priming activity in vitro8, its addition did not enhance the efficiency of restart (Extended Data Fig. 1f).

The observation that restart products were close to their maximum possible length (6.2 kb) indicated that they were initiated a very short distance from the lesion. To obtain a high-resolution view of leading-strand restart, we devised a strategy to map priming sites at near single-nucleotide resolution (Fig. 2a). To do so, products were post-replicatively digested with restriction enzymes that cut upstream and downstream of the lesion to liberate fragments that could be resolved in polyacrylamide sequencing gels. Figure 2b shows that, apart from the stalled leading strand and a minor population of read-through products, a ladder of products was generated upon digestion of the PRIMPOL-containing reaction (lane 4). We conclude that each band in the ladder corresponds to a unique leading-strand repriming site. Notably, most of the PRIMPOL-dependent primers used to restart replication were synthesized within 50 nucleotides of the CPD, even when the PRIMPOL concentration was reduced to 5 nM (Extended Data Fig. 2a). An indistinguishable ladder pattern was observed following replication of the abasic site template (Extended Data Fig. 2b), showing that the chemical nature of the DNA lesion plays no part in priming site specification. Because CMG is likely to continue slowly unwinding DNA after polymerase stalling1,2, these data indicate that PRIMPOL activity is targeted to the leading-strand template immediately after polymerase stalling, which limits the size of the daughter-strand gap to generally <50 nucleotides on this template.

a, Schematic of the predicted products generated from digestion of replication products with SalI and NruI. b, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction processed as in a. c, Schematic of the DNA template in which a 162-nt sequence after the CPD was replaced with an alternative sequence. d, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction containing PRIMPOL, processed as in a. Pol δ was omitted from the experiments in b and d. Und, undamaged.

Previous work established that PRIMPOL exhibits sequence preferences for the initiation of primer synthesis23,24,25. We therefore reasoned that the distinct pattern of restart products in our experiments was a consequence of the DNA sequence downstream of the CPD. To test this, we modified a 162-nt region downstream of the CPD (Fig. 2c). Replication of this modified template in the presence of PRIMPOL generated a distinct pattern of restart products to those from the original CPD template (Fig. 2d, compare lanes 3 and 4). This shows that leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the human replisome is modulated by DNA sequence. Importantly, despite the altered sequence, most restart products were again initiated within <50 nucleotides of the CPD, with one prominent product initiated about 100 nt from the CPD (Fig. 2d, lane 4). This is consistent with both templates containing multiple close matches to the preferred tri-nucleotide primer initiation sequence for PRIMPOL25.

The discovery that PRIMPOL-mediated repriming occurred a short distance from the CPD on two distinct templates suggested that an efficient mechanism directs PRIMPOL to the exposed leading-strand template. We hypothesized that this was mediated by the RBMs in the PRIMPOL C terminus11, recruiting PRIMPOL to RPA bound to the leading-strand template following polymerase stalling at the CPD and continued template unwinding by CMG. To examine this, we generated two PRIMPOL mutants defective in RPA binding: one lacking both RBMs and the other carrying a mutant in RBM-A (RBM-ARA) that abolished PRIMPOL localization to chromatin in human cells11 (Fig. 3a). Figure 3b shows that both PRIMPOL mutants promoted leading-strand restart with comparable efficiency to wild-type PRIMPOL. Moreover, analysis of restart products showed that both mutants exhibited the same repriming site pattern as wild-type PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c). We conclude that RBM-mediated interactions between PRIMPOL and RPA are non-essential for replication fork restart with reconstituted human replisomes.

a, Primary structure diagrams showing full-length PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL point mutants and truncations. b, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction with the indicated PRIMPOL mutants. c, Urea polyacrylamide gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction on the CPD template performed with the indicated PRIMPOL RPA binding mutants. Products were digested post-replicatively with SalI and NruI. d, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction with dropouts of non-essential replisome components on undamaged and CPD templates in the presence of PRIMPOL. e, Silver-stained SDS–PAGE analysis of a pull-down experiment with the indicated proteins. WT, wild type.

The non-essentiality of the PRIMPOL RBMs for fork restart, together with the very close proximity of repriming to the lesion, prompted us to explore the idea that PRIMPOL might be directed to stalled forks through an interaction with the core replisome. Omission of all non-essential core replisome components individually did not abolish leading-strand restart (Fig. 3d). We therefore hypothesized that PRIMPOL might be recruited directly by the CMG helicase. Consistent with this idea, the pull-down experiment in Fig. 3e shows that PRIMPOL interacts specifically with CMG.

To investigate how PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG, and how this might facilitate efficient leading-strand repriming, we determined a structure of PRIMPOL bound to CMG by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Table 1). Well-resolved cryo-EM density was recovered for the PRIMPOL AEP domain alongside the ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 that form part of the C-terminal tier (C-tier) of the two-tiered hexameric MCM ring (Fig. 4a,b). This arrangement is mediated by a conserved 21-aa α-helix at the N terminus of PRIMPOL binding to MCM7 and an approximately 20-aa loop immediately downstream of the helix that is sandwiched between a shallow groove on MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). The PRIMPOL AEP domain is positioned laterally adjacent to the exit of the MCM central pore, through which the unwound leading-strand template emerges. Moreover, superimposing the crystal structure of PRIMPOL bound to primer-template DNA26 onto the AEP domain in our structure shows that its catalytic core is oriented to support primer synthesis directly as template DNA is fed from CMG (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 4c).

a, Cryo-EM density map of the CMG–PRIMPOL structure coloured by subunit occupancy. b, Close-up view of PRIMPOL bound to MCM4 and MCM7. The atomic model is shown in ribbon representation; the cryo-EM density is shown as a semi-transparent surface. c, Primary structure diagram of PRIMPOL with the regions visible in the cryo-EM structure shown in pink. d, Model illustrating the possible path of DNA from CMG to PRIMPOL. The protein structure shown is the CMG–PRIMPOL structure from this study. The DNA in the model was generated by superpositioning the PRIMPOL–DNA structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 5L2X) and CMG-forked DNA structure (PDB: 7PFO) onto the PRIMPOL–CMG structure in this study.

Guided by our cryo-EM structure, to evaluate the role of the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction in replication fork restart, we removed the first 39 aa of PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL∆1–39) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Figure 5b shows that wild-type PRIMPOL but not PRIMPOL∆1–39 was robustly pulled down by CMG, confirming that the PRIMPOL N terminus harbours the primary CMG interaction motifs. PRIMPOL∆1–39 retained primase activity on a ssDNA template (Extended Data Fig. 5b) but was unable to promote fork restart by leading-strand repriming in the human replisome (Fig. 5c,d, lane 4). This defect was not rescued by Pol δ addition (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We conclude that the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is essential for leading-strand repriming by reconstituted human replisomes.

a, Primary structure diagrams of PRIMPOL focusing on the regions in the N terminus that bind to MCM7 and MCM4. Mutants generated within that region are shown. b, Silver-stained and western blot SDS–PAGE analysis of a pull-down experiment with the indicated proteins. c,d, Denaturing agarose (c) and urea polyacrylamide (d) gel analysis of 40-min replication reactions with PRIMPOL mutants. Samples in d were digested post-replicatively with SalI and NruI. e, Close-up view of the interaction between PRIMPOL and MCM4. The model is shown in ribbon representation in semi-transparent cryo-EM density. Amino acid residues targeted for mutagenesis are depicted (sticks). f, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction on the CPD template with the indicated PRIMPOL concentrations. g, Cisplatin sensitivity assay performed for the TK6 cell lines specified. The data are the average of three biological replicates, and error bars represent the standard deviation. P values are the result of statistical testing using two-way analysis of cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (see Extended Data Table 2 for all P values); pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL∆1–39 P** = 0.0064554, primpol/pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL P* = 0.024598.

We next investigated whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG functions exclusively in PRIMPOL recruitment or whether accurate positioning of the AEP domain is necessary for efficient replication fork restart. Abolishing PRIMPOL interaction with MCM7 by removing the α-helix at the extreme N terminus of PRIMPOL (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL∆1–21) resulted in a modest reduction in leading-strand restart (Fig. 5c, denaturing, lane 5), with a disproportionate effect on initiation events that occurred closest to the CPD (Fig. 5d, Urea PAGE, lane 5). Retaining α-helix 1–21 but substituting the ensuing loop (aa 22–39) with a glycine–serine linker (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOLGS22–39), or substituting six residues in the loop to alanine (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL6A loop), resulted in complete loss of restart products (Fig. 5c,d, lanes 6 and 7). These results highlight the importance of this loop, which sits between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain, for leading-strand restart.

Furthermore, targeting three loop residues that sit at the interface with MCM4 (Arg31, Leu32 and Ser33; Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL3A loop) resulted in a less severe defect than a mutant targeting the side chains of Tyr28 and Arg29 to disrupt the bridging interaction between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL2A loop) (Fig. 5c–e). This observation strongly suggests that rigid PRIMPOL positioning alongside the MCM C-tier is necessary for efficient leading-strand restart in the human replisome.

In our reconstituted system, the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG (Fig. 5c), but not between PRIMPOL RBMs and RPA (Fig. 3b), is essential for fork restart. Therefore, because PRIMPOL RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL activity in cells9,11,16,17, we hypothesized that the RBM-mediated interaction might serve to increase the local concentration of PRIMPOL at the replication fork. This function may not be required under our standard in vitro reaction conditions, which use a relatively high concentration (20 nM) of PRIMPOL. To test this idea, we performed a titration of wild-type PRIMPOL and PRIMPOLΔRBM. With wild-type PRIMPOL, leading-strand restart became less efficient only when the protein concentration was reduced to 0.1 nM (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 5d). By contrast, leading-strand restart was compromised at 1 nM PRIMPOLΔRBM and was barely detectable at 0.1 nM. These findings are consistent with a model in which the RBM-mediated interaction between PRIMPOL and RPA facilitates PRIMPOL localization at the replication fork.

Loss of PRIMPOL does not sensitize many human cell lines to DNA damage because of redundant DNA damage tolerance pathways27,28,29. Therefore, to evaluate whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is required for PRIMPOL function in human cells, we took advantage of our recent finding that loss of PRIMPOL sensitizes translesion synthesis (TLS)-deficient TK6 lymphoblastoid cells to cisplatin, most prominently observed in cells unable to ubiquitinate PCNA at lysine 164 (ref. 27). PRIMPOL was removed by CRISPR–Cas9 targeting in pcnaK164R cells. Figure 5g shows that loss of PRIMPOL further sensitized pcnaK164R cells to cisplatin, consistent with our previous work27. Whereas expression of wild-type PRIMPOL fully rescued this phenotype, expression of PRIMPOL∆1–39 did not complement the additional cisplatin sensitivity of pcnaK164R cells (Fig. 5g, Extended Data Fig. 6 and Extended Data Table 2). These data indicate that the interaction between CMG and PRIMPOL, which is essential for fork restart in vitro, is important for PRIMPOL-mediated DNA damage tolerance in human cells.

On the basis of our results and previous work, we propose the following model for replication fork restart by PRIMPOL-dependent repriming (Fig. 6a). Our biochemical reconstitution has demonstrated that the PRIMPOL RBMs are not essential for leading-strand repriming in vitro. However, they do become important for fork restart at low PRIMPOL concentrations, and evidence from cellular studies shows that RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL recruitment to chromatin and fork progression during replication stress9,11,16,17. To accommodate these observations, we propose that the interaction of PRIMPOL with RPA, which is low affinity11 and therefore likely to be transient, serves primarily to localize PRIMPOL to actively replicating genomic loci, which may be necessary because PRIMPOL is a relatively low abundance protein in human cells15,30 (Fig. 6a).

a, Model for CMG-directed replication fork restart by PRIMPOL after the replisome encounters a leading-strand DNA lesion (red triangle). Two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms are shown. In (i), PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG only after fork stalling at the lesion. In (ii), PRIMPOL can associate with CMG and travel with the replisome before fork stalling. b, Composite model of the human replisome showing the positions of PRIMPOL, Pol ε and Pol α–primase. The model is a composite of the following PDB files: 8B9D, 7PFO and 9F6D. The position of the Pol ε catalytic domain (9F6D) is based on a yeast replisome structure42.

On encountering a DNA lesion, leading-strand synthesis by Pol ε is blocked, but CMG continues to translocate along the template at a greatly reduced rate1,2, exposing ssDNA on the leading-strand template between the helicase and polymerase (Fig. 6a). Through its interactions with MCM4 and MCM7, PRIMPOL is positioned to capture the exposed ssDNA to initiate leading-strand repriming (Fig. 6a, pathway (i)). After primer synthesis, Pol ε must reengage the leading strand for optimal fork progression to resume. The anchoring of PRIMPOL on CMG suggests a pathway in which the primer might be handed off directly to the leading-strand PCNA loader CTF18-RFC and then to Pol ε. Alternatively, Pol δ might facilitate the recoupling of leading-strand synthesis by extending the primer made by PRIMPOL until it reaches CMG, at which point the 3′ end is transferred to Pol ε. This pathway has been observed following leading-strand lesion bypass by TLS in the yeast replisome31.

The direct interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG raises the possibility that PRIMPOL could travel with CMG to facilitate its immediate deployment on helicase–polymerase uncoupling (Fig. 6a, pathway (ii)). In this regard, it is noteworthy that PRIMPOL does not clash with any known core replisome protein, including Pol ε (Fig. 6b). However, because the MCM4 and MCM7 ATPase domains undergo conformational changes during CMG translocation that could affect PRIMPOL binding, single-molecule studies will be required to determine if PRIMPOL can stably associate with moving replisomes.

The mechanism of PRIMPOL recruitment via MCM4 and MCM7 ensures that repriming is tightly coupled to CMG progression to limit the size of the ssDNA gap that is left for post-replicative repair pathways. Our work further establishes that PRIMPOL displays a sequence preference for primer synthesis. Based on prior studies, this sequence is short and somewhat degenerate25, which should enable efficient repriming at most genomic loci. However, regions of the genome devoid of optimal priming sites are likely to exist, for example in repetitive DNA, which could limit repriming and bias fork restart and stabilisation towards alternative pathways.

The two-stage model for PRIMPOL recruitment involving both RPA and CMG interactions is analogous to a mechanism proposed for the recruitment of TLS polymerases to the replication fork32. This mechanism has been observed in the E. coli replisome for the TLS polymerase PolIV, where an interaction with the single-stranded DNA-binding protein SSB concentrates PolIV at the fork to promote its interaction with the sliding clamp β33. We also note that RPA will accumulate on the leading-strand template during prolonged uncoupling, which should enhance PRIMPOL recruitment to stressed replication forks.

Apart from its low abundance, PRIMPOL activity is regulated by checkpoint and cell cycle kinases6,34,35,36, suggesting that excessive repriming and daughter-strand gap formation is deleterious. Tight regulation of PRIMPOL might also indicate a capacity of the enzyme to interfere with normal replisome function. We reasoned that this could be a consequence of PRIMPOL being directed to the leading strand by CMG, causing it to interfere with Pol ε by competing for the nascent leading strand. Consistent with this idea, addition of PRIMPOL mildly slowed fork progression on an undamaged template, and this effect was exacerbated by omission of CTF18-RFC, which compromises PCNA loading on the leading strand (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Importantly, this inhibition was dependent on the interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG but not on primase activity (Extended Data Fig. 7b).

The widespread phylogenetic distribution of PRIMPOL37, and the conservation of its CMG interaction motifs, indicates an evolutionary pressure to keep replication forks moving by repriming. It also indicates that in the absence of chronic replication stress, repriming might be the default response of the replisome to impediments to leading-strand synthesis. This raises the possibility that leading-strand synthesis might be considerably more discontinuous in human cells than previously appreciated. It is also interesting to consider that PRIMPOL could access the leading strand for priming potentially in any instance where synthesis is paused, for example during PCNA loading on the leading strand by CTF18-RFC. This is possibly a frequent occurrence because PCNA abundance is reported to be similar on leading and lagging strands in yeast38.

Multiple pathways collaborate to protect and restart stalled replication forks during replication stress. Ablating replication fork reversal factors has been found to promote fork progression in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner6,34,39,40,41, suggesting an interplay between repriming and replication fork remodelling. The factors that dictate the balance between repriming and other fork processing pathways (for example, fork reversal), and how this is influenced by the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction, is an important area for future study, especially given that PRIMPOL promotes chemoresistance in BRCA1 deficient cells34.

For decades, prokaryotic and eukaryotic replisomes were thought to function with a single primase to initiate DNA synthesis on both template strands. This changed with the discovery of PRIMPOL as a second primase in many eukaryotic species, including humans7,8,9. However, although it has been demonstrated that PRIMPOL facilitates replication fork progression during replication stress in a range of metazoan cell lines, evidence for PRIMPOL primase activity being directed specifically to the leading-strand template, and a plausible mechanism for this targeting, was lacking. The work presented here demonstrates that, through its interactions with CMG, PRIMPOL is a dedicated leading-strand primase, establishing a division of labour in the human replisome: Pol α–primase acts on the lagging strand14, while PRIMPOL operates on the leading strand. Our data, together with the strong conservation of CMG-binding motifs in the PRIMPOL N terminus, indicate that many eukaryotic replisomes rely on strand-specific primases to maintain efficient replisome progression, and that this specificity is governed by helicase-directed primase recruitment to the replication fork.

Replication reactions were performed essentially as described previously, with the following modifications. Reactions were assembled stepwise: DNA (2.4 nM) was first incubated with CMG (50 nM) for 10 min in replication buffer supplemented with 0.1 mM AMP-PNP. Following this pre-incubation, the mixture was diluted two-fold with replication buffer containing 30 μM dATP and dCTP. Additional replication factors (20 nM PCNA, 20 nM RFC, 20 nM Pol ε, 10 nM Pol α, 20 nM CLASPIN, 20 nM TIM–TIPIN, 20 nM AND1 and 20 nM CTF18-RFC) were included at this stage unless stated otherwise. Replication was initiated by adding a concentrated start mix supplying 4 mM ATP; 30 µM dTTP and dGTP; 200 µM GTP, CTP and UTP; 33 nM α-[32P]-dCTP; and 100 nM RPA. When present, 20 nM PRIMPOL was added 2–3 min after replication had started. For reactions containing Pol δ, potassium glutamate was increased to 250 mM, and the polymerase was added at 2 nM immediately before the start mix. Leading-strand restart reactions were typically incubated for 20–40 min and terminated with EDTA to 50 mM. Unincorporated radiolabel was removed using Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns. Replication products were separated by alkaline agarose electrophoresis (0.7% agarose, 30 mM NaOH, 2 mM EDTA) run for 16.5 h at 24 V, fixed in cold 5% trichloroacetic acid, dried on Whatman paper, and visualized using an Amersham Typhoon phosphorimager scanner.

For analysis under native conditions, terminated reactions were supplemented with SDS (0.1%) and proteinase K (0.2 mg ml−1; New England Biolabs) and incubated for 10 min at 37 °C. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol extraction (25:24:1; TE-equilibrated) and passed through Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns to remove unincorporated nucleotides. Samples were then digested with SapI–PciI for 30 min at 37 °C to remove the template ends and prevent end-labelled species in gels. Following digestion, reactions underwent a second SDS/proteinase K treatment and phenol:chloroform extraction to ensure complete protein removal. DNA was ethanol-precipitated, washed with 70% ethanol, resuspended in native loading dye (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM EDTA, 10% Ficoll 400, 2% N-lauroylsarcosine sodium salt solution), and resolved on 1% agarose gels run overnight at 24 V in modified 1× TAE buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 40 mM sodium acetate, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0). Gels were dried and imaged as described above.

For two-dimensional (2D) gel analysis, samples were prepared as for native conditions and loaded into two lanes of a native agarose gel, with 10% of the reaction applied to one lane and the remaining 90% to the other. After electrophoresis, the lane containing the bulk of the sample was excised and placed horizontally along the top of a 0.7% denaturing agarose gel for the second dimension, which was run for 16.5 h at 27 V. Gels were then processed and imaged as described for alkaline gels.

For analysis on denaturing polyacrylamide gels, samples were prepared as for native conditions, but digested with SalI–NruI instead, and resuspended in loading dye (95% formamide, 20 mM EDTA, 0.04% Bromophenol Blue and 0.04% xylene cyanol). Samples were boiled for 5 min at 75 °C and resolved on a 40 cm × 20 cm 3.5% denaturing polyacrylamide gel. Gels were run in 1× TBE for 150 min at 40 W and dried as described above.

DNA substrates were prepared following previously published methods1,20. Gapped pZN3 was produced by introducing two adjacent Nt.BbvCI nicks and heating the plasmid to release the short intervening oligonucleotide, which was subsequently displaced using a sequestering oligonucleotide. The resulting gapped plasmid was purified on a Sepharose 4B (Sigma-Aldrich 4B200) gel filtration column. A 10-fold molar excess of a short oligonucleotide containing a CPD lesion, an abasic site or an undamaged control sequence (listed in Supplementary Table 1) was then annealed into the gap and ligated to generate the damaged or control templates. Finally, the DNA was digested with SapI, ligated to a pre-annealed fork structure, and purified again over a Sepharose 4B column.

Replication proteins were expressed in either E. coli or insect cells (Sf9 and Hi-5) and were purified following the methods described previously20,43. For more details about the purification steps, see Supplementary Table 2.

Relevant plasmids for protein expression were transformed into Rosetta2 cells using standard bacterial transformation protocols. A single transformant colony was selected and cultured in 1 l LB media supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and 10 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol overnight at 30 °C without agitation. The following morning, the culture temperature was increased to 37 °C and incubated with shaking at 210 rpm. On reaching an optical density (OD600) of 0.6–0.8, protein expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG for 3 h. Cells were subsequently harvested, washed with PBS and flash-frozen for storage.

Wild-type and mutant PRIMPOL proteins were purified using the following protocol. Cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM TCEP and protease inhibitors (cOmplete, EDTA-free; Roche). The cells were lysed by sonication (three cycles of 1 min each, consisting of 5 s ‘on’ and 5 s ‘off’ pulses at 40% amplitude), and insoluble material was removed by centrifugation at 235,000g for 50 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with 1 ml Strep-Tactin XT Superflow high-capacity resin for 1 h at 4 °C. The resin was then collected and washed extensively with 100 ml lysis buffer, followed by sequential washes with 25 ml lysis buffer containing 0.55 M NaCl and 35 ml lysis buffer containing 0.1 M NaCl to reduce the salt concentration. Bound protein was eluted in 1 ml fractions using eight column volumes of 0.1 M NaCl lysis buffer supplemented with 30 mM biotin. Protein-containing fractions were pooled and loaded onto a 5 ml HiTrap Heparin HP column pre-equilibrated in 0.1 M NaCl buffer. The protein was eluted with a 20 column volume linear gradient from 100 mM to 1 M NaCl. Peak fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 1 l of storage buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 0.3 M potassium acetate, 10% glycerol, 0.02% NP-40-S and 0.5 mM TCEP. Finally, the protein was concentrated using a 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off spin concentrator (Amicon Ultra-30), flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Reactions (20 µl) were performed in buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 150 mM potassium glutamate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 0.05% NP-40, and 1 mM DTT. CMG (5 pmol) was incubated with PRIMPOL (10 pmol; wild-type or Δ1–39) for 30 min on ice. A 2 µl aliquot was removed as input, and the remaining mixture was incubated with 5 µl α-Flag magnetic beads equilibrated in buffer for 30 min at 4 °C with shaking (1,250 rpm). Beads were washed three times with 100 µl reaction buffer, and bound proteins were eluted for 30 min at 4 °C at 1,250 rpm in 20 µl buffer containing 0.2 mg ml−1 Flag peptide. Eluates were mixed with loading buffer and analysed by 4–12% SDS–PAGE alongside input samples, followed by silver staining and western blotting.

Protein samples from pull-down assays with purified proteins were resolved on NuPAGE Novex 4–12% Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher) in MOPS buffer and transferred to PVDF membranes using the iBlot Dry Transfer System (Life Technologies). Membranes were blocked for 30 min at room temperature in 5% milk-TBST. For the detection of PRIMPOL, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with anti-PRIMPOL (Proteintech; 29824-1-AP, see Supplementary Table 3) followed by a secondary antibody incubation for another hour at room temperature (anti-rabbit-HRP, see Supplementary Table 3). For the detection of strep-SLD5, membranes were incubated for 2 h at room temperature with anti-strep-HRP antibody. Both membranes were subsequently incubated with Amersham ECL western blotting detection reagent, and the emitted chemiluminescence was detected on film and developed in an automatic film processor. The films were scanned using an Epson Scan V850 pro.

For the detection of PRIMPOL from TK6 extracts, protein was extracted from cells by lysing cells directly with RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher) supplemented with 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma) for 10 min on ice. To quantify protein concentration, a BCA assay was performed using the Pierce Protein Assay Kit (Thermo) as per kit instructions. Protein lysate (20 µg) was prepared with 1× Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad), supplemented with 10% β-mercaptoethanol. Denatured protein was run using NuPAGE Novex 4–12% Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher). The samples were then transferred onto a PVDF membrane. The membranes were blocked in 5% BSA in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) with 1% Tween (TBS-T) for 2 h at room temperature with rocking. The blocked membranes were incubated in blocking buffer with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 3) at 4 °C for 12–20 h. Membranes were incubated with Licor IRDye 800CW Rabbit secondary antibody at 20,000× dilution in blocking buffer for 30 min at room temperature. Membranes were washed three times with 10 ml fresh TBS-T for 5 min at room temperature with rocking. Antibody detection and image capture were carried out using the Bio-Rad ChemiDoc.

Reactions were adapted from a previously described study11. Human RPA (240 nM) was first incubated with 5 nM M13 single-stranded DNA (New England Biolabs) for 10 min at 37 °C in 10 µl reactions containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 100 mM potassium acetate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, 0.1 mg ml−1 BSA, 400 µM rNTPs, 80 µM dNTPs, 3 mM ATP and 33 nM α-[32P]-dCTP. PRIMPOL (400 nM; wild-type or mutants) was then added, and reactions were incubated for a further 30 min at 37 °C. DNA synthesis was stopped with 50 mM EDTA, and unincorporated radiolabel was removed using illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns. The samples were mixed with loading buffer (95% formamide, 20 mM EDTA, 0.04% Bromophenol Blue and 0.04% xylene cyanol), heated at 75 °C for 5 min, and resolved on a 40 cm × 20 cm 10% denaturing polyacrylamide gel run at 40 W for 105 min. The gels were dried and imaged as described above.

PRIMPOL, purified as described above, was concentrated using an Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter with a 30 kDa MWCO and injected onto a 2.4 ml S200 increase 3.2/300 column equilibrated with 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT. The peak fractions were collected and adjusted with buffer to a concentration of 5.7 µM. CMG was dialysed overnight against 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT, mixed with 1.3-fold molar excess of PRIMPOL, supplemented with 3.3 mM ATP and incubated on ice for at least 20 min before cryo-EM grid preparation. After incubation on ice, 2 µl of the sample was applied to freshly glow-discharged (Edwards Sputter Coater S150B, 45 s at 30 mA) UltrAuFoil R1.2/1.3, manually blotted on the top face for 2 s and immediately plunged into liquid ethane at liquid nitrogen temperature. Two datasets of 8,160 and 8,103 raw movies, respectively, were acquired using a 300 kV TFS Titan Krios microscope equipped with a Falcon 4i direct electron detector operated in electron counting mode using ThermoFisher EPU with AFIS enabled. The movies were collected over a defocus range of −1.0 µm to −2.6 µm, at an effective pixel size of 0.84 Å per pixel.

The data processing pipeline is shown as a schematic in Extended Data Fig. 4a. Raw movies were motion-corrected and dose-weighted using the implementation of a MotionCor2-like program of RELION44,45 (Extended Data Table 1) and then imported to CryoSPARC v.4.7.1 (ref. 46) for further processing. For each dataset, the particles were first ‘blob’-picked and extracted with 4-fold binning (336 Å box size). The 2D classification was run on a subset of 50,000 particles, and classes showing features for CMG in 2D-class averages were selected. Ab initio reconstruction was performed with the selected particles and, separately, with the remaining particles to generate three-dimensional (3D) volumes for either CMG or ‘noise/junk’-classes. The obtained volumes were provided as 3D references in two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement of all extracted particles, the first round of which the particles of the best class were selected for the second round. Independently, 2D class averages were used for template-based picking, and the resulting particles were also subjected to two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement as described above. The particles of the best 3D class from each picking strategy were combined and duplicate particles were removed. The resulting particles were used for homogeneous refinement with minimization over per-particle scale enabled, after which the particle population with poor signal (relative per-particle scale below 0.75) was removed. The remaining particles were subjected to 3D classification using a focus mask around the C-tier of the MCM ring, and particle classes with good definition for secondary structure features in the MCM C-tier were selected. At this stage, particles from datasets 1 and 2 were combined and locally refined using a focus mask around the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The resulting 3D reconstruction displayed density for the AEP domain of PRIMPOL around which a local mask was drawn for 3D classification. The largest class (135,661 particles) also exhibited the strongest signal for PRIMPOL. The particles were recentred on a mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7, re-extracted (280-pixel box, downsampled to 160 pixels, 1.47 Å per pixel) and subjected to signal subtraction with an inverted mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The subtracted particles were used for 3D classification from which the classes with the best density for the PRIMPOL AEP domain were selected (65,500 particles). The 30,000-particle subset with the best per-particle scale was then used for 3DFlex47 to reconstruct the final map for the PRIMPOL AEP domain near the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 (map 1, 3.5 Å resolution). The same particle subset was reverted to the original (non-subtracted) images, re-extracted from the original micrographs without binning (440-pixel box, 0.84 Å per pixel) using particle poses from global refinement on the CMG helicase. The obtained particles were subjected to homogeneous refinement to reconstruct a consensus map (map 2), or to local refinements with either a focus mask on CMG components GINS, CDC45 and the N-tier of the MCM ring (map 3, 3.1 Å resolution), or a focus mask on the C-tier of the MCM ring (map 4, 3.3 Å resolution). Maps coloured by estimated local resolution are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4c. Fourier shell correlation plots are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4d. Focus maps (maps 1, 3 and 4) were fitted into the consensus volume (map 2) using ChimeraX48. An initial atomic model was obtained by rigid-body fitting previously reported structures of CMG (6XTX, 7PFO) and PRIMPOL (5L2X) into the consensus EM volume using ChimeraX26,43,49. The fit-to-density was subsequently refined using ISOLDE50 inside ChimeraX. ATP–ADP ligands and gaps in the model were built de novo in Coot51. The molecular model was then used together with the consensus map and all focus maps to generate a composite EM map using phenix.combine_focused_maps by Thomas Terwilliger. Model geometry and atomic displacement parameters were refined against the composite map using phenix.real_space_refine52, after which model validation was carried out using MolProbity53 inside Phenix. Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between PRIMPOL–CMG (this study) and PRIMPOL–DNA (5L2X) was calculated in PyMOL (www.pymol.org) for 1,987 pairs of common atoms (RMSD = 1.723) or 253 pairs of common Cα atoms (RMSD = 1.374).

All TK6 cell lines were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium with GlutaMAX (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco). The cells were grown at 37 °C and 5% CO2. The cells were maintained between 0.05 cells ml −1 and 1.0 × 106 cells ml−1.

For the generation of plasmids for protein purification, plasmid MT_FB (see Supplementary Table 4 for details) was used as a template to generate the rest of PRIMPOL mutants in this study.

For the generation of plasmids for cellular studies, the m6p-PRIMPOL-WT_GFP_BSD plasmid backbone (wild-type PRIMPOL with GFP tag) (Supplementary Table 4) was used to generate the PRIMPOL ∆1–39 mutant (truncation mutant with GFP co-expression), using the Q5 Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (NEB) as per kit instructions. See Supplementary Table 1 for primers used.

TK6 primpol/pcnaK164R cells were used for expression of mutant and wild-type PRIMPOL–GFP. PRIMPOL Δ1–39 and wild-type PRIMPOL were expressed through plasmids that contained resistance cassettes for blasticidin. Plasmid DNA (15 µg) was electroporated into 20 × 106 cells using the Neon electroporator (Thermo Fisher) with the following conditions: 100 µl Resuspension Buffer R, 1,400 V and 20 ms. The electroporated cells were seeded across 96-well plates in growth media containing 7.5 µg ml−1 blasticidin. The surviving colonies were expanded and subjected to single-cell sorting for positive GFP expression through FACS to generate clonal populations.

Viscous culture medium (5 ml) consisting of 11.9 g l−1 RPMI 1640 powder with l-glutamine supplement (Gibco), 2 g l−1 sodium hydrogen carbonate (Sigma-Aldrich), 10 g l−1 4,000 cP methylcellulose (Thermo Fisher), 100 U l−1 penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) and 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco) was added to wells of six-well plates. The plates were equilibrated at 37 °C, 10% CO2 for a minimum of 1 h. The cells were treated with the indicated dose of cisplatin for 1 h at 37 °C and 10% CO2. The cells were then pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in fresh growth media to stop the cisplatin treatment. Then, 500,000, 50,000 or 5,000 cells were added to duplicate wells of the six-well plates for each cell line or condition. The plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2 until well-defined colonies were visible.

Flow cytometry was used to confirm the expression of GFP in TK6 primpol/pcnaK164R cell lines. A total of 1 × 106 cells were pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in 1 ml PBS supplemented with 2% FBS. The cells were analysed by flow cytometry using a Becton Dickinson LSRFortessa. TK6 primpol and TK6 wild-type cells were used as negative controls for GFP expression. Cell sorting of GFP-positive cells was performed using a Becton Dickinson FACSAria Fusion, with cells sorted into single cells per well of a 96-well plate. Flow cytometry data were plotted using FlowJo.

For the colony survival assay in TK6 human cells in Fig. 5g, individual colonies in each well were counted using a custom macro-script in ImageJ, and the percentage survival relative to untreated cells was calculated to assess clonogenic survival. Statistical testing was performed by the R package CFAssay using two-way analysis of the cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (Extended Data Table 2).

Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. RMSD between PRIMPOL–CMG (this study) and PRIMPOL–DNA (5L2X) was calculated in PyMOL (www.pymol.org) for 1,987 pairs of common atoms (RMSD = 1.723) or 253 pairs of common Cα atoms (RMSD = 1.374).

DNA replication assays were quantified using ImageJ, and data were plotted in Prism.

The experiments in Figs. 1b, 2b,d, 3b,c,e and 5c,d,f and Extended Data Figs. 1b,f, 2a, 3a, 5a,b, 6a,b were performed a minimum of three times. Experiments in Figs. 1c, 3d and 5b and Extended Data Figs. 1a,c–e, 2b, 3b, 5c and 7a,b were performed twice. Colony survival assay in TK6 human cells (Fig. 5g) was performed three times, testing two independent clones of primpol/pcnaK164R + PRIMPOLΔ1–39. Cryo-EM sample preparation was performed twice.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper and the Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.

#1302. Where Every Golden Boy Winner is Now

When looking to predict who will be among football's next crop of global superstars, many will turn to the squads of successful youth teams, or to those who standout in youth international tournaments. However, these generally don't prove to be accurately predictive of who will dominate the game for years to come.

Winners of the under-17 World Cup Player of the Tournament in recent iterations of the competition include Kelechi Nwakali, Kelechi Iheanacho and Julio Gomez – certainly not household names in today's game. However, winners of TuttoSport's Golden Boy Award tend to become pretty special.

While some Golden Boy winners have blossomed, others have bombed...

The accolade is voted on by journalists, and seeks to identify the best player under the age of 21 and playing in one of Europe's major leagues. While most who have claimed the award have enjoyed illustrious playing careers, there have been a few whose careers have stagnated, and they've ultimately failed to fulfill their potential. GIVEMESPORT has taken a look at every single Golden Boy winner, and where they are now.

The award's inaugural winner, Rafael van der Vaart, was applauded for his exceptional year for Ajax in 2003, which had seen him explode into one of the most prolific young midfielders in world football. He'd go onto have an impressive career playing for the likes of Hamburg, Real Madrid and Tottenham, before hanging up his boots in 2019. Nowadays, the Dutchman is mostly commonly seen voicing his critical opinions on an array of players as a pundit for football broadcasts in his home country, having seemingly given up post-retirement careers in coaching and darts.

In 2004, Wayne Rooney was named Golden Boy after bursting onto the scene with Everton and completing a switch to Manchester United. His achievements in the game need no introduction, and he has pursued managerial endeavours, despite struggling in roles at D.C. United and Birmingham City. Now, the Old Trafford legend is focusing on his punditry career and has even thrown himself into the jungle, taking part in 'I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here'.

After Rooney held it aloft, Lionel Messi was granted the award in 2005, and he's certainly not looked back. Still playing at a high level, arguably the greatest footballer of all time plies his trade in Miami. In 2026, he managed to help Argentina to the World Cup final and was in the running for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Cesc Fàbregas, 2006's Golden Boy recipient, retired from playing in the summer of 2023, and is overseeing Como's meteoric rise in Italy as manager. Winning promotion to Serie A with Gli Azzuri, the former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea midfielder has ambitions of forging a lengthy and successful coaching career. Indeed, he steered the club to Champions League football in the 2026/27 season.

Manchester City's record goalscorer, Sergio Aguero, won the award in 2007, and now spends most of his days streaming to his 4.8 million Twitch followers after becoming one of the deadliest hitmen in the history of the Premier League. The Argentine was forced into a premature retirement in 2021 due to a heart condition, and is yet to explore a career in punditry or coaching.

Perhaps the most surprising winner of the Golden Boy award became an assistant manager in Turkey after calling it time on his playing career. Ex-United midfielder, Anderson, worked for Adana Demirspor and had been at the Süper Lig club in some capacity after retiring in 2019, but he is now without a job in management. In September 2025, it was reported that Andeson was ordered to serve time in prison after failing to pay his child maintenance.

The notorious wonderkid Alexandre Pato was the final man to win the award in the noughties. Without a club after being released by Sao Paulo earlier this year, Pato is still only 36 but officially hung up his boots in January 2025 after failing to reach the heights expected of him. In the infancy of his career, he was mooted as the next big thing.

Mario Balotelli was the first Golden Boy winner of the 2010s, and the Italian striker's career has arguably not gone in the direction he might have once hoped. After leaving Genoa in 2025, Balotelli signed for UAE-based side Al-Ittifaq.

Mario Gotze was once Europe's hottest young playmaker, but the Bundesliga journeyman has settled for a squad role at Eintracht Frankfurt in his early 30s. Meanwhile, the German's Spanish counterpart, Isco, who developed at a similar time to Gotze, is fairing slightly better, taking up a talismanic role in his home country with Real Betis.

2013 Golden Boy winner Paul Pogba became a free agent after being released by Juventus in recent years following a doping ban. The suspension came to an end in March 2025, and he moved back to his homeland to join AS Monaco. However, it didn't work out and he left the club after just six appearances. As over November 2026, he was a free agent.

Raheem Sterling's exploits for Liverpool in 2014 earned him the prodigious accolade – but now he is without a club after disapponting spells at Chelsea and Feyenoord. 2015 recipient Anthony Martial continues this trend of winners whose careers have declined slightly earlier than they'd have hoped, with the Frenchman most recently playing with Monterrey. Things didn't start swimmingly, though, and he left the club on June 2026 to become a free agent once more.

Renato Sanches stormed into the footballing landscape in 2016, but hasn't really kicked on since. The former Swansea City loanee is now a free agent, having most recently plied his trade in Greece for Panathinaikos, on loan from Paris Saint-Germain. One of the more successful winners, Kylian Mbappe's 2017 antics have carried forward into years of exceptional productivity. And although he struggled to hit the ground running upon his arrival to Real Madrid, he's now firing on all cylinders.

The first defender to win the Golden Boy award to date, Matthijs de Ligt, left Bayern Munich for Manchester United in the summer of 2024, and has endured a mixed experience at Old Trafford, with the club going through a number of different managers during his time there. The Dutchman claimed the accolade a year prior to another who has also earned his corn in England's top flight: Joao Felix.

Felix – a regular Portugal international – was viewed as a supreme talent in 2019, and subsequently earned a big money move to Atletico Madrid from boyhood club Benfica. Years of stagnation in the Spanish capital saw him wash up at Chelsea, but he eventually didn't make the grade in the English capital. As of the autumn of 2026, he has lined up alongisde compatriot Cristiano Ronaldo at Al-Nassr.

Manchester City's Erling Haaland – who is, without a doubt, widely regarded as one of the best strikers in world football – was nominated as the Golden Boy winner in 2020, after enjoying an outstanding year with Borussia Dortmund. Now the most prolific number nine in Europe, the record-setting Norwegian continues to scale new heights on the goalscoring frontier.

In 2021 and 2022, two Barcelona midfielders emerged from La Masia and flourished on the La Liga and continental stage. First Pedri, and then Gavi, both Spanish midfielders have struggled with injuries in recent campaigns, but they both remain key to Hansi Flick and his entourage when they are fit and raring to go.

Jude Bellingham's incredible 2023 was rewarded with the Golden Boy title, and he's continuing to impress at the Bernabeu with Real Madrid, albeit his astounding goal-scoring exploits have hit something of a brick wall. Lamine Yamal – an inevitable recipient of multiple Ballon d'Or – then followed in Strourbridge-born Bellingham's footsteps the following year.

Yamal became a global superstar overnight, winning Euro 2024 with Spain, leading a resurgent Barcelona and, of course, the Golden Boy award in 2024. Desire Doue – whose name, when translated into English, means 'Desired Gifted' – won the prestigious award in 2025 – and he can attribute his part to play in Paris Saint-Germain's maiden triumph in the Champions League as to why. He and PSG went on to repeat the Champions League feat in 2026, though the Golden Boy award went to World Cup-winning centre-back Pau Cubarsi, who became just the second defender to win it after De Ligt in 2018.
