#1301. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

#1300. Zidane: ‘Italy played better in France, but they won tonight’

Zinedine Zidane feels Italy ‘played better in Paris, but they won this evening’ when inflicting his first defeat as France coach, and defends Chelsea’s Malo Gusto from criticism.

Les Bleus had got off to the ideal start at San Siro when Michael Olise pounced on a Gianluigi Donnarumma howler playing out from the back.

Francesco Pio Esposito equalised, but they felt that when Sebastiano Esposito blazed a penalty wide, it would be a turning point in the match.

Instead, the Azzurri got back on their feet quickly, winning 3-1 with Davide Frattesi and another penalty, this time converted by Pio Esposito.

“We had a good initial approach and held the ball well, but after the break we lost our way, especially defensively,” confessed Zidane in his press conference.

This was an unusual situation, as before tonight France had not scored in the first half in any of their last nine matches.

“We stayed in the game, did good things in possession, but we fell away in the second half, especially after going 2-1 down. It is part of the process.”

France were decimated by injuries, missing Inter’s Marcus Thuram, Juventus defender Pierre Kalulu, Roma midfielder Manu Koné, Kylian Mbappé, Ousmane Dembélé, Aurelien Tchouameni, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

Malo Gusto had terrible problems at right-back dealing with Nicolò Cambiaghi first, then Federico Dimarco.

“Your job is to analyse what you need to analyse, but my focus is on recharging the batteries for the next game,” replied Zidane to questions about the Chelsea defender.

“We are all united, we didn’t defend well in general as a team and need to improve. I won’t change players over one game. Malo Gusto gave away a penalty, but it can happen.”

Olise scored the opener, but then made little impact as the match wore on at San Siro.

“You cannot always play at the top level for 90 minutes. Olise had some good performances, he wasn’t the only one who fell away in the second half, the whole team did.

“We wanted to win the game tonight to ensure we had first place on Sunday, now we must win the final match against Turkiye, but that was the objective anyway regardless of this evening’s result.”

Italy are the only team who Zidane has been unable to defeat as France coach, earning a 1-1 draw in Paris and this 3-1 victory.

“The most important thing is to create chances, and we did hit the woodwork twice. I am not disappointed, I would’ve been if we had not had such good possession play. What we need to analyse is that we weren’t at the right level off the ball.

“I think Italy had a similar performance to in Paris defensively, which is what they do best. I must admit, I thought they played better with the ball at their feet in the first game, but they won tonight and that’s all.”

Mbappé was not even on the bench this evening, but could he recover in time for the final group game with Turkiye on Sunday?

“We hope so, that is the plan and why he has not gone back home. We just decided not to risk it tonight over a slight problem.”

The French are arrogant by nature, and none more so than Zidane.

#1299. Football Italia Show: Azzurri beat arrogant France, we told you about Dimarco!

The latest episode of the Football Italia Show, filmed at San Siro, examines Italy’s 3-1 win over France in the Nations League.

The victory allowed the Azzurri to climb to the top of group A1, level on ten points with Les Blues, while Belgium follow with nine.

France took an early lead through Michael Olise after just 10 minutes, capitalising on a misplaced pass from Gianluigi Donnarumma. However, Italy responded emphatically, with Pio Esposito restoring parity before half-time.

The second half saw further drama, as Rayan Cherki struck the post before Sebastiano Esposito missed a penalty. Davide Frattesi then put the Azzurri ahead, finishing off a move created by Federico Dimarco, before Pio Esposito converted from the spot to complete the 3-1 triumph.

Football Italia was among the accredited media at San Siro, with our editor offering an exclusive pitchside assessment of the encounter at full-time.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1298. ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

#1297. England's new plan of attack: Thomas Tuchel has switched style since World Cup but clunky win over Croatia showed growing pains - Spain will put it to severe test, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 07:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:01 EST, 13 November 2026

It was gone 11pm when Thomas Tuchel was shaking the hands of Harry Kane’s parents on the Wembley pitch while the children of England’s record appearance maker enjoyed the run of the national stadium in front of 90,000 empty seats.

This was time for Kane to fully take in the emotion of an historic night alongside his family and that Tuchel was out there too felt instructive of their relationship.

Kane and Tuchel had frank conversations last month about the World Cup fallout, on how England might be best tinkering with their selection when chasing games.

The manager respects and values his captain’s opinion on these things, recognising that he is almost completely agenda-free, as they attempt to better plot a route to silverware in readiness for the European Championship in 18 months’ time.

If there was uncertainty about identity and style when the World Cup crunch arrived, when Enzo Fernandez was pulling stupid faces and the colour drained from England faces, then players have felt that the detail on how Tuchel wants to move forward has been clear across the first two camps since America.

Thursday night was not vintage against a Croatia team they battered 7-0 a few weeks back. Tuchel and Kane both admitted that afterwards but it is noticeable that there is a defined plan on how they intend to attack in a slightly different way.

Thomas Tuchel embraces Harry Kane's wife Katie at Wembley on Thursday night

Harry Kane (centre) and Co are changing the way they attack after the World Cup

Were Tuchel to have been able to pick a first-choice back four then the win would likely have been more comfortable, Croatia benefiting from individual errors. And a lack of cutting edge inside the box hindered the hosts too.

The idea behind what they were doing appeared well thought out though and that should bring about some gentle encouragement.

The full backs, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Lewis Hall, were both consistently worked into hugely dangerous areas in the inside channels, while the make-up of Tuchel’s midfield felt very deliberate as well.

It is no coincidence that England enjoyed the highest amount of possession in the half spaces ten yards inside Croatia’s half. That is a clear directive, with both Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice drifting wider to create overloads and the full backs pushed into threatening spaces.

‘Declan understands the game like he’s almost a coach on the field and in a perfect position to manage all these things from behind,’ Tuchel said this week. To have a constant interchanging unit, he does need brains.

These are the rotations that the Three Lions didn’t engineer enough of over in the United States, with Kane dropping deep as he does and completing that wonder crossfield pass for the Morgan Rogers opener.

They are the moments that Tuchel is preaching, Jude Bellingham taking up an unusual position in order to stretch Croatia as he squared for the Chelsea forward.

What Tuchel needs now is to work on how that can be translated into making sure his very best players can affect matches more regularly inside the opponent’s box.

Jude Bellingham only touched the ball four times in Croatia's box in the 2-1 win

That Kane only touched it six times inside the 18-yard area and Bellingham on just four occasions points to a team still figuring themselves out.

That will be put to the severe test in Madrid on Sunday. England do not beat the truly elite nations; never have.

And it’ll be interesting to see whether Tuchel sticks to this sort of plan, one designed to dominate, or if he instead relies on the counter-attacking ability of a group he has viewed as a ‘Premier League team’ before now, leaning into their physicality.

If England are feeling confident enough, giving this tweaked style a go against the world champions might offer them some answers on what could be achieved when the proper silverware is on the line.

#1295. Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nic Fleming is a science writer in Bristol, UK.

Container ships were forced to dock at ports in the United Arab Emirates and other Middle Eastern nations after the Iranian government announced that it would close the Strait of Hormuz in July.Credit: AFP via Getty Images

Protesters burnt tyres and blocked roads in Syria over fuel prices. French fishers blockaded a fuel depot and clashed with police. Government and household budgets were squeezed around the world as interest rates rose and the sales of electric vehicles roughly doubled year-on-year in several countries, including Australia, Brazil and India.

These were just some of the many knock-on effects of the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran that began in February. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 25% of the world’s oil trade and 20% of exported liquefied natural gas previously passed, caused what the International Energy Agency (IEA) called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”, as fuel prices spiked worldwide.

The resulting strain has exacerbated the economic pressures already felt from previous shocks, including the Russia–Ukraine war, the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2008 global financial crash, as well as from the continuing effects of climate change. The current global energy-security picture is “really bad on all fronts”, says Dan Marks, an energy-security researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London. “It’s something of a perfect storm.”

Governments seeking to improve national energy security are taking a variety of approaches — from measures to reduce demand and increase electrification to infrastructure updates and incentive programmes to encourage renewable-energy investment. Researchers, meanwhile, are doing their bit, driving scientific and technological advances that have the potential to deliver a stable and sustainable future energy mix.

Human energy consumption is both growing and changing (see ‘Powering the planet’). Use of global primary energy — naturally occurring energy sources that have not undergone any processing by humans — more than doubled between 1980 and 2025. Over that period, consumption increased from around 85,000 terawatt hours (TWh) annually to 178,000 TWh. That’s approximately 71 times the yearly primary-energy consumption of France.

Electrification — the replacement of technologies that burn fossil fuels with alternatives powered by electricity — is advancing in many countries as various industries look into switching to renewables. Worldwide, electricity demand is predicted to increase by around 40% by 2035, compared with current levels (see ‘The road ahead’). Despite this, many industries are still reliant on fossil fuels. Close to 99% of aviation and more than 90% of shipping relies on fossil fuels, for example. One-quarter of extracted natural gas is used to heat industrial buildings, and around 21% is used for heating and cooking in homes worldwide. Most of the rest (40%) is used to generate electricity. Although the share of primary energy generated by renewables is growing, oil, coal and gas still account for about 80% of energy production.

The IEA defines energy security as reliable, affordable access to all fuels and energy sources. Marks and others highlight that priorities vary internationally, with reliability often seen as of primary importance in high-income countries and affordability taking precedence in low-income nations. The impacts of global shocks to fuel supplies and prices also vary according to how reliant countries are on imported fossil fuels. “There isn’t one global energy-security picture, but many different context-dependent pictures,” says Severin Borenstein, an energy economist at the University of California, Berkeley.

Economies that rely on imported oil products are particularly vulnerable to the current shocks. The World Food Programme, part of the United Nations, estimated in March that the US–Iran war could push an extra 45 million people into acute hunger, taking this year’s total to 363 million, as increasing oil and gas costs push up the prices of fuel, food and other crucial products such as fertilizer. “If, like in a lot of African countries, people are dependent on travelling long distances in vehicles and on other imported oil products, large oil-price increases can be existentially problematic,” says Marks. Some high-income nations have also been hit hard. In Japan — which was importing more than 90% of its crude oil from the Middle East before the conflict — household electricity bills have risen to their highest levels in three years, and government borrowing costs have risen to a 30-year high.

By contrast, nations with domestic fuel supplies have been partially insulated. Although car users in the United States have seen big fuel-price increases, the country’s ample supplies of natural gas have shielded the nation from severe economic hardships. “In most developed free-market economies, there isn’t an energy-security issue in the sense of availability,” says Borenstein. “There are price and macro-economic issues. Some countries, like the United States, are better protected than others.”

Global oil prices have jumped since the US–Iran war broke out. Brent Crude futures contracts, a global oil-price benchmark, hit US$126 a barrel in April — up from around $70 before the conflict. This has affected consumers and businesses, but not as much as some previous energy crises. During the Yom Kippur War, coordinated action by oil-producing countries caused prices to more than triple between October 1973 and January 1974. And oil prices more than doubled after the 1978–79 Iranian revolution.

Many economists think that the global economy is better placed to avoid the soaring inflation, unemployment and recessions seen in many industrialized nations after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks. The ‘oil intensity’ of the global economy, that is, how much oil is needed to generate a unit of gross domestic product (GDP) in the form of goods and services, has fallen by more than 50% since the 1970s. And the IEA, established after the 1973 oil crisis, also requires its 32 member countries to keep reserves of at least 90 days’ worth of crude oil to guard against supply shocks. “For most of the developed world, it’s a big inconvenience, and, for some, a substantial budget squeeze, but it’s not the complete disruption of the economy seen in the 1970s,” says Borenstein.

But economic and energy-security challenges are also expected to grow owing to climate change. Droughts are becoming more frequent and severe, resulting in big reductions in hydropower generation in nations such as China, Brazil, the United States, Spain and Zambia. Low water levels in rivers, including the Rhine and Danube in Europe, the Amazon in South America and the Yangtze in China, have caused freight delivery problems. The other effects of climate change include reduced wind-energy generation and increased demand for power to run air-conditioning units.

Governments, policymakers and others who are working to tackle energy-security challenges have various options. Reducing energy demand, especially for oil and gas, by electrifying industrial processes and home heating, for example, helps with these issues, especially in nations that are heavily reliant on imported fossil fuels. Managing demand volatility through improved energy storage and ensuring that power grids can transition towards greater energy generation from renewables are also part of the picture, Marks says.

Although governments and business leaders have parts to play in energy-demand management, electrification and infrastructure investments, researchers are driving scientific and technical innovations that support energy security. Tapping underground heat to produce geothermal energy, for example, emits only small amounts of greenhouse gases and can be used to generate electricity or to heat buildings. However, at present, geothermal energy produces less than 1% of electricity globally because few locations have the right combination of accessible underground heat, water and permeable rock.

That could change thanks to advances in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), in which underground fractures are expanded or created in hot areas, and then fluids are pumped down, heated up and transferred back to the surface, usually to drive turbines and generate electricity.

Russia has been experiencing a fuel crisis since mid-June caused by increased Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries. Credit: Contributor/Getty Images News

There have been small-scale EGS research operations since the 1970s, but drilling times and costs have fallen substantially in the decades since thanks to techniques adapted from the oil and gas industries. These include the fracturing of rock with pressurized fluids, known as fracking, horizontal drilling to increase the exposure of fluid to heat reservoirs and the use of tougher, faster polycrystalline diamond compact drill bits. “It’s hard to overestimate how much of a game changer the new techniques have been,” says Roland Horne, a geothermal-energy engineer at Stanford University in California.

These innovations are driving investments in large commercial plants. One of the biggest of these is the Cape Station project operated by Fervo Energy near Milford in Utah, which began delivering power in September and plans to build the capacity to generate 500 megawatts (MW) by 2028 — enough electricity to power around 500,000 US homes.

However, there are obstacles to overcome. A number of EGS projects have been halted owing to earthquakes that geologists linked to increased underground forces generated by the EGS process. A magnitude-5.5 earthquake that injured 90 people was probably triggered by hydraulic fracturing at an EGS plant in Pohang, South Korea, in 2017. Lessons have been learnt from this and other incidents. For example, EGS developers are deploying networks of sensors to better predict seismic risks and using multistage stimulation. This involves the use of pressurised fluids or chemical agents to fracture rock sequentially and more gently at several points rather than at fewer locations.

Horne says that he expects the levelized cost of electricity — the average cost of generating a unit of electricity across a power plant’s lifetime — for EGS to drop to a commercially competitive $80 per megawatt hour (MWh) by 2027. The IEA says that this could drop to $50 by 2035 and that geothermal energy could generate 8% of global electricity supplies by 2050.

Efforts to develop more efficient solar cells could also help countries to improve their energy security by increasing sustainable domestic electricity supplies. In 2025, 9% of the world’s electricity came from solar, up from 3% in 2020. Today’s solar cells are mostly silicon-based and can typically convert light into electricity with efficiencies of around 20–24%.

A worker inspects newly installed solar panels at the Fuendetodos II solar park near Zaragoza, Spain.Credit: Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images

When sunlight hits a solar, or photovoltaic, cell, electrons inside the semiconductor material that it is made from are knocked loose, creating an electrical imbalance that produces a voltage and generates electricity. Researchers are now developing next-generation solar cells that use metal halide perovskites, a family of crystalline compounds with high light absorption and charge-transport capabilities.

#1294. What Italy need to win Nations League group after 3-1 France victory

Italy picked up their first victory at home against France in 64 years on Thursday evening and have overtaken their opponents into first place in their Nations League group in the process. Here is what the Azzurri need to seal their spot as group winners or to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals.

A brace from Pio Esposito and another goal from Davide Frattesi sent Italy on their way to a 3-1 victory over France in San Siro on Thursday evening, following a 10th-minute opener from Bayern Munich’s Michael Olise.

This result means that Italy are top of the group on 10 points, France are in second on 10 (trailing on goal difference and head-to-head), Belgium are in third on nine points and Turkey are still without a point after the fifth round of group stage fixtures.

The final round of group stage fixtures in Nations League group A will take place on Sunday evening. Roberto Mancini and his players will take on Belgium in Brussels.

Italy can qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners, as runners-up, or as one of the two best-ranked third-place teams.

Following Thursday’s victory over France, Italy are guaranteed to finish no lower than third place, regardless of the results on Sunday evening. This means that they cannot be relegated from League A.

A draw against Belgium on Sunday will guarantee a second-place finish and a spot in the quarter-finals for Italy, but will require France to either lose or draw against Turkey (without a point after five matches) if they are to finish as group leaders.

A victory against Belgium in Brussels will guarantee Italy’s status as group winners.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

So basically we’ve qualified? To be honest though it’s the performances that are the main thing and they have been a massive improvement.

#1293. Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa

From the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa said. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

Konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

The victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also says plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

Probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

Brilliant play from Oscar Bobb as he cuts inside on his left foot and bends a shot into the far bottom corner for the away side.

Treatment is needed for Zubimendi after he is caught on the nose by Barry.

Big chance for Everton. Garner whips a teasing cross into the box, Dewsbury-Hall meets it with his head on the run but the ball flies just wide of the post.

EvertonOFF Johnson, Mykolenko ON Dibling, Hackney

Tarkowski is the latest yellow card for Everton after a foul on Havertz.

Eze with a poor cross into the box. He fails to run back quickly and Arteta sprints to the edge of the touchline and goes berserk at the midfielder.

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

It is a lovely move with slick one-touch passing. The ball is fed to White making a run down the outside and he clips the ball to the far post for Gabriel to head home.

OFF Merino, Lewis-Skelly, GyokeresON Calafiori, Guimaraes, Havertz

Garner is booked for Everton now after barging into Merino off the ball.

Arteta is shown a yellow card for something. Not sure what for yet. But the Arsenal manager is looking to make some changes off the bench.

Arsenal have been guilty of overplaying today. Opting for the extra pass rather than taking a shot. The game is open at the moment and that makes things dangerous for the home side.

Yellow card for Lewis-Skelly after bringing down Johnson. Gabriel is back on the pitch and seems happy enough to continue.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Gabriel immediately raised his hand for medical attention after making that clearance. He really extended his leg to get the ball away. Looks to be in a lot of pain.

Latest corner from Arsenal after Eze’s shot is blocked by Rohl. Rice’s delivery into the near post is headed clear to Odegaard, who shoots ambitiously from distance and Pickford collects the ball comfortably.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

Before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

Yellow card for Mykolenko after he catches White wide on the right. Rice whips the ball in and Merino meets it with a flick goalwards but the ball goes over the bar.

That is the final touch of the half and the players are running off to get dry!

Big chance for Everton. White thinks he has time when he heads the ball back to Raya but he does not connect well and Barry is there to pick it up and he flicks a shot at goal but Raya reacts quickly to parry the ball.

Raya is penalised for taking too long with the ball and Everton have a cheap corner. Danger is cleared by Arsenal as they force Everton back into their half.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Madueke should do better. Rice finds him and the winger drives into the box. He takes a shot but drags a right-footed effort wide.

Chance for Arsenal. Rice finds space behind the Everton midfield and drives forward. He plays a pass to Lewis-Skelly, who lays it off to Eze. The England midfielder sidefoots a cross into the box but no one in an Arsenal shirt is there to meet it.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

George is looking lively for Everton. He tries to come inside and whip an effort to the far corner but the ball deflects wide.

From the corner, Gabriel clears off the line after Raya loses track of the ball.

Everton have responded impressively to the Konsa goal and have been the better team since falling behind. Midfielders Garner and Armstrong are growing into the game quite nicely.

Everton have responded well to going behind here. The early goal against them will have ripped up any plans to sit deep and play on the counter.

Set-pieces are back on the menu for Arsenal. Ezri Konsa’s first goal for the club is their first goal from a corner this season, which will come as a relief to set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. “Set piece again, ole ole,” sing the Arsenal fans. Arteta’s side had started the game on the front foot.

Arsenal had not scored from a corner this season... until now. Konsa breaks the deadlock after a melee in the box and his pokes the ball into the net.

A couple of early set pieces from Declan Rice. Everton do well to clear the danger. But have another one now...

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

After a minute’s applause in honour of Ken Friar, the match makes a prompt start at the Emirates.

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

“They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”

“Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz

Everton: Pickford, Tarkowski, O’Brien, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George, Barry, Garner, Mykolenko, JohnsonSubs: Travers, King, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Dibling, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Braiden Graham

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

#1292. Esposito earning Kane and Riva comparisons after brace in 3-1 France victory

Pio Esposito was voted as the player of the match by the vast majority of outlets in Italy following his brace during Thursday’s 3-1 Nations League victory over France, and one newspaper has compared the Inter striker to Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane: ‘A complete performance’.

Esposito’s brace against France means that he is now up to nine goals from his first 14 caps, and at his current goalscoring rate, is on course to smash Italy’s all-time goalscoring record, currently held by Gigi Riva on 35.

The Corriere dello Sport gave Esposito a rating of 9/10 for his performance on Thursday night, labelling him a ‘constant thorn’ in France’s side. ‘He fought like a lion, often left alone against everyone,’ their report read.

Sky gave Esposito a rating of 8/10 and agreed that he is the ‘heir to Gigi Riva’s throne’ as Italy’s all-time record goalscorer. ‘Exuberant, courageous and combative,’ was their assessment.

La Gazzetta dello Sport, meanwhile, gave Esposito a rating of 8/10 and compared his performance to England captain and 2026 Ballon d’Or winner Kane: ‘His movement, which make everyone lose track of him, a complete performance,” wrote the Pink Paper.

TMW also gave Esposito a rating of 8/10, adding that his performance is ‘nothing new’. They add that Italy now have a ‘great centre-forward’, and that it has been ‘too long’. The Corriere della Sera also agreed with the 8/10 rating.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

It’s taken 20 years but do we finally have the great forward we have been looking for? it’s looking like it and with potentially Cisse if he keeps pushing on we could have a formidable attack for years to come. I think we are a Jorginho midfielder away from being a very good side. The defence is looking a lot stronger too and with Palma, Leoni and Ahanor coming through the future is looking bright.

#1291. Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jia Yu is at the Center for Social Research, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China.

China’s one-child policy is probably the best-known population-control programme in history, yet in its first decade it barely changed the country’s fertility rate. Writing in Nature, Meng et al.1 show that the biggest drop in fertility after the policy’s introduction was driven by a change in how officials were incentivized to enforce it. This change accounts for about half of the fall in the country’s fertility rate during the 1990s.

#1289. Referees selected for Italy’s final Nations League group stage clash against Belgium

Italy have one game to go in their Nations League group following Thursday evening’s 3-1 victory over France in San Siro, and will be officiated by Norwegian referee Espen Eskas when they take on Belgium in Brussels on Sunday evening.

Italy sit at the top of their Nations League group heading into the final round of group stage fixtures thanks to Thursday’s 3-1 victory over France in San Siro. The Azzurri have 10 points, as do France (behind on goal difference and head-to-head), Belgium have nine points and Turkey are still on zero after five matches.

Italy just need a draw away against Belgium to guarantee themselves a spot in the Nations League quarter-finals. A draw could be enough to finish in first place, but will require a favour from Turkey in their game against France. A win for Italy in Belgium will guarantee their status as group winners.

It has recently been confirmed that Norwegian official Espen Eskas will be the referee for Italy’s final Nations League group stage clash away against Belgium on Sunday.

Eskas will be joined by Norwegian assistant referees Jan Erik Engan and Alf Olav Rossland, with fourth official Sigur Kringstad, also from Norway.

German official Christian Dingert will be the VAR and will be assisted by Norwegian Kristoffer Hagenes.

Curiously, Eskas has already refereed a game between Italy and Belgium before, ending in a 2-2 draw at the Stadio Olimpico back in October 2024, also in the Nations League group stage under the reign of Luciano Spalletti.

Italy had led by two goals in that game thanks to Andrea Cambiaso and Mateo Retegui, but conceded twice before full-time after Lorenzo Pellegrini was sent off after a VAR review that saw his yellow card for a foul on Arthur Theate upgraded to a red.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1288. Italy rise in FIFA World Rankings after 3-1 victory over France

Italy have risen two places in the FIFA World Rankings following Thursday’ evening’s 3-1 victory over France in the Nations League, and as things stand, the Azzurri are currently rated as the 13th-best national team in the world.

A brace from Pio Esposito and another goal from Davide Frattesi sent Italy on their way to a 3-1 victory at home against France in San Siro on Thursday evening, the first time that the Azzurri had beaten Les Bleus on home soil in 64 years.

As a result of Thursday’s victory, Italy have risen two places in the FIFA World Rankings, from 15th up to 13th, overtaking Germany (14th) and Croatia (15th) in the process.

The Azzurri will be hoping for a positive result away against Belgium on Sunday evening in order to push them closer to their next targets: Switzerland in 12th, Colombia in 11th and Mexico in 10th.

A further update to the FIFA rankings will arrive next week (November 18).

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1286. Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby

Henry Pollock was at the centre of an East Midlands derby flare-up that sparked a second-half Leicester onslaught as Northampton were overpowered at a sodden Mattioli Woods Welford Road.

The England back row, never knowingly far from controversy, escalated a brawl at the end of the first half that Leicester prop Joe Heyes revealed “added fuel to the fire” of a Tigers side who roared impressively when they returned after the break.

The incident fired up a sell-out crowd and Leicester brought what had up to that point been a drab game to life with a storming second-half performance.

Three tries in a pulverising 13-minute spell overturned a half-time deficit and put the hosts on course for a bonus-point win over their arch-rivals that took them to second place in the Prem table.

Pollock, withdrawn after 52 minutes, may wish to reflect on the wisdom of riling the Tigers in their own lair.

“That was a proper Tigers second half and a really pleasing performance,” Geoff Parling, their director of rugby, said.

“We got on the front foot and showed our power. The way the guys problem-solved was brilliant and I’m just really pleased with the emotional energy they threw into that game.

“The way we were physically for each other – I’m really pleased.

“The challenge for us, if we want to be a title-winning team, is to play like that when it isn’t Northampton Saints. We have to play with that heart – the fire we showed in our chests – but also the calmness we showed too.

“I think if we play our game to the best of our ability we can knock over anyone.”

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

In the pack, Joe Heyes joins Archie van der Flier and Jamie Blamire who retain their places in the front row, while the second row make up of Cameron Henderson and Ollie Chessum remains unchanged.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Leicester: F Steward; A Radwan, W Wand, S Kata; G Hamer-Webb; B Searle, J van Poortvliet; A van der Flier, J Blamire, J Heyes, C Henderson, O Chessum, A Wainwright, F Carnduff, O Cracknell.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

#1282. Zidane sets an unfortunate double record against Italy after 3-1 San Siro defeat

It was a night to forget for the France national team, who lost 3-1 to Italy in San Siro on Thursday evening, and head coach Zinedine Zidane has now become the first Frenchman to lose against Italy both as a player and a coach.

Italy exceeded expectations with an impressive 3-1 victory over the third-ranked nation in the world in their penultimate Nations League group stage fixture on Thursday night. Italy had not beaten France on home soil since 1962 and had lost all of their previous three games at home against Les Bleus.

It was a brace from Pio Esposito, now being tipped to break Gigi Riva’s national team goalscoring record, and an individual goal from Davide Frattesi that sent the Azzurri on their way to victory in Milan on Thursday night.

Italy have now overtaken France into first place in their Nations League group and now require just a draw against Belgium on Sunday in order to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals.

Zidane, meanwhile, will be hoping to bounce back against Turkey on Sunday night. They have not picked up any points in any of their five Nations League group stage matches last night.

As pointed out by Cronache di Spogliatoio, Zidane has now become the first Frenchman to lose against Italy both as a player and as a coach. His final international appearance was famously in the 2006 World Cup final, which ended in glory for the Azzurri and a red card for Zidane after headbutting Marco Materazzi.

#1278. Chelsea Confidential: Mike Penders' Vaseline goalkeeping hack revealed, Emi Martinez fitness update, why Estevao started against 'weak' Man United and the £750 'dressing room experience' for Blues fans

Published: 07:03 EST, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 14:51 EST, 4 November 2026

One of the secrets to Chelsea goalkeeper Mike Penders stopping Manchester United from scoring at Stamford Bridge was to smear a stash of Vaseline on his goalpost.

The 21-year-old Belgian used the petroleum jelly to add grip to his gloves during the game and particularly before corners. Prior to one United set-piece, Penders walked to the woodwork to rub his hands with the substance which was hidden up high towards his crossbar. He then caught the ball when Bruno Fernandes’ cross came into his box.

It seems counterintuitive to smear a greasy substance on gloves to aid catching but it is an old goalkeeper hack – and perfectly legal in the laws of the game – with former England keeper Ben Foster once saying on his podcast: ‘It’s hard to explain, but if we were in a training session, I could tell you if one of us had Vaseline on our gloves, because as soon as I grab the ball, it does make it grippier.’

Penders may have learned the trick from Sweden’s Karl-Johan Johnsson. They were both at Chelsea’s sister side Strasbourg last season – Penders as No 1 and Johnsson as No 2.

Johnsson is now 36 and without a club. He did not respond when contacted by Confidential, but he does have an old YouTube channel. His most popular video – viewed 54,000 times and uploaded in 2021 when he was a goalkeeper for Copenhagen – is about the benefits of Vaseline.

While Johnsson would apply it from the blue-topped tub in the changing room before kick-off, he would also add a chunk to his goalpost so he could easily top up mid-match if needed.

Mike Penders has a novel trick he uses to help keep the ball out of the Chelsea net

Penders saves Ryan Gravenberch's penalty kick in the Carabao Cup shootout against Liverpool at Anfield

The Vaseline tip has tended to be passed on from ‘keeper to ‘keeper. Ask Foster and he will say he learned it from Joe Hart. Ask Hart and he will credit Kasper Schmeichel. And so on.

For Johnsson, he believes there is a psychological benefit as it not only gave greater grip to his gloves but made him feel more confident in goal, particularly in wet weather.

Stamford Bridge was soaking when Penders struggled in his first Premier League start as Tottenham Hotspur visited Chelsea. That was a match played in the midst of Storm Boelo. At one corner, the youngster filling in for Emiliano Martinez mistimed a punch for an own goal. With that lead, Spurs went on to win 2-0, their first victory at the Bridge since 2018.

It is not known if Penders used the Vaseline hack in that derby defeat, but sources told Confidential to look out for his use of it in their following two fixtures versus Liverpool and United.

Penders put in a fine performance at Liverpool in the Carabao Cup, despite Chelsea losing on penalties at Anfield after a 1-1 draw. Had Emmanuel Emegha scored his spot-kick, Xabi Alonso’s side would have reached the quarter-finals after Penders denied Ryan Gravenberch from 12 yards.

In Chelsea’s 2-0 Premier League victory over United, Penders made sure of his clean sheet with several saves, including a world-class stop as he tipped Bryan Mbeumo’s rocket on to his crossbar.

As mentioned, the hack is entirely legal. IFAB – football’s lawmakers – have no rule against Vaseline or any other petroleum jelly being applied to goalkeepers’ gloves in their regulations on player equipment.

Penders saves from Liverpool's Ronald Araujo during the Carabao Cup match

Penders punches a slippery ball into his own net against Tottenham on a miserable evening at Stamford Bridge

In more goalkeeper news, Martinez has been privately pushing to play in Chelsea’s trip to Sunderland this Sunday, per sources who also revealed how he has been insisting to club colleagues that he wants to represent Argentina during the upcoming international break.

Since this information was relayed to Confidential earlier this week, Martinez has indeed been called up by Lionel Scaloni for his country’s friendlies versus Uruguay and Costa Rica. He is also understood to have returned to Chelsea training on Wednesday, albeit with strapping around his jaw.

Alonso confirmed at his last press conference that ‘there is a chance’ his goalkeeper could return before the break. That would leave Chelsea’s manager with a decision to make – whether to stick with Penders, who has shown his potential in the last two games, or turn to Martinez, who has seen a specialist while sidelined about having a face-mask fitted.

The 34-year-old broke his jaw in Chelsea’s 2-0 Premier League win away at Everton in mid-October. He had surgery, and said at the time that he would be ‘back in a few weeks’. That will be three weeks ago this weekend when Alonso’s squad travel to Sunderland.

Meanwhile, Aaron Anselmino has also been called up by Argentina, despite having not played a single minute for Chelsea this season. He has only made the match-day squad once as an unused substitute in their first game in the Carabao Cup against Luton Town in August.

Then he disappeared. But Confidential did spy Anselmino last Saturday for the first time in a while as he took a seat behind the bench, and now he is in Scaloni's squad. That is despite Alonso telling us at his last press conference that he was injured.

Chelsea goalkeeper Emi Martinez breaks his jaw in a clash with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite last month

Marintez receives treatment on the Hill Dickinson Stadium turf - but is pushing for a return to action this weekend

SUNDERLAND WOULD PREFER PENDERS OVER MARTINEZ

Confidential asked former Sunderland striker Kevin Phillips whether he would rather face Penders or Martinez.

The 53-year-old, who scored 92 Premier League goals, told us: ‘The obvious one would be Penders, with his lack of experience, coming to the Stadium of Light, which is going to be a hostile, noisy occasion.

‘Emiliano, he's got the experience, played an awful long time at Villa. Obviously, he's had his injury, but he's an experienced international, been there, seen it and done it. So you would say Penders for his inexperience. But it looks like Martinez might be the one who starts, with a mask on, which, from Sunderland's point of view, means you're going to have to test him.’

Phillips spoke to us via Best Betting Sites and when asked if Martinez’s recent injury would impact Sunderland’s approach if he is in goal, he said: ‘The natural one with Martinez is that nobody wants to go and hurt him again. It's a terrible injury, so you don't want a recurrence.

‘So anything physical, no. But from a wide point of view, getting the ball in the box, from set-plays, put the ball in high, just to see if he's confident to come for crosses, come and punch it. That would be my advice, certainly not to get physical with him.

‘Take every opportunity to shoot. Put him under pressure early and see how he copes. But from Chelsea's point of view, if he wasn't 100 per cent, they wouldn't risk him.’

Chelsea sources who were consulted by Confidential after Estevao was suddenly handed his first Premier League start of the season have explained why Manchester United were deliberately picked as the opponents.

We are told Alonso has had concerns about the 19-year-old Brazilian’s physicality and Chelsea’s fitness staff have been tasked with working on building him up. But United, managed by Michael Carrick, were seen as ideal opposition for him to face from the beginning.

United were considered weaker than the Premier League's other physical sides, which lessened Alonso’s reservations. Estevao did indeed have fun, could not be tamed by Diogo Dalot, and was unfortunate not to get among the goals in the 2-0 win.

It remains to be seen if Estevao will now keep his place away at Sunderland, where Chelsea crumbled on the final day of last season to end up out of Europe.

Estevao (left) was given a rare start against Manchester United at the weekend when he teamed up nicely with Morgan Rogers

There were some interesting quotes from Regis Le Bris last week as the Sunderland boss praised his centre back Omar Alderete after they beat Brentford in the Carabao Cup.

'We spoke about the style of play,’ Le Bris said. ‘We try to press high. It’s more or less the trend of the Premier League. You press up, and it means your opponent will go long. If your centre backs are not strong, consistent and able to manage one v ones, it’s over. Thank you, Omar.’

Except, Alderete is now suspended for the visit of Chelsea, and despite Le Bris liking to press high, the statistics say only Coventry have won possession in the final third fewer times than Sunderland this season.

It is a big game for Le Bris, who has avoided losing his job while his side sit bottom of the Premier League with a vote of confidence coming from his board in the build-up to Chelsea’s visit.

This weekend's Chelsea match is a big one for Regis Le Bris, the under-pressure Sunderland manager

Chelsea are making significant money on having fans lay out their favourite player’s kit and boots in the changing room on a matchday, while the supporter can also leave a good-luck message.

The ‘VVIP dressing room experience’ is already a sell-out for Chelsea’s next Premier League home game versus Leeds United on Saturday, November 21 at £750 per person.

There are other perks which come with that package – you aren’t just paying to do the kit-man’s job for him – but it is another example of Chelsea’s outside-of-the-box hospitality ideas.

#1277. Italy fans mock Domenech for classless tweet during France defeat at San Siro

Former France national team head coach Raymond Domenech was widely mocked by Italy fans on social media after posting a classless tweet during Thursday evening’s Nations League match between the two countries in San Siro: ‘You really never understood football’.

Italy claimed their first win at home against France in 64 years with a 3-1 victory in San Siro on Thursday evening: Michael Olise, Pio Esposito (x2) and Davide Frattesi with the goals. #

This result saw the Azzurri leapfrog Les Bleus into first place in their Nations League group heading into the final round of group stage fixtures on Sunday night. Roberto Mancini and his players only require a draw against Belgium to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals.

The media response in Italy has been overwhelmingly positive, Tuttosport claiming that the Azzurri ‘are back’ and the Corriere dello Sport thanking Mancini on the front page of Friday morning’s paper.

The reaction in France, however, has understandably been less positive. Former head coach Domenech did not enjoy what he saw on the night, but opened himself up for criticism after criticising Italy’s performance on the night.

Italie France 1/1 c’est inespéré pour les Italiens . Quelle faiblesse dans tous les secteurs mais le plus surprenant est leur niveau technique , que d’erreurs dans des passes faciles c’est affolant .

— Raymond Domenech (@RaymondDomenech) November 12, 2026

Shortly after Esposito had levelled the scores at 1-1, Domenech tweeted: “Italy 1-1 France, it’s beyond the Italians’ wildest dreams. So weak in every department, but what’s most surprising is their technical level. So many mistakes from easy passes, it’s alarming.”

Frattesi would go on to score for 2-1 in the second half and Esposito added a third just over 10 minutes later, not forgetting that his brother Sebastiano had also missed a penalty.

Domenech has since been treated to a round of mocking responses from Italy supporters on social media.

The most common response to Domenech’s tweet was a video or gif of Fabio Cannavaro lifting the 2006 World Cup trophy, after beating Domenech’s France side in the final in Berlin.

One fan wrote: “You always provide, dear Raymond, thank you for the entertainment.”

“Keep reading your horoscopes, Raymond,” another added.

“You’re as bad an expert as you were a coach,” another taunted. “You really nevery understood football,” wrote another.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

I mean, he wasn’t wrong about the mistakes in the first half. Italy did make a lot of them – one famously resulted in a goal.

He’s bitter still, I’d rather be Italy than France right now. Also wait until the right wingers are starting, added a position in midfield still up for debate, R Cassano eventually perhaps.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Chelsea and Tottenham at Stamford Bridge.

It’s Xabi Alonso’s first taste of the bitter rivalry and has hyped up the atmosphere ahead of the clash. “We are expecting a good atmosphere,” he said. “Electric, with good energy, knowing that in a derby this passion is really in the air in the stadium.

#1271. Bastoni avoids suspension despite yellow card confusion during Italy 3-1 France

Alessandro Bastoni will be available for selection when Italy take on Belgium in their final Nations League group stage fixture on Sunday evening as he did not pick up a yellow card during Thursday’s 3-1 victory over France, despite reports from UEFA suggesting that he had.

In UEFA Nations League matches, players earn one-match suspensions for every even number of yellow cards they receive, i.e. after every second, fourth and sixth booking.

Bastoni was one of five players in Italy’s matchday squad against France who had been carrying a yellow card, along with Gianluigi Donnarumma, Nicolo Fagioli, Antonio Vergara and Gianluca Scamacca. Moise Kean, Daniel Maldini, Gianluca Mancini and Matteo Ruggeri had also been booked before the France game, but were not in the squad on Thursday night.

There were momentary fears on Thursday night when UEFA reported that Bastoni had been shown a yellow card during the second half of the France victory, which would have earned him a suspension for Sunday’s test away against Belgium.

However, it has since been confirmed by the FIGC that this was an error in reporting and that the yellow card had actually been shown to Davide Frattesi. Neither Bastoni nor Frattesi will be suspended against Belgium.

Pio Esposito was also booked against France, but this was his first yellow card of the Nations League campaign and he also remains eligible to face Belgium on Sunday.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.
